questions.question_text: In an ideal AC circuit with only a capacitor, what is the relationship between the rates of change of voltage and current?
options: Current is proportional to the rate of change of voltage
Voltage is proportional to the rate of change of current
They are out of phase by 180°
questions.explanation: In a capacitor, \( I = C \frac{dV}{dt} \), meaning the current is directly proportional to the rate of change of voltage. Conversely, the rate of change of current relates to the second derivative of voltage, but the primary relationship is that current depends on \( \frac{dV}{dt} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 220 \, \text{V} \) (rms), \( 50 \, \text{Hz} \) AC source is connected to a \( 44 \, \text{mH} \) inductor. Calculate the inductive reactance.
questions.explanation: Inductive reactance: \( X_L = \omega L \), where \( \omega = 2\pi f \). Given: \( f = 50 \, \text{Hz} \), \( L = 44 \, \text{mH} = 0.044 \, \text{H} \). \( \omega = 2 \times 3.14 \times 50 = 314 \, \text{rad/s} \). \( X_L = 314 \times 0.044 = 13.816 \, \Omega \approx 13.82 \, \Omega \).

questions.question_text: In an LCR circuit with \( R = 3 \, \Omega \), \( X_L = 8 \, \Omega \), \( X_C = 4 \, \Omega \), what is the power factor?
questions.explanation: Impedance: \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = \sqrt{3^2 + (8 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5 \, \Omega \). Power factor: \( \cos \phi = \frac{R}{Z} = \frac{3}{5} = 0.6 \).

questions.question_text: A \( 165 \, \text{V} \) (rms) AC source supplies a \( 55 \, \Omega \) resistor. What is the average power consumed?
questions.explanation: RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{165}{55} = 3 \, \text{A} \). Average power: \( P = I^2 R = 3^2 \times 55 = 495 \, \text{W} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 268.7 \, \text{V} \) (peak) AC source is connected to a \( 95 \, \Omega \) resistor. What is the average power consumed?
questions.explanation: RMS voltage: \( V = \frac{v_m}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{268.7}{1.414} \approx 190 \, \text{V} \). RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{190}{95} = 2 \, \text{A} \). Average power: \( P = I^2 R = 2^2 \times 95 = 380 \, \text{W} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 200 \, \text{V} \) (rms) AC source is connected to a series LCR circuit with \( R = 20 \, \Omega \) at resonance. What is the power dissipated?
questions.explanation: At resonance, \( Z = R = 20 \, \Omega \). RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{200}{20} = 10 \, \text{A} \). Power: \( P = I^2 R = 10^2 \times 20 = 2000 \, \text{W} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 17 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is connected to a \( 110 \, \text{V} \), \( 60 \, \text{Hz} \) AC source. What is the rms current?
questions.explanation: \( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} \), \( \omega = 2\pi \times 60 = 376.8 \, \text{rad/s} \). \( C = 17 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{F} \). \( X_C = \frac{1}{376.8 \times 17 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 156 \, \Omega \). RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{X_C} = \frac{110}{156} \approx 0.705 \, \text{A} \).

questions.question_text: In an AC circuit containing only a resistor, what happens to the power dissipated if the frequency of the source is doubled?
questions.explanation: In a purely resistive AC circuit, power dissipated is \( P = I^2 R \), where \( I = \frac{V}{R} \), and \( R \) is constant. Since resistance does not depend on frequency, and assuming the rms voltage remains constant, the power dissipated remains unchanged when frequency doubles.

questions.question_text: A series LCR circuit has \( L = 1.5 \, \text{H} \), \( C = 35 \, \mu\text{F} \). What is the resonant frequency in Hz?
questions.explanation: Resonant angular frequency: \( \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L C}} \). \( L = 1.5 \, \text{H} \), \( C = 35 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{F} \). \( \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1.5 \times 35 \times 10^{-6}}} \approx 138.3 \, \text{rad/s} \). \( f_0 = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi} = \frac{138.3}{6.28} \approx 22 \, \text{Hz} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 60 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is connected to a \( 110 \, \text{V} \), \( 60 \, \text{Hz} \) AC supply. What is the peak current in the circuit?
questions.explanation: Capacitive reactance: \( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} \), where \( \omega = 2\pi f \). \( f = 60 \, \text{Hz} \), \( C = 60 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{F} \). \( \omega = 2 \times 3.14 \times 60 = 376.8 \, \text{rad/s} \). \( X_C = \frac{1}{376.8 \times 60 \times 10^{-6}} = 44.24 \, \Omega \). RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{X_C} = \frac{110}{44.24} = 2.487 \, \text{A} \). Peak current: \( i_m = \sqrt{2} I = 1.414 \times 2.487 \approx 3.52 \, \text{A} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 70 \, \Omega \) resistor and \( 14 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor are in series with a \( 210 \, \text{V} \), \( 50 \, \text{Hz} \) source. What is the impedance?
A \( 23 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is connected to a \( 110 \, \text{V} \), \( 60 \, \text{Hz} \) source. What is the rms current?
questions.explanation: \( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} \), \( \omega = 2\pi \times 60 = 376.8 \, \text{rad/s} \). \( C = 23 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{F} \). \( X_C = \frac{1}{376.8 \times 23 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 115.4 \, \Omega \). RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{X_C} = \frac{110}{115.4} \approx 0.953 \, \text{A} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 180 \, \text{V} \) (rms) AC source supplies a \( 90 \, \Omega \) resistor. What is the average power consumed?
questions.explanation: RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{180}{90} = 2 \, \text{A} \). Average power: \( P = I^2 R = 2^2 \times 90 = 360 \, \text{W} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 45 \, \text{mH} \) inductor is connected to a \( 230 \, \text{V} \), \( 50 \, \text{Hz} \) source. What is the peak current?
questions.explanation: \( X_L = \omega L \), \( \omega = 2\pi \times 50 = 314 \, \text{rad/s} \). \( L = 45 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{H} \). \( X_L = 314 \times 0.045 = 14.13 \, \Omega \). RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{X_L} = \frac{230}{14.13} \approx 16.28 \, \text{A} \). Peak current: \( i_m = \sqrt{2} I = 1.414 \times 16.28 \approx 23.02 \, \text{A} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 10 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is connected to a \( 230 \, \text{V} \), \( 50 \, \text{Hz} \) source. What is the rms current?
questions.explanation: \( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} \), \( \omega = 2\pi \times 50 = 314 \, \text{rad/s} \). \( C = 10 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{F} \). \( X_C = \frac{1}{314 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 318.5 \, \Omega \). RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{X_C} = \frac{230}{318.5} \approx 0.722 \, \text{A} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 35 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is connected to a \( 230 \, \text{V} \), \( 50 \, \text{Hz} \) AC source. What is the peak current?
questions.explanation: \( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} \), \( \omega = 2\pi \times 50 = 314 \, \text{rad/s} \). \( C = 35 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{F} \). \( X_C = \frac{1}{314 \times 35 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 91 \, \Omega \). RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{X_C} = \frac{230}{91} \approx 2.527 \, \text{A} \). Peak current: \( i_m = \sqrt{2} I = 1.414 \times 2.527 \approx 3.57 \, \text{A} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 120 \, \Omega \) resistor is connected to a \( 240 \, \text{V} \) (rms) AC source. What is the rms current?
questions.explanation: RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{R} \). Given: \( V = 240 \, \text{V} \), \( R = 120 \, \Omega \). \( I = \frac{240}{120} = 2 \, \text{A} \).

questions.question_text: A series LCR circuit has \( R = 25 \, \Omega \), \( X_L = 45 \, \Omega \), \( X_C = 20 \, \Omega \). What is the power factor?
questions.explanation: \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = \sqrt{25^2 + (45 - 20)^2} = \sqrt{625 + 625} = \sqrt{1250} \approx 35.36 \, \Omega \). Power factor: \( \cos \phi = \frac{R}{Z} = \frac{25}{35.36} \approx 0.707 \).

questions.question_text: A \( 40 \, \text{mH} \) inductor is connected to a \( 230 \, \text{V} \), \( 50 \, \text{Hz} \) AC source. What is the rms current?
questions.explanation: \( X_L = \omega L \), \( \omega = 2\pi \times 50 = 314 \, \text{rad/s} \). \( L = 40 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{H} \). \( X_L = 314 \times 0.04 = 12.56 \, \Omega \). RMS current: \( I = \frac{V}{X_L} = \frac{230}{12.56} \approx 18.31 \, \text{A} \).

questions.question_text: A series LCR circuit has \( R = 70 \, \Omega \), \( X_L = 40 \, \Omega \), \( X_C = 20 \, \Omega \). What is the impedance?
What is the primary purpose of using laminated cores in transformers?
questions.explanation: Laminated cores in transformers reduce eddy current losses. By dividing the core into thin, insulated layers, the induced currents are confined to smaller paths, minimizing energy loss as heat and improving efficiency.

questions.question_text: What is the effect on the impedance of a series LCR circuit when the frequency is increased beyond the resonant frequency?
questions.explanation: Beyond the resonant frequency, the inductive reactance (\( X_L = \omega L \)) increases with frequency, while the capacitive reactance (\( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} \)) decreases. Since \( X_L \) grows faster than \( X_C \) decreases, the net reactance (\( X_L - X_C \)) becomes positive, increasing the impedance (\( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} \)).

questions.question_text: Why does a step-down transformer increase the current in the secondary coil compared to the primary coil?
questions.explanation: In a step-down transformer (\( V_s < V_p \), \( N_s < N_p \)), power is conserved (\( V_p I_p = V_s I_s \)). Since \( V_s \) is lower, \( I_s \) must be higher than \( I_p \) (\( I_s = I_p \times \frac{N_p}{N_s} \), where \( \frac{N_p}{N_s} > 1 \)) to maintain the same power output.

questions.question_text: What characterizes the emission line spectrum of a hydrogen atom?
options: Dark lines on a bright background
Bright lines on a dark background
questions.explanation: The emission line spectrum consists of bright lines on a dark background, corresponding to specific wavelengths emitted during electron transitions.

questions.question_text: In Bohr’s model, what defines the stationary orbits of an electron?
questions.explanation: Bohr’s second postulate defines stationary orbits as those where the angular momentum is an integral multiple of \( h/2\pi \).

questions.question_text: In Bohr’s model, what is the state of a hydrogen atom when its electron is in the \( n = \infty \) orbit?
questions.explanation: At \( n = \infty \), the energy is zero, meaning the electron is ionized and no longer bound to the nucleus.

questions.question_text: What does the de Broglie hypothesis suggest about the electron in Bohr’s model?
questions.explanation: De Broglie suggests that electrons exhibit wave-like behavior, forming standing waves in orbits where the circumference is an integer multiple of the wavelength.

questions.question_text: In the Bohr model, how many de Broglie wavelengths fit into the circumference of the \( n = 6 \) orbit?
questions.explanation: \( 2\pi r_n = n\lambda \). For \( n = 6 \), number of wavelengths = 6.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about Rutherford’s nuclear model?
options: Electrons maintain stable orbits without radiating
Positive charge is concentrated in the nucleus
Most of the atom is empty space
questions.explanation: Rutherford’s model does not explain atomic stability, as it predicts electrons would emit radiation and collapse into the nucleus, not maintain stable orbits.

questions.question_text: An electron in a hydrogen atom transitions from \( n = 3 \) to \( n = 1 \). What is the energy of the emitted photon? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
What is the total energy of an electron in the \( n = 4 \) state of a hydrogen atom? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))

What is the wavelength of the photon emitted when an electron drops from \( n = 2 \) to \( n = 1 \) in a hydrogen atom? (Use \( h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \), 1 eV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta E = 10.2 \, \text{eV} = 1.632 \times 10^{-18} \, \text{J} \). \( \lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{1.632 \times 10^{-18}} \approx 1.21 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{m} \).

questions.question_text: What is the energy difference between the \( n = 5 \) and \( n = 3 \) states in a hydrogen atom? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
An electron beam of 11.0 eV excites a hydrogen atom in the ground state. What is the highest energy level reached? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
In Rutherford’s scattering experiment, what happens to an alpha-particle with a large impact parameter?
questions.explanation: For a large impact parameter, the alpha-particle experiences minimal deflection (\( \theta \approx 0 \)) and goes nearly undeviated.

questions.question_text: What is the energy required to excite a hydrogen atom from \( n = 1 \) to \( n = 3 \)? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
Which of the following statements is correct about the Bohr model’s prediction of hydrogen spectra?
questions.explanation: The model predicts discrete frequencies because photon energy equals the difference between quantized energy levels, not continuous radiation.

questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom is excited to the \( n = 4 \) state and returns to the ground state. What is the maximum energy of the emitted photon? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
An electron in a hydrogen atom has an angular momentum of \( 1.05 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \). What is its principal quantum number? (Use \( h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \))
In a hydrogen atom, the radius of the first orbit is \( 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \). What is the circumference of the third orbit?
questions.explanation: \( r_n = n^2 r_1 \), \( r_3 = 3^2 \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11} = 4.77 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m} \). Circumference = \( 2\pi r_3 = 2 \times 3.14 \times 4.77 \times 10^{-10} \approx 3.0 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{m} \).

questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the radius of the \( n = 4 \) orbit to the \( n = 2 \) orbit in a hydrogen atom?
What is the significance of the negative total energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom according to Bohr’s model?
options: Electron is bound to the nucleus
questions.explanation: The negative total energy indicates that the electron is bound to the nucleus, requiring energy to be supplied to free it.

questions.question_text: What is the total energy of an electron in the \( n = 2 \) state of a hydrogen atom? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))

An alpha-particle with 4.0 MeV kinetic energy approaches a gold nucleus (Z = 79). What is the distance of closest approach? (Use \( \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \), 1 MeV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \, \text{J} \))
questions.explanation: \( d = \frac{2Ze^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 K} \). \( K = 4.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13} = 6.4 \times 10^{-13} \, \text{J} \). \( d = \frac{2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2 \times 9 \times 10^9}{6.4 \times 10^{-13}} \). \( d = \frac{3.641 \times 10^{-28}}{6.4 \times 10^{-13}} \approx 5.69 \times 10^{-14} \, \text{m} \approx 57 \, \text{fm} \).

questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom absorbs a photon of energy 1.89 eV from the \( n = 2 \) state. To which energy level does it jump? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
In Bohr’s model, what is the physical basis for the quantization of angular momentum?
questions.explanation: Bohr’s second postulate states that the angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of \( h/2\pi \), introducing quantization to ensure stable orbits.

questions.question_text: What does de Broglie’s hypothesis explain in the context of Bohr’s model?
questions.explanation: De Broglie’s hypothesis explains the quantization of angular momentum by proposing that electrons form standing waves, with the orbit circumference being an integral multiple of the wavelength.

questions.question_text: Why does the classical electromagnetic theory predict that an atom should collapse?
questions.explanation: An accelerating electron in orbit emits radiation, losing energy and spiraling into the nucleus, leading to collapse according to classical theory.

questions.question_text: According to Bohr’s model, what happens when an electron in a hydrogen atom transitions from a higher orbit to a lower orbit?
questions.explanation: Bohr’s third postulate states that a photon is emitted with energy equal to the difference between the initial and final energy states.

questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom absorbs a photon of energy 12.75 eV from the ground state. To which energy level does it jump? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))

An alpha-particle with kinetic energy 6.0 MeV approaches a gold nucleus (Z = 79). What is the distance of closest approach? (Use \( \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \), 1 MeV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \, \text{J} \))
questions.explanation: \( d = \frac{2Ze^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 K} \). \( K = 6.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13} = 9.6 \times 10^{-13} \, \text{J} \). \( d = \frac{2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2 \times 9 \times 10^9}{9.6 \times 10^{-13}} \). \( d = \frac{3.641 \times 10^{-28}}{9.6 \times 10^{-13}} \approx 3.79 \times 10^{-14} \, \text{m} \approx 38 \, \text{fm} \).

questions.question_text: A 13.0 eV electron beam excites a hydrogen atom in the ground state. What is the highest energy level reached? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
According to Thomson’s model of the atom, how is the positive charge distributed?
questions.explanation: In Thomson’s model, the positive charge is uniformly distributed throughout the volume of the atom, with electrons embedded in it like seeds in a watermelon.

questions.question_text: In Rutherford’s scattering experiment, what percentage of alpha-particles scatter by more than 1°?
questions.explanation: Given: 0.14% of alpha-particles scatter by more than 1°. Percentage = 0.14%.

questions.question_text: What is the angular momentum of an electron in the \( n = 2 \) state of a hydrogen atom? (Use \( h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = n \frac{h}{2\pi} \). For \( n = 2 \): \( L = 2 \times \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{2 \times 3.14} \approx 2.1 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \).

questions.question_text: A photon of energy 10.2 eV is absorbed by a hydrogen atom in the ground state. To which energy level does the electron jump? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))

In an alpha-particle scattering experiment, a 5.5 MeV alpha-particle approaches a gold nucleus (Z = 79). What is the approximate distance of closest approach? (Take \( \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \), 1 MeV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \, \text{J} \))
questions.explanation: Energy conservation: \( K = \frac{2Ze^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 d} \). \( d = \frac{2Ze^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 K} \). \( K = 5.5 \, \text{MeV} = 5.5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13} = 8.8 \times 10^{-13} \, \text{J} \). \( d = \frac{2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2 \times 9 \times 10^9}{8.8 \times 10^{-13}} \). \( d = \frac{158 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38} \times 9 \times 10^9}{8.8 \times 10^{-13}} \approx 4.13 \times 10^{-14} \, \text{m} \approx 41 \, \text{fm} \). Rounded to 40 fm for simplicity.

questions.question_text: Why did Rutherford’s nuclear model fail to explain the stability of atoms?
questions.explanation: In classical theory, an accelerating electron (in circular orbit) emits radiation, losing energy and spiraling into the nucleus, contradicting atomic stability.

questions.question_text: What is the orbital period of an electron in the \( n = 2 \) orbit of a hydrogen atom if \( v_1 = 2.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \) and \( r_1 = 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \)?
What is the potential energy of an electron in the \( n = 5 \) state of a hydrogen atom? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
What does the line spectrum of hydrogen indicate about its atomic structure?
questions.explanation: The line spectrum suggests that electrons occupy discrete energy levels, emitting photons of specific wavelengths when transitioning between them.

questions.question_text: What is the orbital period of an electron in the first orbit of a hydrogen atom if its speed is \( 2.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \) and radius is \( 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \)?
questions.explanation: \( T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2 \times 3.14 \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}}{2.2 \times 10^6} \approx 1.51 \times 10^{-16} \, \text{s} \).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the hydrogen atom’s energy levels in Bohr’s model?
options: Energy is negative in bound states
Energy is positive in all orbits
Energy approaches zero as \( n \) increases
questions.explanation: Energy levels are discrete and negative, becoming less negative with increasing \( n \), not positive or continuous as in classical models.

questions.question_text: What is the total energy of an electron in the \( n = 5 \) state of a hydrogen atom? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
The radius of the first orbit in a hydrogen atom is \( 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \). What is the circumference of the fourth orbit?
questions.explanation: \( r_n = n^2 r_1 \), \( r_4 = 4^2 \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11} = 8.48 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m} \). Circumference = \( 2\pi r_4 = 2 \times 3.14 \times 8.48 \times 10^{-10} \approx 5.33 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{m} \).

questions.question_text: In the Bohr model, what is the ground state of a hydrogen atom?
questions.explanation: The ground state is the lowest energy state, where the electron is in the orbit with \( n = 1 \), having an energy of -13.6 eV.

questions.question_text: In Rutherford’s scattering experiment, what fraction of alpha-particles scatter by more than 90° out of 8000 incident particles?
questions.explanation: Given: 1 in 8000 alpha-particles deflect by more than 90°. Fraction = \( \frac{1}{8000} = 0.000125 \).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key feature of Bohr’s model for the hydrogen atom?
questions.explanation: Bohr’s model introduces quantization, where electrons revolve in stable orbits with angular momentum as integral multiples of \( h/2\pi \).

questions.question_text: In Rutherford’s model, what is the order of magnitude of the ratio of the atomic size to the nuclear size?
questions.explanation: Atomic size \( \approx 10^{-10} \, \text{m} \), nuclear size \( \approx 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \). Ratio = \( \frac{10^{-10}}{10^{-15}} = 10^5 \).

questions.question_text: In Rutherford’s model, what provides the centripetal force for an electron orbiting the nucleus in a hydrogen atom?
questions.explanation: The electrostatic force between the electron and nucleus provides the centripetal force: \( \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} = \frac{m v^2}{r} \).

questions.question_text: An electron in a hydrogen atom has a speed of \( 2.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \) in the first orbit. What is its kinetic energy? (Mass of electron = \( 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \), 1 eV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))

What is the wavelength of the photon emitted when an electron in a hydrogen atom drops from \( n = 3 \) to \( n = 2 \)? (Use \( h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \), 1 eV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))
Which of the following statements is correct about Thomson’s model of the atom?
options: Positive charge is spread uniformly with electrons embedded in it
Positive charge is concentrated in a small nucleus
Electrons orbit the nucleus like planets
Atom consists of discrete energy levels
questions.explanation: Thomson’s model describes the atom as a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, resembling a plum pudding, not a nuclear structure.

questions.question_text: The radius of the first orbit in a hydrogen atom is \( 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \). What is the radius of the second orbit?
Which of the following statements is correct about the energy levels in a hydrogen atom according to Bohr’s model?
options: Energy is constant for all orbits
Energy is zero in the ground state
questions.explanation: The energy becomes less negative (increases) as the principal quantum number \( n \) increases, approaching zero at \( n = \infty \).

questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom in the \( n = 5 \) state emits a photon and returns to the ground state. What is the maximum energy of the photon? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
How many de Broglie wavelengths fit into the circumference of the \( n = 4 \) orbit of a hydrogen atom?
questions.explanation: Circumference = \( 2\pi r_n = n\lambda \). For \( n = 4 \), number of wavelengths = 4.

questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the kinetic energy to the potential energy of an electron in the ground state of a hydrogen atom? (Given total energy = -13.6 eV)

What is the wavelength of a photon emitted when an electron drops from \( n = 4 \) to \( n = 3 \) in a hydrogen atom? (Use \( h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \), 1 eV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta E = 0.66 \, \text{eV} = 1.056 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \). \( \lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{1.056 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 1.875 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m} \).

questions.question_text: What is the angular momentum of an electron in the \( n = 5 \) state of a hydrogen atom? (Use \( h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = n \frac{h}{2\pi} \). For \( n = 5 \): \( L = 5 \times \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{2 \times 3.14} \approx 5.25 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \).

questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom absorbs a photon and jumps from \( n = 1 \) to \( n = 2 \). What is the energy of the photon? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
In Rutherford’s model, what is the primary force keeping electrons in orbit around the nucleus?
questions.explanation: The electrostatic force of attraction between the positively charged nucleus and negatively charged electrons provides the centripetal force for orbiting.

questions.question_text: The radius of the third orbit in a hydrogen atom is how many times the radius of the first orbit if \( r_1 = 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \)?
Why does the Bohr model predict discrete spectral lines for hydrogen?
questions.explanation: Discrete spectral lines arise because electrons transition between fixed energy levels, emitting photons with energies equal to the differences between these levels.

questions.question_text: In Bohr’s model, what prevents an electron from emitting radiant energy while revolving in a stable orbit?
questions.explanation: Bohr’s first postulate states that electrons in certain stable orbits (stationary states) do not emit radiant energy, contrary to classical electromagnetic theory.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct about the ionization energy of a hydrogen atom in Bohr’s model?
options: It is zero in the ground state
It is negative for all states
It is 13.6 eV from the ground state
questions.explanation: The ionization energy is the energy required to remove the electron from the ground state (\( n = 1 \), -13.6 eV) to infinity (0 eV), which is 13.6 eV.

questions.question_text: What is the primary reason Rutherford’s model could not explain the line spectra of atoms?
questions.explanation: Rutherford’s model lacks quantized energy levels, predicting continuous radiation as electrons accelerate, not discrete spectral lines.

questions.question_text: What is the energy required to ionize a hydrogen atom from its ground state? (Ground state energy = -13.6 eV)
questions.explanation: Ionization energy = energy to reach \( E = 0 \) from ground state. \( E_1 = -13.6 \, \text{eV} \), \( E_\infty = 0 \, \text{eV} \). Energy required = \( 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6 \, \text{eV} \).

questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom in the ground state is bombarded with a 12.5 eV electron beam. What is the maximum energy level the electron can reach? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
In Rutherford’s scattering experiment, what does a small fraction of alpha-particles rebounding back indicate?
questions.explanation: It indicates that the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a small nucleus, causing strong repulsion in head-on collisions.

questions.question_text: In a hydrogen atom, the total energy of an electron in the ground state is -13.6 eV. What is the magnitude of its potential energy?
What does the presence of discrete wavelengths in the hydrogen spectrum indicate?
options: Electrons move randomly in the atom
Atom has a uniform charge distribution
questions.explanation: Discrete wavelengths indicate that electrons transition between specific energy levels, emitting or absorbing photons of fixed energies.

questions.question_text: In Rutherford’s experiment, what does the scattering of alpha-particles at small angles indicate?
options: Alpha-particles pass far from the nucleus
questions.explanation: Small-angle scattering occurs when alpha-particles pass far from the nucleus (large impact parameter), experiencing weak repulsion.

questions.question_text: What is the frequency of a photon emitted when an electron drops from \( n = 2 \) to \( n = 1 \) in a hydrogen atom? (Use \( h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \), 1 eV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta E = 10.2 \, \text{eV} = 1.632 \times 10^{-18} \, \text{J} \). \( \nu = \frac{\Delta E}{h} = \frac{1.632 \times 10^{-18}}{6.6 \times 10^{-34}} \approx 2.47 \times 10^{15} \, \text{Hz} \).

questions.question_text: In Rutherford’s scattering experiment, what causes the large deflection of some alpha-particles?
questions.explanation: Large deflections occur due to the strong repulsive force from the positively charged nucleus when alpha-particles approach it closely.

questions.question_text: What is a limitation of Bohr’s model when applied to the hydrogen atom’s spectrum?
questions.explanation: Bohr’s model cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines, as it does not account for transition probabilities.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct about the absorption process in a hydrogen atom?
options: Electron remains in the same orbit
Electron jumps to a higher energy level
questions.explanation: Absorption occurs when an electron jumps to a higher energy level by absorbing a photon matching the energy difference between levels.

questions.question_text: What is the frequency of a photon emitted when an electron drops from \( n = 3 \) to \( n = 1 \) in a hydrogen atom? (Use \( h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \), 1 eV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))
In Bohr’s model, what happens to the energy required to ionize a hydrogen atom as the electron’s orbit number increases?
questions.explanation: As \( n \) increases, the energy becomes less negative (closer to zero), so less energy is required to ionize the atom from higher orbits.

questions.question_text: In a hydrogen atom, the total energy of an electron in the \( n = 3 \) state is -1.51 eV. What is its potential energy?
What is the orbital period of an electron in the \( n = 4 \) orbit if \( v_1 = 2.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \) and \( r_1 = 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \)?
What assumption in Rutherford’s model contradicts classical electromagnetic theory?
questions.explanation: Rutherford assumes electrons orbit the nucleus like planets, but classical theory predicts they would radiate energy and collapse, not remain stable.

questions.question_text: In the Bohr model, how many de Broglie wavelengths fit into the circumference of the \( n = 3 \) orbit?
questions.explanation: \( 2\pi r_n = n\lambda \). For \( n = 3 \), number of wavelengths = 3.

questions.question_text: In Rutherford’s nuclear model, why do most alpha-particles pass through the gold foil without deflection?
questions.explanation: Most of the atom is empty space, with the nucleus occupying a very small volume, so most alpha-particles do not encounter the nucleus and pass through undeflected.

questions.question_text: What is the role of the impact parameter in Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering?
options: Indicates the size of the foil
questions.explanation: The impact parameter determines the scattering angle; a smaller impact parameter leads to a larger deflection due to closer approach to the nucleus.

questions.question_text: An electron beam of 12.0 eV excites a hydrogen atom in the ground state. What is the highest energy level reached? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
In the Bohr model, what is the ratio of the radius of the \( n = 5 \) orbit to the \( n = 1 \) orbit?
What is the speed of an electron in the \( n = 4 \) orbit of a hydrogen atom if its speed in \( n = 1 \) is \( 2.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \)?
What is the energy of a photon emitted when an electron drops from \( n = 5 \) to \( n = 4 \) in a hydrogen atom? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
The radius of the first orbit in a hydrogen atom is \( 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \). What is the radius of the fifth orbit?
Which of the following statements is incorrect about de Broglie’s explanation of Bohr’s model?
options: Electrons form standing waves in orbits
Circumference is an integer multiple of wavelength
questions.explanation: De Broglie’s hypothesis supports quantization by proposing standing waves, not continuous waves, which fit an integer number of wavelengths into the orbit.

questions.question_text: In a hydrogen atom, the total energy of the electron in the ground state is -13.6 eV. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Total energy \( E = K + U \), where \( K = \frac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 r} \), \( U = -\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} \). \( E = K - 2K = -K \). \( E = -13.6 \, \text{eV} = -K \Rightarrow K = 13.6 \, \text{eV} \).

questions.question_text: What limitation of Bohr’s model prevents it from explaining the spectrum of helium?
questions.explanation: Bohr’s model applies only to hydrogenic (single-electron) atoms and cannot account for electron-electron interactions in multi-electron atoms like helium.

questions.question_text: What was the primary evidence from Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment that led to the nuclear model of the atom?
options: Some alpha-particles were deflected by large angles
Alpha-particles were absorbed by the foil
questions.explanation: The observation that a small fraction of alpha-particles were deflected by large angles (e.g., more than 90°) indicated a small, dense, positively charged nucleus at the atom’s center.

questions.question_text: In Rutherford’s scattering experiment, what does the small number of alpha-particles undergoing head-on collisions suggest?
questions.explanation: The rarity of head-on collisions (1 in 8000 rebounding back) suggests that the nucleus, containing most of the mass and charge, is very small compared to the atom.

questions.question_text: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from \( n = 4 \) to \( n = 2 \). What is the energy of the emitted photon? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
In Rutherford’s model, what is the ratio of the size of the nucleus to the size of the atom if the nuclear radius is \( 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \) and atomic radius is \( 10^{-10} \, \text{m} \)?
questions.explanation: Ratio = \( \frac{\text{nuclear radius}}{\text{atomic radius}} = \frac{10^{-15}}{10^{-10}} = 10^{-5} \).

questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom emits a photon when an electron drops from \( n = 5 \) to \( n = 2 \). What is the energy of the photon? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
A hydrogen atom in the \( n = 3 \) state emits a photon and returns to the ground state. What is the maximum energy of the photon? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
What is the speed of an electron in the \( n = 3 \) orbit of a hydrogen atom if its speed in \( n = 1 \) is \( 2.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \)?
What is the angular momentum of an electron in the \( n = 3 \) state of a hydrogen atom? (Use \( h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = n \frac{h}{2\pi} \). For \( n = 3 \): \( L = 3 \times \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{2 \times 3.14} \approx 3.15 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J·s} \).

questions.question_text: What is the frequency of revolution of an electron in the first orbit of a hydrogen atom if its speed is \( 2.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \) and radius is \( 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \)?
questions.explanation: \( v = \frac{v}{2\pi r} \). \( v = \frac{2.2 \times 10^6}{2 \times 3.14 \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}} \approx 6.6 \times 10^{15} \, \text{Hz} \).

questions.question_text: What is the minimum energy required to excite a hydrogen atom from its ground state to the first excited state? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))

The kinetic energy of an alpha-particle is 7.7 MeV. If it approaches a nucleus with atomic number 79, what is its distance of closest approach? (Use constants: \( \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \), 1 MeV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \, \text{J} \))
What is the speed of an electron in the \( n = 5 \) orbit of a hydrogen atom if its speed in \( n = 1 \) is \( 2.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \)?
In the Bohr model, what is the ratio of the kinetic energy of an electron in the \( n = 2 \) state to that in the \( n = 1 \) state?
questions.explanation: \( K = \frac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 r} \), \( r_n \propto n^2 \). \( K_n \propto \frac{1}{n^2} \). Ratio = \( \frac{K_2}{K_1} = \frac{1/2^2}{1/1^2} = \frac{1}{4} \).

questions.question_text: An electron in a hydrogen atom has a total energy of -3.4 eV. What is its kinetic energy?
Which of the following statements is incorrect about Thomson’s model?
options: Electrons are embedded in positive charge
Described as a plum pudding model
questions.explanation: Thomson’s model does not include a nucleus; it proposes a uniform positive charge distribution, unlike Rutherford’s nuclear model.

questions.question_text: In the Bohr model, how many de Broglie wavelengths fit into the circumference of the \( n = 5 \) orbit?
questions.explanation: \( 2\pi r_n = n\lambda \). For \( n = 5 \), number of wavelengths = 5.

questions.question_text: What does the absorption spectrum of a hydrogen atom reveal?
options: Bright lines on a dark background
Dark lines in a continuous spectrum
questions.explanation: The absorption spectrum shows dark lines at wavelengths where photons are absorbed, matching the emission line wavelengths, indicating specific energy level transitions.

questions.question_text: What is the kinetic energy of an electron in the \( n = 4 \) state of a hydrogen atom? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
What is the orbital period of an electron in the \( n = 3 \) orbit if \( v_1 = 2.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \) and \( r_1 = 5.3 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \)?
What is the energy difference between the \( n = 4 \) and \( n = 2 \) states in a hydrogen atom? (Use \( E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \))
The binding energy of a nucleus is \( 240 \, \text{MeV} \) and its mass number is 30. What is the binding energy per nucleon?
What is the radius of a nucleus with mass number 32? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
A nucleus with mass number 70 has a binding energy of \( 595 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
What is the energy equivalent of a neutron with mass \( 1.6749 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \) in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
What happens to the nuclear force when nucleons are separated by more than a few femtometres?
questions.explanation: The nuclear force is short-ranged and drops rapidly to zero beyond a few femtometres, leaving only weaker forces like Coulomb repulsion or gravity to act between nucleons.

questions.question_text: What role does the binding energy play in nuclear stability?
questions.explanation: Higher binding energy indicates a more tightly bound nucleus, making it more stable as it requires more energy to break apart, reflecting the strength of the nuclear force.

questions.question_text: Why does the nuclear force not distinguish between protons and neutrons?
options: It is weakened by Coulomb force
questions.explanation: The nuclear force is charge-independent, acting equally between neutron-neutron, proton-neutron, and proton-proton pairs, as it is a fundamental property unrelated to electric charge.

questions.question_text: What is the mass defect of a nucleus with binding energy \( 216 \, \text{MeV} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta M = \frac{E_b}{c^2} \). \( \Delta M = \frac{216}{931.5} \approx 0.232 \, \text{u} \approx 0.23 \, \text{u} \).

questions.question_text: A nucleus with mass number 40 has a binding energy of \( 320 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
What is the significance of the mass-energy equivalence in nuclear physics?
questions.explanation: Einstein’s \( E = m c^2 \) explains how mass defect converts into binding energy, unifying mass and energy conservation and enabling the understanding of energy release in nuclear reactions.

questions.question_text: What is the mass defect of a nucleus with binding energy \( 167.67 \, \text{MeV} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta M = \frac{E_b}{c^2} \). \( \Delta M = \frac{167.67}{931.5} \approx 0.18 \, \text{u} \).

questions.question_text: How much energy is released when \( 5 \, \text{g} \) of matter is converted into energy? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
What is the volume of a nucleus with radius \( 3.0 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
Which characteristic of the nuclear force explains its dominance over the Coulomb force in the nucleus?
questions.explanation: The nuclear force is much stronger than the Coulomb force at short distances (within the nucleus), allowing it to overcome proton repulsion and bind nucleons together.

questions.question_text: What is the approximate mass number of a nucleus with radius \( 3.3 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
What is the radius of a nucleus with mass number 4? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: The radius of a nucleus is given by \( R = R_0 A^{1/3} \), where \( A = 4 \). \( A^{1/3} = 4^{1/3} \approx 1.59 \). \( R = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \times 1.59 \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \).

questions.question_text: What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.25 \, \text{g} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
What is the key requirement for nuclei to undergo fusion?
questions.explanation: Fusion requires nuclei to overcome the Coulomb barrier (electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei), which is achieved by providing high kinetic energy through elevated temperatures.

questions.question_text: Why is the mass of a nucleus less than the sum of its constituent nucleons?
questions.explanation: The mass defect occurs because some mass is converted into binding energy, which holds the nucleus together, as per Einstein’s \( E = m c^2 \).

questions.question_text: What is the approximate mass number of a nucleus with radius \( 4.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
What is the primary advantage of controlled thermonuclear fusion as an energy source?
questions.explanation: Controlled thermonuclear fusion could provide nearly unlimited energy by fusing light nuclei (e.g., hydrogen), utilizing abundant fuel sources and producing minimal radioactive waste.

questions.question_text: Calculate the nuclear density of a nucleus if its mass is \( 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \) and radius is \( 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \). (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
questions.explanation: Density = \( \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \), Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \). \( R^3 = (1.2 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 1.728 \times 10^{-45} \, \text{m}^3 \). Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 1.728 \times 10^{-45} = 7.24 \times 10^{-45} \, \text{m}^3 \). Density = \( \frac{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{7.24 \times 10^{-45}} \approx 2.31 \times 10^{17} \, \text{kg/m}^3 \).

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the nuclear force at distances greater than 0.8 fm?
questions.explanation: At distances greater than 0.8 fm, the nuclear force is attractive and dominates over the Coulomb force, binding nucleons together until it drops off rapidly beyond a few femtometres.

questions.question_text: What is the mass defect of a nucleus with binding energy \( 70 \, \text{MeV} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta M = \frac{E_b}{c^2} \). \( \Delta M = \frac{70}{931.5} \approx 0.075 \, \text{u} \).

questions.question_text: What is the primary reason nuclear reactions release more energy than chemical reactions?
questions.explanation: Nuclear reactions involve changes in nuclear binding energy, which operates on a scale of MeV, vastly exceeding the eV scale of chemical bond energy, due to the strong nuclear force.

questions.question_text: Which force is responsible for overcoming the repulsion between protons in the nucleus?
questions.explanation: The nuclear force, being much stronger than the Coulomb force, binds protons and neutrons together, overcoming the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged protons.

questions.question_text: What is the nuclear density of a nucleus with mass \( 2.33 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 1.7 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
questions.explanation: Density = \( \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \), Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \). \( R^3 = (1.7 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 4.913 \times 10^{-45} \, \text{m}^3 \). Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 4.913 \times 10^{-45} \approx 2.06 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Density = \( \frac{2.33 \times 10^{-27}}{2.06 \times 10^{-44}} \approx 1.13 \times 10^{17} \, \text{kg/m}^3 \).

questions.question_text: What is the ratio of nuclear radii of two nuclei with mass numbers 64 and 8?
Why does nuclear fission release more energy than chemical reactions?
options: Larger energy scale of nuclear processes
questions.explanation: Nuclear fission involves changes in nuclear binding energy (order of MeV), which is about a million times larger than the energy from chemical bond changes (order of eV).

questions.question_text: What is the outcome when two light nuclei fuse into a heavier nucleus?
questions.explanation: Fusion of light nuclei increases the binding energy per nucleon, making the resulting nucleus more tightly bound and releasing energy as a result of this increased stability.

questions.question_text: What does the mass defect of a nucleus represent?
options: Mass of the electrons in the atom
Excess mass due to nuclear repulsion
questions.explanation: The mass defect is the difference between the total mass of the individual protons and neutrons and the actual mass of the nucleus, representing the mass converted into binding energy that holds the nucleus together.

questions.question_text: Why does the binding energy per nucleon remain nearly constant for nuclei with mass numbers between 30 and 170?
options: Due to the short-range nature of nuclear force
Due to the long-range nature of Coulomb force
Because of the increase in proton repulsion
Due to the variation in nuclear density
questions.explanation: The nuclear force is short-ranged, affecting only neighboring nucleons. In medium-sized nuclei (A = 30 to 170), most nucleons are inside the nucleus, surrounded by a constant number of neighbors, leading to a saturation effect and nearly constant binding energy per nucleon.

questions.question_text: What is the ratio of nuclear radii of nuclei with mass numbers 125 and 27?
What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.02 \, \text{kg} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
What is the ratio of nuclear radii of nuclei with mass numbers 216 and 8?
What is the volume of a nucleus with radius \( 4.8 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
What happens to the binding energy per nucleon when a heavy nucleus undergoes fission?
questions.explanation: For heavy nuclei (A > 170), the binding energy per nucleon is lower (~7.6 MeV). Fission into intermediate mass fragments (A ≈ 120) increases it to ~8.5 MeV, releasing energy.

questions.question_text: A nucleus with mass number 60 has a binding energy of \( 510 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
What is the nuclear density of a nucleus with mass \( 7.01 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 2.5 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
questions.explanation: Density = \( \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \), Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \). \( R^3 = (2.5 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 1.5625 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 1.5625 \times 10^{-44} \approx 6.54 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Density = \( \frac{7.01 \times 10^{-27}}{6.54 \times 10^{-44}} \approx 1.07 \times 10^{17} \, \text{kg/m}^3 \).

questions.question_text: What is the binding energy of a nucleus with mass defect \( 0.14 \, \text{u} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( E_b = \Delta M \cdot c^2 \). \( \Delta M = 0.14 \, \text{u} \). \( E_b = 0.14 \times 931.5 = 130.41 \, \text{MeV} \).

questions.question_text: What is the mass defect of a nucleus with binding energy \( 102.3 \, \text{MeV} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta M = \frac{E_b}{c^2} \). \( \Delta M = \frac{102.3}{931.5} \approx 0.11 \, \text{u} \).

questions.question_text: A nucleus with mass number 80 has a binding energy of \( 680 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
What is the volume of a nucleus with radius \( 3.6 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
Which of the following is true about the nuclear force at very short distances (less than 0.8 fm)?
questions.explanation: The nuclear force becomes strongly repulsive at distances less than 0.8 fm, preventing nucleons from collapsing into each other, as shown in the potential energy plot.

questions.question_text: What is the energy equivalent of \( 1 \, \text{kg} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
Why is nuclear fusion more likely to release energy when light nuclei are involved?
options: Increase in binding energy per nucleon
questions.explanation: In light nuclei (A < 30), the binding energy per nucleon is lower. When they fuse into a heavier nucleus, the binding energy per nucleon increases, releasing energy as the final system is more tightly bound.

questions.question_text: What is the approximate radius of a nucleus with mass number 8? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: The radius of a nucleus is given by \( R = R_0 A^{1/3} \), where \( A = 8 \). \( A^{1/3} = 8^{1/3} = 2 \). \( R = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \times 2 = 2.4 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \).

questions.question_text: What is the mass defect of a nucleus with binding energy \( 93.15 \, \text{MeV} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
What is the main source of energy in nuclear reactors?
questions.explanation: Nuclear reactors produce energy through nuclear fission, where heavy nuclei split into lighter fragments, releasing energy due to the increase in binding energy per nucleon.

questions.question_text: The radius of a nucleus is \( 6.0 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \). What is its approximate mass number? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
What is the mass defect of a nucleus if its binding energy is \( 186 \, \text{MeV} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( E_b = \Delta M \cdot c^2 \). \( \Delta M = \frac{E_b}{c^2} = \frac{186}{931.5} \approx 0.2 \, \text{u} \).

questions.question_text: InEinstein's mass-energy equivalence, what does the term \( c^2 \) represent?
options: Square of the speed of light
questions.explanation: In \( E = m c^2 \), \( c^2 \) is the square of the speed of light in a vacuum, acting as the conversion factor between mass and energy, indicating the immense energy equivalent of a small mass.

questions.question_text: What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.5 \, \text{g} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
What is the radius of a nucleus with mass number 108? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
What is the nuclear density of a nucleus with mass \( 6.68 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 2.4 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
questions.explanation: Density = \( \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \), Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \). \( R^3 = (2.4 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 1.382 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 1.382 \times 10^{-44} \approx 5.79 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Density = \( \frac{6.68 \times 10^{-27}}{5.79 \times 10^{-44}} \approx 1.15 \times 10^{17} \, \text{kg/m}^3 \).

questions.question_text: What is the binding energy per nucleon if a nucleus with mass number 56 has a total binding energy of \( 490 \, \text{MeV} \)?
What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.002 \, \text{kg} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
A nucleus has a radius of \( 3.6 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \). What is its approximate mass number? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.1 \, \text{g} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
Which process is responsible for the energy release in an atomic bomb?
questions.explanation: The energy in an atomic bomb comes from uncontrolled nuclear fission, where a heavy nucleus splits into lighter fragments, releasing energy due to increased binding energy per nucleon.

questions.question_text: What is the radius of a nucleus with mass number 200? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
What is the energy equivalent of \( 2 \, \text{kg} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
Which factor primarily determines the nuclear radius?
questions.explanation: The nuclear radius is given by \( R = R_0 A^{1/3} \), where \( A \) (mass number) is the key factor determining the size, as the radius scales with the cube root of the number of nucleons.

questions.question_text: What is the ratio of nuclear radii of two nuclei with mass numbers 27 and 125?
What is the nuclear density of a nucleus with mass \( 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 1.5 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
questions.explanation: Density = \( \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \), Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \). \( R^3 = (1.5 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 3.375 \times 10^{-45} \, \text{m}^3 \). Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 3.375 \times 10^{-45} \approx 1.41 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Density = \( \frac{1.66 \times 10^{-27}}{1.41 \times 10^{-44}} \approx 1.18 \times 10^{17} \, \text{kg/m}^3 \).

questions.question_text: A nucleus has a mass defect of \( 0.05 \, \text{u} \). What is its binding energy in MeV? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Binding energy = \( \Delta M \cdot c^2 \). \( \Delta M = 0.05 \, \text{u} \). \( E_b = 0.05 \times 931.5 = 46.575 \, \text{MeV} \approx 46.58 \, \text{MeV} \).

questions.question_text: What is the primary challenge in achieving controlled thermonuclear fusion?
questions.explanation: Controlled thermonuclear fusion requires extremely high temperatures (e.g., \( 10^8 \, \text{K} \)), producing a plasma that no container can withstand, making confinement (e.g., using magnetic fields) a major challenge.

questions.question_text: What is the approximate radius of a nucleus with mass number 64? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: The radius of a nucleus is given by \( R = R_0 A^{1/3} \), where \( A = 64 \). \( A^{1/3} = 64^{1/3} = 4 \). \( R = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \times 4 = 4.8 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \).

questions.question_text: A nucleus with mass number 50 has a binding energy of \( 425 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.15 \, \text{g} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
Why does nuclear fusion require extremely high temperatures?
questions.explanation: High temperatures provide nuclei with enough kinetic energy to overcome the electrostatic repulsion (Coulomb barrier) between positively charged nuclei, enabling fusion via the nuclear force.

questions.question_text: What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.05 \, \text{g} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
Why is the nuclear density nearly constant across all nuclei?
questions.explanation: The volume of a nucleus is proportional to \( A \) (since \( R \propto A^{1/3} \) and \( V \propto R^3 \)), and the mass is also proportional to \( A \), making the density (mass/volume) independent of \( A \).

questions.question_text: Why is the binding energy per nucleon a useful measure of nuclear stability?
questions.explanation: It represents the average energy needed to remove a nucleon, with higher values indicating a more stable nucleus due to stronger binding against disruptive forces like Coulomb repulsion.

questions.question_text: What is the significance of the binding energy per nucleon curve?
questions.explanation: The binding energy per nucleon curve shows how tightly nucleons are bound, indicating that energy is released in fission (heavy nuclei) or fusion (light nuclei) when transitioning to higher binding energy states.

questions.question_text: The mass of a proton is \( 1.67262 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \). What is its energy equivalent in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
Which of the following forces is negligible in holding the nucleus together?
questions.explanation: The gravitational force is much weaker than the nuclear force and Coulomb force, playing a negligible role in binding nucleons within the tiny nuclear volume, where the strong nuclear force dominates.

questions.question_text: Which property of the nuclear force leads to the saturation of binding energy in large nuclei?
questions.explanation: The short-range nature of the nuclear force means it only affects nearby nucleons, not all nucleons in the nucleus, leading to a saturation effect where adding more nucleons does not significantly increase the binding energy per nucleon in large nuclei.

questions.question_text: What is the key difference between nuclear and chemical energy sources?
questions.explanation: Nuclear energy arises from changes in nuclear binding energy (MeV scale), while chemical energy comes from electron rearrangements (eV scale), making nuclear energy millions of times greater.

questions.question_text: What is the binding energy of a nucleus with a mass defect of \( 0.09 \, \text{u} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Binding energy = \( \Delta M \cdot c^2 \). \( \Delta M = 0.09 \, \text{u} \). \( E_b = 0.09 \times 931.5 = 83.835 \, \text{MeV} \approx 83.84 \, \text{MeV} \).

questions.question_text: What is the nuclear density of a nucleus with mass \( 8.35 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 2.7 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
questions.explanation: Density = \( \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \), Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \). \( R^3 = (2.7 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 1.9683 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 1.9683 \times 10^{-44} \approx 8.25 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Density = \( \frac{8.35 \times 10^{-27}}{8.25 \times 10^{-44}} \approx 1.01 \times 10^{17} \, \text{kg/m}^3 \).

questions.question_text: What is the binding energy of a nucleus with mass defect \( 0.12 \, \text{u} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( E_b = \Delta M \cdot c^2 \). \( \Delta M = 0.12 \, \text{u} \). \( E_b = 0.12 \times 931.5 = 111.78 \, \text{MeV} \).

questions.question_text: What is the energy released when \( 2 \, \text{g} \) of matter is completely converted into energy? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
Why is the binding energy per nucleon lower in very heavy nuclei?
questions.explanation: In very heavy nuclei (A > 170), the increased Coulomb repulsion between protons reduces the net binding energy per nucleon, as the nuclear force cannot fully counteract this effect.

questions.question_text: What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.001 \, \text{kg} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
A nucleus has a mass defect of \( 0.136 \, \text{u} \). What is its binding energy in MeV? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Binding energy = \( \Delta M \cdot c^2 \). \( \Delta M = 0.136 \, \text{u} \). Energy = \( 0.136 \times 931.5 \approx 126.7 \, \text{MeV} \).

questions.question_text: Which process cannot produce elements beyond the peak of the binding energy curve?
questions.explanation: Fusion produces heavier nuclei with higher binding energy per nucleon up to the peak (around A = 56), but beyond this, further fusion does not release energy, limiting element synthesis.

questions.question_text: What is the volume of a nucleus with radius \( 2.7 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
What is the nuclear density of a nucleus with mass \( 5.01 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 2.1 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
questions.explanation: Density = \( \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \), Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \). \( R^3 = (2.1 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 9.261 \times 10^{-45} \, \text{m}^3 \). Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 9.261 \times 10^{-45} \approx 3.88 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Density = \( \frac{5.01 \times 10^{-27}}{3.88 \times 10^{-44}} \approx 1.29 \times 10^{17} \, \text{kg/m}^3 \).

questions.question_text: A nucleus with mass number 216 has a radius of \( 7.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \). What is the value of \( R_0 \)?
What is the primary outcome of nuclear fission in terms of energy?
questions.explanation: Nuclear fission converts mass defect into energy, initially as kinetic energy of fragments and neutrons, which is eventually transferred as heat, due to the increase in binding energy per nucleon.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the nuclear force?
questions.explanation: The nuclear force is a strong, short-range attractive force that binds protons and neutrons in the nucleus, overcoming the Coulomb repulsion between protons. It is much stronger than the Coulomb force and does not depend on the electric charge of the nucleons.

questions.question_text: What is the binding energy of a nucleus if its mass defect is \( 0.15 \, \text{u} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( E_b = \Delta M \cdot c^2 \). \( \Delta M = 0.15 \, \text{u} \). \( E_b = 0.15 \times 931.5 = 139.725 \, \text{MeV} \approx 139.73 \, \text{MeV} \).

questions.question_text: A nucleus with mass number 100 has a binding energy of \( 850 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
A nucleus with mass number 36 has a binding energy of \( 288 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
Which statement is true about the energy release in nuclear processes?
options: Energy is absorbed in all cases
Energy is released when binding increases
questions.explanation: Nuclear processes (fission and fusion) release energy when less tightly bound nuclei transform into more tightly bound ones, increasing the binding energy per nucleon.

questions.question_text: Why is the nuclear force considered saturated in large nuclei?
questions.explanation: The nuclear force is short-ranged, affecting only a fixed number of neighboring nucleons, so adding more nucleons in large nuclei does not proportionally increase the binding energy, leading to saturation.

questions.question_text: A nucleus with mass number 12 has a binding energy of \( 96 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
What is the role of high temperature in nuclear fusion?
questions.explanation: High temperatures provide nuclei with sufficient kinetic energy to overcome the Coulomb barrier (electrostatic repulsion), allowing them to come close enough for the nuclear force to cause fusion.

questions.question_text: What is the nuclear density of a nucleus with mass \( 3.67 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 2.0 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Use \( \pi = 3.14 \))
questions.explanation: Density = \( \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \), Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \). \( R^3 = (2.0 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 8.0 \times 10^{-45} \, \text{m}^3 \). Volume = \( \frac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 8.0 \times 10^{-45} \approx 3.35 \times 10^{-44} \, \text{m}^3 \). Density = \( \frac{3.67 \times 10^{-27}}{3.35 \times 10^{-44}} \approx 1.10 \times 10^{17} \, \text{kg/m}^3 \).

questions.question_text: What is the radius of a nucleus with mass number 16? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))
A nucleus has a binding energy of \( 127.5 \, \text{MeV} \) and mass number 16. What is its binding energy per nucleon?
questions.explanation: \( E_{bn} = \frac{E_b}{A} \). \( E_b = 127.5 \, \text{MeV} \), \( A = 16 \). \( E_{bn} = \frac{127.5}{16} \approx 7.97 \, \text{MeV} \approx 8 \, \text{MeV} \).

questions.question_text: A nucleus with mass number 28 has a binding energy of \( 224 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
A nucleus with mass number 18 has a binding energy of \( 144 \, \text{MeV} \). What is its binding energy per nucleon?
What is the primary factor limiting the size of stable nuclei?
questions.explanation: In large nuclei, the Coulomb repulsion between protons increases with atomic number, counteracting the nuclear force and reducing stability, limiting the size of stable nuclei.

questions.question_text: How much energy is equivalent to a mass defect of \( 0.1 \, \text{u} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Energy = \( \Delta M \cdot c^2 \). \( \Delta M = 0.1 \, \text{u} \). Energy = \( 0.1 \times 931.5 = 93.15 \, \text{MeV} \).

questions.question_text: The binding energy per nucleon of a nucleus is \( 8.5 \, \text{MeV} \). What is the total binding energy for a nucleus with mass number 20?
questions.explanation: Total binding energy = \( E_{bn} \times A \). \( E_{bn} = 8.5 \, \text{MeV} \), \( A = 20 \). \( E_b = 8.5 \times 20 = 170 \, \text{MeV} \).

questions.question_text: What is the primary source of energy in stars like the Sun?
questions.explanation: The energy in stars like the Sun is generated through nuclear fusion, where light nuclei (e.g., hydrogen) combine to form heavier nuclei (e.g., helium), releasing energy due to increased binding energy per nucleon.

questions.question_text: What is the mass defect of a nucleus with binding energy \( 149.04 \, \text{MeV} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta M = \frac{E_b}{c^2} \). \( \Delta M = \frac{149.04}{931.5} \approx 0.16 \, \text{u} \).

questions.question_text: Which process involves the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two intermediate mass fragments?
questions.explanation: Nuclear fission is the process where a heavy nucleus splits into two intermediate mass fragments, releasing energy due to the higher binding energy per nucleon in the resulting nuclei.

questions.question_text: What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.005 \, \text{kg} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
What is the energy equivalent of \( 0.01 \, \text{kg} \) of matter in Joules? (Given \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
What is the mass defect of a nucleus with binding energy \( 186.3 \, \text{MeV} \)? (Given \( 1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV/c}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta M = \frac{E_b}{c^2} \). \( \Delta M = \frac{186.3}{931.5} \approx 0.2 \, \text{u} \).

questions.question_text: What is the mass number of a nucleus with radius \( 5.4 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \)? (Given \( R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{m} \))

tests.chapter: Behaviour of Perfect Gas and Kinetic Theory
tests.title: Behaviour of Perfect Gas and Kinetic Theory Chapter-Wise Test 1

questions.question_text: The mean free path of a gas is \(9 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{m}\) with a number density of \(1.0 \times 10^{25} \, \text{m}^{-3}\). What is the molecular diameter?
The mean free path of a gas molecule is \(4 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{m}\) at 2 atm. What will it be at 4 atm if temperature remains constant?
questions.explanation: \(l \propto \frac{1}{n}\), \(n \propto P\). If \(P\) doubles, \(n\) doubles, \(l\) halves. New \(l = \frac{4 \times 10^{-7}}{2} = 2 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{m}\).

questions.question_text: A gas at 1.5 atm and 300 K has a volume of 24 litres. If the temperature increases to 600 K at constant pressure, what is the new volume?
The mean free path of a gas is \(6.0 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{m}\) with a number density of \(2.0 \times 10^{25} \, \text{m}^{-3}\). What is the molecular diameter?
A solid has a molar specific heat capacity of \(25.5 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). How many degrees of freedom per atom does it have? (\(R = 8.31 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\))
questions.explanation: \(C = f \times \frac{R}{2}\), \(25.5 = f \times \frac{8.31}{2}\). \(f = \frac{25.5 \times 2}{8.31} \approx 6.14 \approx 6\).

questions.question_text: What is the total internal energy of 0.8 moles of a triatomic gas at 500 K with no vibrational modes? (\(R = 8.31 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\))
questions.explanation: Triatomic gas: 6 degrees of freedom, \(U = 3 \mu R T\). \(U = 3 \times 0.8 \times 8.31 \times 500 = 9969.6 \, \text{J} \approx 9.97 \, \text{kJ}\).

questions.question_text: A gas has a \(C_v\) of \(24.93 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). What is the ratio of specific heats (\(\gamma\))? (\(R = 8.31 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\))
How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 0.25 moles of a monatomic gas by 40 K at constant volume? (\(R = 8.31 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\))
questions.explanation: Monatomic gas: \(C_v = \frac{3}{2} R\). \(Q = \mu C_v \Delta T = 0.25 \times \frac{3}{2} \times 8.31 \times 40 = 124.65 \, \text{J} \approx 124.7 \, \text{J}\).

questions.question_text: The rms speed of a gas is 300 m/s at 150 K. At what temperature will the rms speed be 600 m/s?
A gas at 1.5 atm and 300 K has a density of \(0.72 \, \text{kg m}^{-3}\). What is its molecular mass? (\(R = 8.31 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\), 1 atm = \(1.01 \times 10^5 \, \text{Pa}\))
questions.explanation: \(P = \frac{\rho R T}{M}\), \(M = \frac{\rho R T}{P}\). \(P = 1.5 \times 1.01 \times 10^5 = 1.515 \times 10^5 \, \text{Pa}\). \(M = \frac{0.72 \times 8.31 \times 300}{1.515 \times 10^5} = 0.01185 \, \text{kg/mol} \approx 11.85 \, \text{g/mol} \approx 12 \, \text{g/mol}\).

tests.title: Behaviour of Perfect Gas and Kinetic Theory Chapter-Wise Test 2

questions.question_text: A gas at 1 atm and 273 K has a volume of 11.2 litres. If the temperature increases to 546 K at constant pressure, what is the new volume?
A gas mixture has equal numbers of nitrogen and oxygen molecules at 300 K. What is the ratio of their rms speeds? (Molecular mass: \(N_2 = 28 \, \text{u}\), \(O_2 = 32 \, \text{u}\))
questions.explanation: \(v_{\text{rms}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\), \(\frac{v_{\text{N}_2}}{v_{\text{O}_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{m_{\text{O}_2}}{m_{\text{N}_2}}}\). \(\frac{v_{\text{N}_2}}{v_{\text{O}_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{32}{28}} \approx \sqrt{1.1429} \approx 1.069\).

questions.question_text: The mean free path of a gas molecule is \(8 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{m}\) at 1 atm. What will it be at 0.25 atm if temperature remains constant?
questions.explanation: \(l \propto \frac{1}{n}\), \(n \propto P\). If \(P\) reduces to \(\frac{1}{4}\), \(n\) reduces to \(\frac{1}{4}\), \(l\) increases 4 times. New \(l = 8 \times 10^{-7} \times 4 = 3.2 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m}\).

questions.question_text: The rms speed of argon molecules is 430 m/s at 300 K. What is the rms speed of neon molecules at the same temperature? (Atomic mass: Ar = 39.9 u, Ne = 20.2 u)
questions.explanation: \(v_{\text{rms}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\), \(\frac{v_{\text{Ne}}}{v_{\text{Ar}}} = \sqrt{\frac{m_{\text{Ar}}}{m_{\text{Ne}}}}\). \(\frac{v_{\text{Ne}}}{430} = \sqrt{\frac{39.9}{20.2}} \approx \sqrt{1.975} \approx 1.405\). \(v_{\text{Ne}} = 430 \times 1.405 \approx 604 \, \text{m/s}\).

questions.question_text: A gas has a \(C_v\) of \(12.7 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). What is the ratio of specific heats (\(\gamma\))? (\(R = 8.31 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\))
A solid has a molar specific heat capacity of \(26.5 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). How many degrees of freedom per atom does it have? (\(R = 8.31 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\))
questions.explanation: \(C = f \times \frac{R}{2}\), \(26.5 = f \times \frac{8.31}{2}\). \(f = \frac{26.5 \times 2}{8.31} \approx 6.38 \approx 6\).

questions.question_text: The mean free path of a gas molecule is \(2.0 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m}\) at 0.1 atm. What will it be at 0.4 atm if temperature remains constant?
questions.explanation: \(l \propto \frac{1}{n}\), \(n \propto P\). If \(P\) increases by 4 times (\(0.1 \, \text{to} \, 0.4\)), \(n\) increases 4 times, \(l\) reduces to \(\frac{1}{4}\). New \(l = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-6}}{4} = 5.0 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{m}\).

questions.question_text: A gas has a \(C_p\) of \(35.4 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). What is the ratio of specific heats (\(\gamma\))? (\(R = 8.31 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\))
A solid has a molar specific heat capacity of \(24.4 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). How many degrees of freedom per atom does it have? (\(R = 8.31 \, \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\))
questions.explanation: \(C = f \times \frac{R}{2}\), \(24.4 = f \times \frac{8.31}{2}\). \(f = \frac{24.4 \times 2}{8.31} \approx 5.87 \approx 6\).
