questions.explanation: The existence of a threshold frequency, below which no emission occurs regardless of intensity, contradicts the wave theory’s continuous energy absorption model.

questions.question_text: The work function of a metal is \( 1.8 \, \text{eV} \). What is the threshold frequency for this metal? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( 1 \, \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))
The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass \( 3.0 \times 10^{-30} \, \text{kg} \) moving at \( 1.0 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \) is:

An electron is accelerated through \( 50 \, \text{V} \). What is its de Broglie wavelength? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
questions.explanation: \( K = e V = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 50 = 8.0 \times 10^{-18} \, \text{J} \). \( p = \sqrt{2 m K} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 8.0 \times 10^{-18}} \approx 3.816 \times 10^{-24} \, \text{kg m/s} \). \( \lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{3.816 \times 10^{-24}} \approx 1.737 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m} = 0.1737 \, \text{nm} \).

questions.question_text: The work function of a metal is \( 3.0 \, \text{eV} \). Light of frequency \( 8.0 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \) is incident on it. What is the stopping potential? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))

A \( 30 \, \text{kV} \) X-ray tube produces X-rays. What is the minimum wavelength of the emitted X-rays? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
questions.explanation: Energy \( E = e V = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 30 \times 10^3 = 4.8 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{J} \). \( \lambda_{\min} = \frac{h c}{E} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{4.8 \times 10^{-15}} \approx 4.14 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} = 0.0414 \, \text{nm} \).

questions.question_text: Light of wavelength \( 300 \, \text{nm} \) produces a stopping potential of \( 1.5 \, \text{V} \). What is the work function of the metal in eV? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))

tests.title: Dual Nature of Matter Chapter-Wise Test 3

questions.question_text: A light source emits \( 6.0 \times 10^{15} \) photons per second with a power of \( 3.0 \, \text{mW} \). What is the energy of each photon in joules?
A photon’s energy is \( 3.0 \, \text{eV} \). What is its momentum? (Take \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \), \( 1 \, \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))
questions.explanation: \( E = 3.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 4.8 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \). For a photon, \( p = \frac{E}{c} = \frac{4.8 \times 10^{-19}}{3 \times 10^8} = 1.6 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg m/s} \).

questions.question_text: The maximum speed of photoelectrons is \( 7.0 \times 10^5 \, \text{m/s} \). What is the maximum kinetic energy in joules? (Take \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \))
questions.explanation: \( K_{\max} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\max}^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times (7.0 \times 10^5)^2 \). \( K_{\max} = \frac{1}{2} \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 4.9 \times 10^{11} \approx 2.231 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is \( 2.5 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \). What is the stopping potential? (Take \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
Why do macroscopic objects not exhibit measurable wave-like properties according to de Broglie’s hypothesis?
questions.explanation: The de Broglie wavelength \( \lambda = \frac{h}{p} \) is extremely small for macroscopic objects due to their large momentum, making wave effects negligible.

questions.question_text: Light of frequency \( 7.5 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \) produces a stopping potential of \( 0.9 \, \text{V} \). What is the work function in eV? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \))

The maximum speed of photoelectrons is \( 6.0 \times 10^5 \, \text{m/s} \) when light of wavelength \( 400 \, \text{nm} \) is used. What is the work function in eV? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \), \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \))
Which process allows electrons to escape from a metal surface when illuminated by light of suitable frequency?
questions.explanation: Photoelectric emission occurs when light of sufficient frequency provides energy to overcome the work function, ejecting electrons.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the minimum energy required for an electron to escape from a metal surface?
questions.explanation: The minimum energy required for an electron to escape from a metal surface is called the work function, denoted as \( \phi_0 \).

questions.question_text: In the photoelectric effect, what happens to the photocurrent when the intensity of incident light increases, keeping frequency constant?
questions.explanation: The photocurrent increases linearly with intensity because more photons eject more electrons per second, while frequency affects energy, not number.

tests.title: Dual Nature of Matter Chapter-Wise Test 4

questions.question_text: Light of frequency \( 6.5 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \) is incident on a metal with work function \( 2.3 \, \text{eV} \). What is the maximum kinetic energy in eV? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \))

The work function of a metal is \( 2.4 \, \text{eV} \). Light of wavelength \( 350 \, \text{nm} \) is incident on it. What is the maximum speed of emitted electrons? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \), \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \))
Which of the following observations contradicts the wave theory of light in the photoelectric effect?
questions.explanation: The wave theory predicts energy absorption over time, but photoelectric emission is instantaneous (within \( 10^{-9} \, \text{s} \)), supporting the photon model.

questions.question_text: Which phenomenon provided evidence that light behaves as if it consists of quanta of energy?
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect demonstrated that light interacts with matter in discrete packets (photons), explained by Einstein’s quantum theory.

questions.question_text: The threshold frequency of a metal is \( 5.0 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \). What is the stopping potential for light of frequency \( 7.0 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \)? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
A photon of frequency \( 7.0 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \) has what momentum? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
The de Broglie wavelength of an electron is \( 0.15 \, \text{nm} \). What is its speed? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \))

A photon of energy \( 2.5 \, \text{eV} \) strikes a metal surface. The stopping potential is \( 0.8 \, \text{V} \). What is the maximum speed of emitted electrons? (Take \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \))
questions.explanation: \( K_{\max} = e V_0 = 0.8 \, \text{eV} = 0.8 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 1.28 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \). \( K_{\max} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\max}^2 \Rightarrow v_{\max} = \sqrt{\frac{2 K_{\max}}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.28 \times 10^{-19}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}} \approx 5.3 \times 10^5 \, \text{m/s} \).

questions.question_text: A particle of mass \( 2.5 \times 10^{-29} \, \text{kg} \) has a de Broglie wavelength of \( 0.5 \, \text{nm} \). What is its speed?

Light of frequency \( 7.5 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \) is incident on a metal with work function \( 2.5 \, \text{eV} \). What is the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons in eV? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( 1 \, \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))

tests.title: Dual Nature of Matter Chapter-Wise Test 5

questions.question_text: What is the nature of the relationship between the stopping potential and the frequency of incident light in the photoelectric effect?
questions.explanation: The stopping potential \( V_0 \) varies linearly with frequency (\( e V_0 = h v - \phi_0 \)), as shown by experimental graphs and Einstein’s equation.

questions.question_text: The threshold frequency of a metal is \( 3.0 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \). What is the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted by light of wavelength \( 500 \, \text{nm} \)? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
What characteristic of light quanta (photons) is directly proportional to their frequency?
questions.explanation: The energy of a photon is given by \( E = h v \), making it directly proportional to frequency.

questions.question_text: A photon has a momentum of \( 1.8 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg m/s} \). What is its wavelength? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \))
Light of wavelength \( 400 \, \text{nm} \) is incident on a metal with a stopping potential of \( 1.2 \, \text{V} \). What is the threshold wavelength? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))
Which property of incident light determines the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons, assuming the metal remains the same?
questions.explanation: According to Einstein’s photoelectric equation, \( K_{\max} = h v - \phi_0 \), the maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency of the incident light.

questions.question_text: A light source emits photons of energy \( 4.5 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \) at a rate of \( 2.0 \times 10^{16} \) photons per second. What is the wavelength of the light? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
questions.explanation: \( \lambda = \frac{h c}{E} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{4.5 \times 10^{-19}} = 4.42 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{m} = 442 \, \text{nm} \).

questions.question_text: A photon of wavelength \( 300 \, \text{nm} \) is incident on a metal. What is its energy in eV? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))
questions.explanation: Energy \( E = \frac{h c}{\lambda} \). \( E = \frac{1240}{300} \approx 4.13 \, \text{eV} \).

questions.question_text: Light of frequency \( 6.2 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \) is incident on a metal with work function \( 2.1 \, \text{eV} \). What is the stopping potential? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
Which of the following particles was historically identified as a universal constituent of matter through cathode ray experiments?
questions.explanation: J.J. Thomson’s experiments with cathode rays led to the discovery of electrons as fundamental negatively charged particles in matter.

tests.title: Dual Nature of Matter Chapter-Wise Test 6

questions.question_text: A light source emits photons of energy \( 3.0 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \) at a rate of \( 4.0 \times 10^{15} \) photons per second. What is the power emitted?
questions.explanation: Power \( P = N \times E \). \( P = 4.0 \times 10^{15} \times 3.0 \times 10^{-19} = 1.2 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{W} = 1.2 \, \text{mW} \).

questions.question_text: A particle of mass \( 1.0 \times 10^{-28} \, \text{kg} \) has the same momentum as a photon of wavelength \( 600 \, \text{nm} \). What is its speed? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \))
questions.explanation: Photon momentum \( p = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{600 \times 10^{-9}} = 1.105 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg m/s} \). For particle, \( p = m v \Rightarrow v = \frac{p}{m} = \frac{1.105 \times 10^{-27}}{1.0 \times 10^{-28}} = 1.105 \times 10^1 = 11.05 \, \text{m/s} \).

questions.question_text: The stopping potential for photoelectrons emitted from a metal surface is \( 1.2 \, \text{V} \). What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in joules? (Take \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
questions.explanation: Maximum kinetic energy \( K_{\max} = e V_0 \). \( K_{\max} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.2 = 1.92 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: In the photoelectric effect, what does the saturation current depend on, assuming a fixed frequency above the threshold?
questions.explanation: Saturation current depends on the intensity of light, as it determines the number of photons and thus the number of photoelectrons emitted per second.

questions.question_text: A light source emits \( 5.0 \times 10^{15} \) photons per second with a power of \( 2.0 \, \text{mW} \). What is the energy of each photon in joules?
questions.explanation: Power \( P = N \times E \). \( E = \frac{P}{N} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}{5.0 \times 10^{15}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A light source emits \( 3.0 \times 10^{16} \) photons per second with a power of \( 9.0 \, \text{mW} \). What is the wavelength of the light? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
The maximum frequency of X-rays from a \( 35 \, \text{kV} \) tube is: (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))

The threshold frequency of a metal is \( 6.0 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \). What is its work function in eV? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( 1 \, \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))

The minimum wavelength of X-rays from a \( 15 \, \text{kV} \) tube is: (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
questions.explanation: \( E = e V = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 15 \times 10^3 = 2.4 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{J} \). \( \lambda_{\min} = \frac{h c}{E} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{2.4 \times 10^{-15}} \approx 8.2875 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} = 0.082875 \, \text{nm} \).

questions.question_text: The work function of a metal is \( 2.0 \, \text{eV} \). What is the threshold frequency for photoelectric emission from this metal? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( 1 \, \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \))
questions.explanation: Work function \( \phi_0 = 2.0 \, \text{eV} = 2.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \). Threshold frequency \( v_0 = \frac{\phi_0}{h} = \frac{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} \approx 4.83 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \).

tests.title: Dual Nature of Matter Chapter-Wise Test 7

questions.question_text: A photon has a momentum of \( 2.0 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg m/s} \). What is its energy in joules? (Take \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
questions.explanation: For a photon, \( p = \frac{E}{c} \). \( E = p c = 2.0 \times 10^{-27} \times 3 \times 10^8 = 6.0 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Light of wavelength \( 400 \, \text{nm} \) produces photoelectrons with a stopping potential of \( 0.8 \, \text{V} \) from a metal. What is the work function of the metal in eV? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))
questions.explanation: Photon energy \( E = \frac{h c}{\lambda} = \frac{1240}{400} = 3.1 \, \text{eV} \). \( K_{\max} = e V_0 = 0.8 \, \text{eV} \). \( \phi_0 = E - K_{\max} = 3.1 - 0.8 = 2.3 \, \text{eV} \).

questions.question_text: A particle of mass \( 1.5 \times 10^{-30} \, \text{kg} \) has the same momentum as a photon of wavelength \( 500 \, \text{nm} \). What is its speed? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \))
questions.explanation: Photon momentum \( p = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{500 \times 10^{-9}} = 1.326 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg m/s} \). \( v = \frac{p}{m} = \frac{1.326 \times 10^{-27}}{1.5 \times 10^{-30}} = 8.84 \times 10^2 = 884 \, \text{m/s} \).

questions.question_text: A photon has a wavelength of \( 200 \, \text{nm} \). What is its momentum? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \))
The threshold wavelength of a metal is \( 620 \, \text{nm} \). What is the work function in eV? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))
A photon has a wavelength of \( 250 \, \text{nm} \). What is its energy in joules? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \))
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{h c}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{250 \times 10^{-9}} = 7.974 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: The work function of a metal is \( 1.5 \, \text{eV} \). Light of wavelength \( 400 \, \text{nm} \) is incident on it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons in eV? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))

An electron moves with a speed of \( 3.0 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \). What is its de Broglie wavelength? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \))
questions.explanation: Momentum \( p = m v = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 3.0 \times 10^6 = 2.733 \times 10^{-24} \, \text{kg m/s} \). \( \lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2.733 \times 10^{-24}} \approx 2.425 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m} = 0.2425 \, \text{nm} \).

questions.question_text: A photon of frequency \( 8.0 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \) has what energy in joules? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \))

The maximum speed of photoelectrons emitted from a surface is \( 5.0 \times 10^5 \, \text{m/s} \). What is the stopping potential? (Take \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))

tests.title: Dual Nature of Matter Chapter-Wise Test 8

questions.question_text: What happens to photoelectric emission if the frequency of incident light is below the threshold frequency?
questions.explanation: No photoelectric emission occurs if the frequency is below the threshold frequency, as the photon energy (\( h v \)) is less than the work function (\( \phi_0 \)).

questions.question_text: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass \( 5.0 \times 10^{-30} \, \text{kg} \) moving at \( 2.0 \times 10^5 \, \text{m/s} \) is:
questions.explanation: Momentum \( p = m v = 5.0 \times 10^{-30} \times 2.0 \times 10^5 = 1.0 \times 10^{-24} \, \text{kg m/s} \). \( \lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{1.0 \times 10^{-24}} = 6.63 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m} = 0.663 \, \text{nm} \).

questions.question_text: The threshold frequency of a metal is \( 4.8 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \). What is the maximum kinetic energy for light of frequency \( 6.8 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \)? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \))
The maximum frequency of X-rays produced by a \( 20 \, \text{kV} \) tube is: (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
questions.explanation: Energy \( E = e V = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 20 \times 10^3 = 3.2 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{J} \). \( v_{\max} = \frac{E}{h} = \frac{3.2 \times 10^{-15}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} \approx 4.83 \times 10^{18} \, \text{Hz} \).

questions.question_text: The threshold wavelength for a metal is \( 600 \, \text{nm} \). What is its work function in eV? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))
questions.explanation: Work function \( \phi_0 = \frac{h c}{\lambda_0} \). \( \phi_0 = \frac{1240}{600} \approx 2.07 \, \text{eV} \).

questions.question_text: The minimum wavelength of X-rays from a \( 25 \, \text{kV} \) tube is: (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
questions.explanation: \( E = e V = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 25 \times 10^3 = 4.0 \times 10^{-15} \, \text{J} \). \( \lambda_{\min} = \frac{h c}{E} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{4.0 \times 10^{-15}} = 4.9725 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m} \approx 0.0497 \, \text{nm} \).

questions.question_text: The momentum of a photon is \( 2.21 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{kg m/s} \). What is its wavelength? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \))
questions.explanation: For a photon, \( p = \frac{h}{\lambda} \). \( \lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2.21 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 3.0 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{m} = 300 \, \text{nm} \).

questions.question_text: Light of wavelength \( 450 \, \text{nm} \) is incident on a metal with work function \( 1.9 \, \text{eV} \). What is the maximum kinetic energy in eV? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{h c}{\lambda} = \frac{1240}{450} \approx 2.756 \, \text{eV} \). \( K_{\max} = E - \phi_0 = 2.756 - 1.9 \approx 0.856 \, \text{eV} \).

questions.question_text: Which scientist proposed that moving particles of matter exhibit wave-like properties?
questions.explanation: Louis de Broglie proposed the wave-particle duality of matter, suggesting that particles like electrons have associated wavelengths (\( \lambda = \frac{h}{p} \)).

questions.question_text: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron is \( 0.2 \, \text{nm} \). What is its speed? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \))

tests.title: Dual Nature of Matter Chapter-Wise Test 9

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key feature of photons that distinguishes them from charged particles?
questions.explanation: Photons are electrically neutral and thus not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, unlike charged particles such as electrons.

questions.question_text: A light beam emits \( 2.5 \times 10^{15} \) photons per second, each of energy \( 4.0 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J} \). What is the power of the beam?
questions.explanation: Power \( P = N \times E \). \( P = 2.5 \times 10^{15} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-19} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{W} = 1.0 \, \text{mW} \).

questions.question_text: Light of frequency \( 8.5 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \) is incident on a metal with threshold frequency \( 4.0 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \). What is the stopping potential? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
Which of the following properties of photoelectrons is independent of the intensity of incident light?
questions.explanation: The maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency (\( K_{\max} = h v - \phi_0 \)), not intensity, which only affects the number of electrons.

questions.question_text: The stopping potential for photoelectrons from a metal is \( 2.0 \, \text{V} \) when illuminated with light of frequency \( 6.0 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \). What is the work function in eV? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \))
The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass \( 2.0 \times 10^{-30} \, \text{kg} \) moving at \( 1.5 \times 10^6 \, \text{m/s} \) is:
Light of wavelength \( 500 \, \text{nm} \) is incident on a metal with stopping potential \( 0.6 \, \text{V} \). What is the threshold wavelength? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))
What is the significance of the stopping potential in the photoelectric effect?
questions.explanation: The stopping potential is the minimum negative voltage that stops the most energetic photoelectrons, directly related to their maximum kinetic energy (\( e V_0 = K_{\max} \)).

questions.question_text: Light of wavelength \( 450 \, \text{nm} \) is incident on a metal. The stopping potential is \( 0.5 \, \text{V} \). What is the threshold wavelength of the metal? (Take \( h c = 1240 \, \text{eV nm} \))
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{h c}{\lambda} = \frac{1240}{450} \approx 2.76 \, \text{eV} \). \( K_{\max} = e V_0 = 0.5 \, \text{eV} \). \( \phi_0 = E - K_{\max} = 2.76 - 0.5 = 2.26 \, \text{eV} \). \( \lambda_0 = \frac{h c}{\phi_0} = \frac{1240}{2.26} \approx 549 \, \text{nm} \).

questions.question_text: Light of frequency \( 5.5 \times 10^{14} \, \text{Hz} \) produces photoelectrons with a maximum speed of \( 4.0 \times 10^5 \, \text{m/s} \). What is the work function in eV? (Take \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \), \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{kg} \))

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 1

questions.question_text: A closed surface has a net flux of \( 6.78 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). What is the charge enclosed?
questions.explanation: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( q = \phi \varepsilon_0 = 6.78 \times 10^5 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} = 6 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} = 6 \, \mu\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A uniform field \( E = 7 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the z-axis. What is the flux through a circle of radius 25 cm in the xy-plane?
questions.explanation: Area: \( A = \pi (0.25)^2 = 0.1963 \, \text{m}^2 \). Flux: \( \phi = E A \cos 0^\circ = 7 \times 10^3 \times 0.1963 = 1374 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 11 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the center of a cube of edge 45 cm. What is the total flux through the cube?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( \phi = \frac{11 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 1.242 \times 10^6 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A glass rod loses \( 6.4 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \) of charge when rubbed with silk. How many electrons were transferred from it?
questions.explanation: Losing charge means electrons are removed, so charge is positive. \( q = n e \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{6.4 \times 10^{-8}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 4 \times 10^{11} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +8 \, \mu\text{C}, -4 \, \mu\text{C}, +2 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1.8 m. What is the force magnitude on \( +8 \, \mu\text{C} \)?
Which principle underlies the fact that the electric field due to a system of charges can be analyzed by considering each charge independently?
questions.explanation: The superposition principle allows the total electric field to be the vector sum of fields from individual charges, assuming each field is unaffected by others. This linearity stems from the nature of electrostatic forces, enabling independent analysis.

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +5 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -7 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 35 cm apart. What is the electric field magnitude at the midpoint?
questions.explanation: Midpoint distance = 17.5 cm = 0.175 m. \( E_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.175)^2} = 1.47 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -7 \, \mu\text{C} \)). \( E_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{7 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.175)^2} = 2.06 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -7 \, \mu\text{C} \)). Net \( E = 1.47 \times 10^6 + 2.06 \times 10^6 = 3.53 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane remain unaffected by the distance from the plane?
questions.explanation: The infinite extent of the plane ensures uniform field distribution, as contributions from all parts balance out distance effects. Gauss’s law confirms the field is \( \sigma/2\varepsilon_0 \), independent of distance due to symmetry.

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 22 cm has \( q = 15 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 26 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{15 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.26)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{15 \times 10^{-6}}{0.0676} = 1.996 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Three equal charges \( q = 3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1 m. What is the electric field at the centroid?
questions.explanation: Distance from vertex to centroid: \( r = \frac{l}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \, \text{m} \). \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{(1/\sqrt{3})^2} = 81 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) per charge. By symmetry (all \( +q \)), vectors cancel, so \( E_{\text{net}} = 0 \).

questions.question_text: Two point charges \( -3 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) and \( 5 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) are 80 cm apart in vacuum. What is the magnitude of the force between them?
A dipole with charges \( +4 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 2 mm is in a field \( 7 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) at 30°. What is the torque?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a = 4 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 8 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \). Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta = 8 \times 10^{-9} \times 7 \times 10^4 \times \sin 30^\circ = 5.6 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.5 = 2.8 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with moment \( p = 5 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 60° to a uniform field \( E = 4 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque magnitude?
questions.explanation: Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 5 \times 10^{-9} \times 4 \times 10^4 \times \sin 60^\circ = 20 \times 10^{-5} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 1.732 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 7 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 45° to a field \( E = 4 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque?
questions.explanation: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 7 \times 10^{-9} \times 4 \times 10^4 \times \sin 45^\circ = 28 \times 10^{-5} \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 1.98 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: What explains why the electric field due to a dipole can be zero at certain points along its equatorial plane?
questions.explanation: In the equatorial plane, the fields from the dipole’s positive and negative charges are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction at the midpoint. Their vector sum cancels out, resulting in a zero field at that specific location.

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 2

questions.question_text: What ensures that the electric field is always radial for an infinitely long, uniformly charged wire?
questions.explanation: The cylindrical symmetry of an infinitely long, uniformly charged wire means the field must be radial (perpendicular to the wire) and uniform along its length. Any non-radial component would violate symmetry, and Gauss’s law confirms this radial dependence.

questions.question_text: What principle explains why the net electric flux through a closed surface depends only on the charge enclosed within it?
questions.explanation: Gauss’s law states that the electric flux through a closed surface is proportional to the net charge enclosed, regardless of its position or distribution inside. External charges do not contribute to the net flux due to the inverse-square nature of the field.

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge produces \( E = 3.6 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at 5 cm. What is \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \). \( 3.6 \times 10^5 = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times \lambda}{0.05} \). \( \lambda = \frac{3.6 \times 10^5 \times 0.05}{18 \times 10^9} = 1 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +7 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 60 cm apart. What is the electric field magnitude at the midpoint?
questions.explanation: Midpoint distance = 30 cm = 0.3 m. \( E_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{7 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.3)^2} = 7 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \)). \( E_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.3)^2} = 5 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \)). Net \( E = 7 \times 10^5 + 5 \times 10^5 = 1.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( E = 4.5 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at 4 cm. What is \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \). \( 4.5 \times 10^5 = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times \lambda}{0.04} \). \( \lambda = \frac{4.5 \times 10^5 \times 0.04}{18 \times 10^9} = 1 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \).

questions.question_text: A uniform field \( E = 7 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the z-axis. What is the flux through a circle of radius 10 cm in the xy-plane?
questions.explanation: Area: \( A = \pi (0.1)^2 = 0.0314 \, \text{m}^2 \). Flux: \( \phi = E A \cos 0^\circ = 7 \times 10^3 \times 0.0314 = 219.8 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A plane sheet has \( \sigma = 8.85 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field near it?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{8.85 \times 10^{-11}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 32 cm has \( q = 9 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 25 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Inside shell (\( r < R \)): \( E = 0 \) (Gauss’s law).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( 7 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 4 m along the y-axis?
Three charges \( +6 \, \mu\text{C}, -3 \, \mu\text{C}, +3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1 m. What is the force magnitude on \( +6 \, \mu\text{C} \)?
questions.explanation: \( F_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 3 \times 10^{-12}}{1^2} = 0.162 \, \text{N} \) (attractive). \( F_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 3 \times 10^{-12}}{1^2} = 0.162 \, \text{N} \) (repulsive). Angle 60°. Net \( F = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2 F_1 F_2 \cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{0.162^2 + 0.162^2 + 0.026244} = 0.28 \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: What ensures that the electric field outside a uniformly charged spherical shell behaves as if all charge were concentrated at its center?
questions.explanation: Spherical symmetry and Gauss’s law show that for a uniform spherical shell, the field outside depends only on the total charge and distance, mimicking a point charge at the center. Inside, symmetry cancels the field, leaving zero.

questions.question_text: A body loses \( 8.0 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \) of charge when rubbed. How many electrons were transferred from it?
questions.explanation: Losing charge means electrons are removed, so charge is positive. \( q = n e \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{8.0 \times 10^{-8}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 5 \times 10^{11} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 18 cm has a charge of \( 12 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 20 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell (\( r > R \)): \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( q = 12 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \), \( r = 0.2 \, \text{m} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{12 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.2)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{12 \times 10^{-6}}{0.04} = 2.7 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( 15 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 6 m along the y-axis?
A body loses \( 3.2 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \) of charge when rubbed. How many electrons were transferred from it?
questions.explanation: Losing charge means electrons are removed, so charge is positive. \( q = n e \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{3.2 \times 10^{-8}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2 \times 10^{11} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 3

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +10 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 50 cm apart. What is the distance from \( +10 \, \mu\text{C} \) where the electric field is zero?
Why does the electric field due to an electric dipole decrease with distance as \( 1/r^3 \) rather than \( 1/r^2 \) as for a single charge?
questions.explanation: For a dipole, the net charge is zero, and the field results from the combined effect of two equal and opposite charges. At large distances, the fields from each charge partially cancel, leading to a faster fall-off (\( 1/r^3 \)) compared to the \( 1/r^2 \) dependence of a single charge.

questions.question_text: A closed surface has a net flux of \( 5.65 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). What is the charge enclosed?
questions.explanation: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( q = \phi \varepsilon_0 = 5.65 \times 10^5 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} = 5 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} = 5 \, \mu\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +8 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -2 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 20 cm apart. What is the distance from \( +8 \, \mu\text{C} \) where the electric field is zero?
Why does the electric field near an infinite charged plane not depend on the nature of the material it’s made of?
questions.explanation: The field depends only on the surface charge density (\( \sigma/2\varepsilon_0 \)), as derived from Gauss’s law for an infinite plane. The material affects charge distribution, but for a given \( \sigma \), the field is universal, assuming infinite extent and uniformity.

questions.question_text: Why do electric field lines tend to be closer together near regions of high charge density?
questions.explanation: High charge density produces a stronger electric field. The convention of field lines dictates that their closeness (density) reflects field strength, so they cluster near regions where the charge per unit area or volume is greater.

questions.question_text: A dipole with charges \( +7 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -7 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 3 mm is in a field \( 4 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) at 60°. What is the torque?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a = 7 \times 10^{-6} \times 3 \times 10^{-3} = 2.1 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C m} \). Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta = 2.1 \times 10^{-8} \times 4 \times 10^4 \times \sin 60^\circ = 8.4 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 7.28 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: Why does an electric dipole experience a torque but no net force when placed in a uniform electric field?
questions.explanation: In a uniform field, the forces on the positive and negative charges of the dipole are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, resulting in no net force. However, these forces act at different points, creating a torque that tends to align the dipole with the field.

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 16 cm has an electric field of \( 5 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 40 cm from its center. What is the charge?
Two charges \( +9 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 70 cm apart. What is the electric field magnitude at the midpoint?
questions.explanation: Midpoint distance = 35 cm = 0.35 m. \( E_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.35)^2} = 6.61 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \)). \( E_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.35)^2} = 2.2 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \)). Net \( E = 6.61 \times 10^5 + 2.2 \times 10^5 = 8.81 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 23 cm has a surface charge density of \( 35 \, \mu\text{C/m}^2 \). What is the total charge?
questions.explanation: Surface area: \( A = 4 \pi r^2 = 4 \pi (0.23)^2 = 0.2116 \pi \, \text{m}^2 \). Charge: \( q = \sigma A = 35 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.2116 \pi = 2.33 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at \( x = 3 \, \text{m} \)?
A charge of \( 3 \, \mu\text{C} \) is enclosed in a cube of edge 15 cm. What is the flux through one face?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 3.39 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). Flux per face (6 faces): \( \phi_{\text{face}} = \frac{3.39 \times 10^5}{6} = 5.65 \times 10^4 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: What is the total charge of a system containing three charges: \( +3 \, \mu\text{C} \), \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \), and \( +2 \, \mu\text{C} \)?
questions.explanation: Total charge is the algebraic sum (additivity of charges). \( q_{\text{total}} = (+3 \times 10^{-6}) + (-5 \times 10^{-6}) + (+2 \times 10^{-6}) = 3 - 5 + 2 = 0 \, \mu\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +4 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -8 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 40 cm apart. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 20 cm from each charge (forming an equilateral triangle)?
questions.explanation: \( E_1 = \frac{k |q_1|}{r^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.2)^2} = 9 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (away). \( E_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.2)^2} = 1.8 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards). Angle between \( E_1 \) and \( E_2 \) is 60°. Net \( E = \sqrt{E_1^2 + E_2^2 + 2 E_1 E_2 \cos 60^\circ} \). \( E = \sqrt{(9 \times 10^5)^2 + (1.8 \times 10^6)^2 + 2 \times 9 \times 10^5 \times 1.8 \times 10^6 \times 0.5} = 2.29 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 4

questions.question_text: A plane sheet has \( \sigma = 5.31 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field near it?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{5.31 \times 10^{-11}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 3 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +5 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 30 cm apart. What is the potential energy of the system?
questions.explanation: Potential energy: \( U = k \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} \). \( U = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{(5 \times 10^{-6}) \times (-5 \times 10^{-6})}{0.3} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{-25 \times 10^{-12}}{0.3} = -0.75 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: How many electrons must be added to a neutral body to give it a charge of \( -8 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \)?
A charge of \( 5 \, \mu\text{C} \) is enclosed in a cube of edge 30 cm. What is the flux through one face?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 5.65 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). Flux per face (6 faces): \( \phi_{\text{face}} = \frac{5.65 \times 10^5}{6} = 9.42 \times 10^4 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with charges \( +2 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -2 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 1 mm is in a field of \( 6 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) at 90°. What is the torque?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 1 \times 10^{-3} = 2 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \). Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta = 2 \times 10^{-9} \times 6 \times 10^4 \times \sin 90^\circ = 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( -2 \, \mu\text{C} \) produces a flux of \( -2.26 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \) through a spherical surface. What is the radius of the surface?
questions.explanation: Flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \), \( q = -2 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \), \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2/\text{Nm}^2 \). \( \phi = \frac{-2 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = -2.26 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \), matches given flux, so radius is irrelevant (total flux is constant). Question likely tests understanding; flux is independent of radius.

questions.question_text: What fundamental concept explains why the electric field just outside a charged conductor is perpendicular to its surface?
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero. If the field just outside had a tangential component, charges would move along the surface, contradicting equilibrium. Thus, the field must be normal to the surface.

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a charged insulator depend on the distribution of charges within it?
questions.explanation: Fixed charges in an insulator create a field based on their spatial arrangement. Gauss’s law shows the field at a point depends on the enclosed charge, which varies with position due to the immovable nature of the charges.

questions.question_text: A uniform field \( E = 8 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the y-axis. What is the flux through a circle of radius 15 cm in the xz-plane at 30° to the y-axis?
questions.explanation: Area: \( A = \pi (0.15)^2 = 0.0707 \, \text{m}^2 \). Flux: \( \phi = E A \cos 30^\circ = 8 \times 10^3 \times 0.0707 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 489.7 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 30 cm has a charge of \( 18 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 36 cm from the center?
An infinite line charge has a linear charge density \( \lambda = 2 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at 5 cm from the wire?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\lambda}{2 \pi \varepsilon_0 r} \), \( k = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \), so \( \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0} = 4 \pi \times 9 \times 10^9 \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{2 \pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.05} = 7.19 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). Or, \( E = \frac{2k\lambda}{r} = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-6}}{0.05} = 7.2 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 14 cm has an electric field of \( 7 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 28 cm from its center. What is the charge?
Three charges \( +7 \, \mu\text{C}, -5 \, \mu\text{C}, +3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 2 m. What is the force magnitude on \( +7 \, \mu\text{C} \)?
A uniform field \( E = 5 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the x-axis. What is the net flux through a cube of side 30 cm with faces parallel to coordinate planes?
questions.explanation: Flux through face at \( x = 0 \): \( \phi = E \times A = 5 \times 10^3 \times (0.3)^2 = 450 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \) (inward). Flux through face at \( x = 0.3 \): \( 450 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \) (outward). Net flux: \( 450 - 450 = 0 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \) (no charge enclosed).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 11 cm has \( q = 5 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 9 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Inside shell (\( r < R \)): \( E = 0 \) (Gauss’s law).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 5

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +4 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 30 cm apart. What is the electric field at a point 15 cm from \( +4 \, \mu\text{C} \) along the line joining them?
questions.explanation: Distance from \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} = 15 \, \text{cm} = 0.15 \, \text{m} \). \( E_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.15)^2} = 1.6 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (away). \( E_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.15)^2} = 2.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards). Net \( E = 2.4 \times 10^6 - 1.6 \times 10^6 = 8 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \)).

questions.question_text: What explains why an electric dipole aligns with an external field when free to rotate?
questions.explanation: The torque on a dipole (\( \tau = pE \sin \theta \)) acts to minimize potential energy, aligning the dipole with the field (where \( \theta = 0 \), torque = 0). This rotational force drives the dipole to a stable orientation parallel to the field.

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +4 \, \mu\text{C}, -2 \, \mu\text{C}, +5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1.2 m. What is the force magnitude on \( +4 \, \mu\text{C} \)?
A charge \( 6 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the center of a cube of edge 20 cm. What is the total electric flux through the cube?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( \phi = \frac{6 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 6.78 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole has charges \( +q = 3 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -q = -3 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 2 mm. What is the dipole moment?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a \), where \( 2a = 2 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{m} \), \( q = 3 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \). \( p = 3 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 6 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \).

questions.question_text: Two point charges \( 8 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) and \( -4 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) are 60 cm apart in vacuum. What is the magnitude of the force between them?
Why does the torque on an electric dipole in a uniform field depend on the sine of the angle between the dipole and the field?
questions.explanation: Torque (\( \tau = pE \sin \theta \)) arises from the couple formed by forces on the dipole’s charges. The perpendicular component of the field to the dipole axis determines the rotational effect, which is maximum at 90° and zero when aligned (sin 0° = 0).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 6 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 60° to a field \( E = 3 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque?
questions.explanation: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 6 \times 10^{-9} \times 3 \times 10^4 \times \sin 60^\circ = 18 \times 10^{-5} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 1.56 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A closed surface has a net flux of \( 4.52 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). What is the charge enclosed?
questions.explanation: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( q = \phi \varepsilon_0 = 4.52 \times 10^5 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} = 4 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} = 4 \, \mu\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A closed surface has a net flux of \( 2.26 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). What is the charge enclosed?
questions.explanation: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( q = \phi \varepsilon_0 = 2.26 \times 10^5 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} = 2 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} = 2 \, \mu\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: Two point charges \( 4 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) and \( -8 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) are 90 cm apart in vacuum. What is the magnitude of the force between them?
What ensures that the electric field outside a neutral conductor in an external field is altered by induced charges?
questions.explanation: Induced charge separation occurs as the external field polarizes the conductor, creating surface charges. These charges generate an additional field that superposes with the external field, modifying the total field outside the conductor.

questions.question_text: Which property of electric charges is responsible for the fact that charges on a conductor in equilibrium reside only on its surface?
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor must be zero. If charges existed inside, they would create a field, causing further movement. Thus, charges redistribute to the surface, where they can maintain zero internal field due to their mobility.

questions.question_text: A plastic rod gains a charge of \( -1.92 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) when rubbed. How many electrons were transferred to it?
questions.explanation: Negative charge means electrons gained. \( q = n e \), \( e = -1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{1.92 \times 10^{-7}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.2 \times 10^{12} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field due to an infinite charged sheet remain constant regardless of its thickness?
questions.explanation: For an infinite sheet, Gauss’s law shows the field depends only on the surface charge density (\( \sigma/2\varepsilon_0 \)). Thickness doesn’t affect the planar symmetry or enclosed charge per unit area, keeping the field constant.

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 6

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +3 \, \mu\text{C}, +3 \, \mu\text{C}, -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 2 m. What is the force on \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \)?
A uniform field \( E = 4 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the z-axis. What is the flux through a rectangle of 30 cm × 20 cm in the xy-plane?
questions.explanation: Area: \( A = 0.3 \times 0.2 = 0.06 \, \text{m}^2 \). Flux: \( \phi = E A \cos 0^\circ = 4 \times 10^3 \times 0.06 = 240 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 2 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the z-axis. What is the flux through a rectangle of 30 cm × 50 cm in the xy-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = 0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15 \, \text{m}^2 \) along z-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = 2 \times 10^3 \times 0.15 = 300 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with charges \( +5 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 6 mm is in a field \( 3 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) at 30°. What is the torque?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a = 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 6 \times 10^{-3} = 3 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C m} \). Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta = 3 \times 10^{-8} \times 3 \times 10^4 \times \sin 30^\circ = 9 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.5 = 4.5 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A plane sheet has \( \sigma = 2.66 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field near it?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{2.66 \times 10^{-11}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 1.5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell vanish, regardless of the position within it?
questions.explanation: Gauss’s law explains this: for a spherical shell with uniform charge, a Gaussian surface inside encloses no charge (since all charge resides on the surface). Thus, the electric flux through the Gaussian surface is zero, implying the electric field inside is zero due to symmetry.

questions.question_text: A body gains a charge of \( -1.6 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) when rubbed. How many electrons were transferred to it?
questions.explanation: Negative charge means electrons gained. \( q = n e \), \( e = -1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-7}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 1 \times 10^{12} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 20 cm has a surface charge density of \( 30 \, \mu\text{C/m}^2 \). What is the total charge?
questions.explanation: Surface area: \( A = 4 \pi r^2 = 4 \pi (0.2)^2 = 0.16 \pi \, \text{m}^2 \). Charge: \( q = \sigma A = 30 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.16 \pi = 1.507 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 25 cm has an electric field of \( 2 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 50 cm from its center. What is the charge?
A thin spherical shell of radius 31 cm has \( q = 20 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 35 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{20 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.35)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{20 \times 10^{-6}}{0.1225} = 1.469 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 9 \, \mu\text{C} \) is enclosed in a cube of edge 40 cm. What is the flux through one face?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 1.016 \times 10^6 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). Flux per face (6 faces): \( \phi_{\text{face}} = \frac{1.016 \times 10^6}{6} = 1.693 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A closed surface has a net flux of \( 3.39 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). What is the charge enclosed?
questions.explanation: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( q = \phi \varepsilon_0 = 3.39 \times 10^5 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} = 3 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} = 3 \, \mu\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with charges \( +4 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 8 mm is in a field \( 5 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) at 45°. What is the torque?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a = 4 \times 10^{-6} \times 8 \times 10^{-3} = 3.2 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C m} \). Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta = 3.2 \times 10^{-8} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times \sin 45^\circ = 1.6 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 1.13 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 7 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the center of a cube of edge 35 cm. What is the total flux through the cube?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( \phi = \frac{7 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 7.91 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A glass rod loses \( 9.6 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \) of charge when rubbed with silk. How many electrons were transferred from it?
questions.explanation: Losing charge means electrons are removed, so charge is positive. \( q = n e \), \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{9.6 \times 10^{-8}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 6 \times 10^{11} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 7

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 7 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 45° to a field \( E = 9 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque?
questions.explanation: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 7 \times 10^{-9} \times 9 \times 10^4 \times \sin 45^\circ = 63 \times 10^{-5} \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 4.45 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 20 cm has a charge of \( 14 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 25 cm from the center?
Why does the electric field due to a uniformly charged wire drop off more slowly with distance compared to a point charge?
questions.explanation: The wire’s linear charge distribution leads to a cylindrical field pattern (\( 1/r \)), as per Gauss’s law, spreading over a surface area proportional to \( r \). A point charge’s spherical spread (\( 1/r^2 \)) over \( r^2 \) results in a faster drop-off.

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 4 \, \mu\text{C} \) is placed at the center of a cube of edge 10 cm. What is the electric flux through one face?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 4.52 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). Flux through one face (cube has 6 faces): \( \phi_{\text{face}} = \frac{\phi}{6} = \frac{4.52 \times 10^5}{6} = 7.53 \times 10^4 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +q, +q, -q \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 3 m. What is the net force magnitude on \( +q \) at one vertex?
questions.explanation: Force between \( +q \) and \( +q \): \( F = \frac{k q^2}{(3)^2} = \frac{k q^2}{9} \) (repulsive). Force between \( +q \) and \( -q \): \( F = \frac{k q^2}{9} \) (attractive). Angle between forces is 60°. Resultant: \( F_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{F^2 + F^2 + 2F^2 \cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{3} F = \frac{\sqrt{3} k q^2}{9} \).

questions.question_text: Which principle explains why rubbing two neutral objects can result in one becoming positively charged and the other negatively charged?
questions.explanation: The conservation of charge ensures that the total charge remains zero. Rubbing transfers electrons from one object to another due to differing electron affinities, leaving one with a net positive charge (electron loss) and the other negative (electron gain).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +14 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 100 cm apart. What is the distance from \( +14 \, \mu\text{C} \) where the electric field is zero?
What allows the electric field to be discontinuous across a charged surface, such as a conductor’s boundary?
questions.explanation: Surface charge density creates a field discontinuity. Inside a conductor, the field is zero, while just outside, it’s proportional to the surface charge density (\( E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0 \)), as per Gauss’s law applied to a pillbox surface straddling the boundary.

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 10 cm has a surface charge density of \( 20 \, \mu\text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside its surface?
questions.explanation: For a conductor, \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{20 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 2.26 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +12 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 90 cm apart. What is the distance from \( +12 \, \mu\text{C} \) where the electric field is zero?
Two charges \( +3 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 15 cm apart. What is the force on a \( 2 \, \mu\text{C} \) charge placed at the midpoint?
questions.explanation: Electric field at midpoint: \( E_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.075)^2} = 4.8 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \)). \( E_2 = 4.8 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \)). Net \( E = 4.8 \times 10^6 + 4.8 \times 10^6 = 9.6 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \). Force: \( F = q E = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 9.6 \times 10^6 = 19.2 \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( \lambda = 8 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at 20 cm?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 8 \times 10^{-7}}{0.2} = 7.2 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 8 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the center of a cube of edge 25 cm. What is the total flux through the cube?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( \phi = \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 9.03 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A uniform field \( E = 9 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the x-axis. What is the flux through a rectangle of 15 cm × 20 cm in the yz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area: \( A = 0.15 \times 0.2 = 0.03 \, \text{m}^2 \). Flux: \( \phi = E A \cos 0^\circ = 9 \times 10^3 \times 0.03 = 270 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 5 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 90° to a field \( E = 5 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque?
questions.explanation: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 5 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times \sin 90^\circ = 25 \times 10^{-5} \times 1 = 2.5 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 8

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 3 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the y-axis. What is the flux through a square of side 60 cm in the xz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = (0.6)^2 = 0.36 \, \text{m}^2 \) along y-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = 3 \times 10^3 \times 0.36 = 1080 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 13 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the center of a cube of edge 50 cm. What is the flux through one face?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{13 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 1.468 \times 10^6 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). Flux per face (6 faces): \( \phi_{\text{face}} = \frac{1.468 \times 10^6}{6} = 2.447 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 6 cm has \( q = 5 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 8 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.08)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{0.0064} = 7.03 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a charged spherical shell remain zero even if the shell is irregular but closed?
questions.explanation: Gauss’s law applies to any closed surface: if no charge is enclosed within the shell, the net flux through a Gaussian surface inside is zero. For a conductor, charges reside on the outer surface, ensuring no field inside, regardless of shape.

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 5 cm has \( q = 2 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 3 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Inside shell (\( r < R \)): \( E = 0 \) (Gauss’s law).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( -8 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 4 m along the z-axis?
Why is the electric field inside a conductor zero when it is placed in an external electric field?
questions.explanation: In a conductor, free charges redistribute in response to an external field until the internal field cancels the external field completely. This equilibrium condition ensures no net field exists inside, as any field would cause charge motion, violating static conditions.

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field strength near a charged object increase as the density of field lines increases?
questions.explanation: The density of electric field lines represents the magnitude of the field. Closer lines indicate a stronger field because the field strength is proportional to the number of lines per unit area, a convention derived from the inverse-square law and field intensity.

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( \lambda = 6 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at 12 cm?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 6 \times 10^{-6}}{0.12} = 9 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +6 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 50 cm apart. What is the electric field magnitude at the midpoint?
questions.explanation: Midpoint distance = 25 cm = 0.25 m. \( E_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.25)^2} = 8.64 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \)). \( E_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.25)^2} = 4.32 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \)). Net \( E = 8.64 \times 10^5 + 4.32 \times 10^5 = 1.296 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 9

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 8 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the y-axis. What is the flux through a rectangle of 20 cm × 60 cm in the xz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = 0.2 \times 0.6 = 0.12 \, \text{m}^2 \) along y-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = 8 \times 10^3 \times 0.12 = 960 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( 12 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 8 m along the x-axis?
An infinite line charge has \( \lambda = 3 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at 15 cm?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 3 \times 10^{-6}}{0.15} = 3.6 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 8 cm has \( q = 4 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 6 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Inside shell (\( r < R \)): \( E = 0 \) (Gauss’s law).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 17 cm has a surface charge density of \( 15 \, \mu\text{C/m}^2 \). What is the total charge?
questions.explanation: Surface area: \( A = 4 \pi r^2 = 4 \pi (0.17)^2 = 0.1156 \pi \, \text{m}^2 \). Charge: \( q = \sigma A = 15 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.1156 \pi = 5.45 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 12 cm has a total charge of \( 9 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 15 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell (\( r > R \)): \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( q = 9 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \), \( r = 0.15 \, \text{m} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.15)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{0.0225} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: What property of electric charges allows them to be treated as scalars despite their ability to attract or repel?
questions.explanation: The additivity of charges means their total value is the algebraic sum of individual charges, treating them as scalars with magnitude and sign (positive or negative). The directional forces (attraction/repulsion) arise from field interactions, not the charge itself.

questions.question_text: What ensures that the electric field lines from a negative charge always terminate on it rather than extend to infinity?
questions.explanation: Negative charges attract positive test charges, so field lines, representing the force direction on a positive charge, point inward toward the negative charge. This attraction defines their termination, unlike positive charges where lines extend outward.

questions.question_text: A point charge \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 3 m along the y-axis?
Two charges \( +2 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( +3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 10 cm apart. What is the electric field at a point 5 cm from \( +2 \, \mu\text{C} \) along the line joining them?
questions.explanation: Distance from \( +3 \, \mu\text{C} \) = 5 cm. \( E_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.05)^2} = 7.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (away). \( E_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.05)^2} = 1.08 \times 10^7 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards). Net \( E = 1.08 \times 10^7 - 7.2 \times 10^6 = 3.6 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( +3 \, \mu\text{C} \)).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 10

questions.question_text: A uniform field \( E = 6 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the y-axis. What is the flux through a rectangle of 40 cm × 25 cm in the xz-plane at 45° to the y-axis?
questions.explanation: Area: \( A = 0.4 \times 0.25 = 0.1 \, \text{m}^2 \). Flux: \( \phi = E A \cos 45^\circ = 6 \times 10^3 \times 0.1 \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 424.26 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +12 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 60 cm apart. What is the distance from \( +12 \, \mu\text{C} \) where the electric field is zero?
A point charge \( 10 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 5 m along the z-axis?
An infinite line charge has \( E = 6.3 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at 7 cm. What is \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \). \( 6.3 \times 10^5 = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times \lambda}{0.07} \). \( \lambda = \frac{6.3 \times 10^5 \times 0.07}{18 \times 10^9} = 2.45 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +10 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -2 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 80 cm apart. What is the distance from \( +10 \, \mu\text{C} \) where the electric field is zero?
A point charge \( -9 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 6 m along the x-axis?
A conducting sphere of radius 27 cm has an electric field of \( 6 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 54 cm from its center. What is the charge?
A plastic rod gains \( 4.8 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \) of negative charge when rubbed. How many electrons were transferred to it?
questions.explanation: Negative charge means electrons are gained. \( q = n e \), \( e = -1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{4.8 \times 10^{-8}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 3 \times 10^{11} \).

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( \lambda = 1.2 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at 40 cm?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-6}}{0.4} = 5.4 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A glass rod is rubbed with silk and acquires a charge of \( +2.5 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \). How many electrons were transferred from the glass rod to the silk?
questions.explanation: Charge on glass rod is positive, so electrons are transferred from glass to silk. Charge of one electron \( e = -1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). Number of electrons: \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{2.5 \times 10^{-7}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.5625 \times 10^{12} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 11

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 26 cm has a surface charge density of \( 45 \, \mu\text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside its surface?
questions.explanation: For a conductor: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{45 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 5.08 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( -10 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 10 m along the x-axis?
Why does the electric field outside a charged conducting sphere resemble that of a point charge located at its center?
questions.explanation: The spherical symmetry of the charge distribution on the conductor’s surface ensures that the field outside behaves as if all charge were at the center, as per Gauss’s law. This symmetry simplifies the field to a radial, point-charge-like pattern.

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 22 cm has a surface charge density of \( 40 \, \mu\text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside its surface?
questions.explanation: For a conductor: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{40 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 4.52 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A plane sheet has \( \sigma = 1.77 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field near it?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{1.77 \times 10^{-11}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 1 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 8 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 30° to a field \( E = 5 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque magnitude?
questions.explanation: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 8 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times \sin 30^\circ = 8 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times 0.5 = 2 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 13 cm has a charge of \( 9 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 18 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell (\( r > R \)): \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( q = 9 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \), \( r = 0.18 \, \text{m} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.18)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{0.0324} = 2.5 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( E = 4.5 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at 8 cm. What is \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \). \( 4.5 \times 10^5 = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times \lambda}{0.08} \). \( \lambda = \frac{4.5 \times 10^5 \times 0.08}{18 \times 10^9} = 2 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \).

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has a linear charge density of \( 4 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at a distance of 8 cm?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 4 \times 10^{-6}}{0.08} = 9 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a charged conducting shell remain zero even when an external field is applied?
questions.explanation: Charges on the conductor’s surface redistribute to cancel any external field inside, creating an electrostatic shield. This shielding effect ensures the internal field is zero, as charges adjust to maintain equilibrium within the conductor.

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 12

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +11 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 80 cm apart. What is the electric field magnitude at the midpoint?
questions.explanation: Midpoint distance = 40 cm = 0.4 m. \( E_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{11 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.4)^2} = 6.1875 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \)). \( E_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.4)^2} = 2.8125 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \)). Net \( E = 6.1875 \times 10^5 + 2.8125 \times 10^5 = 9 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 24 cm has a charge of \( 16 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 30 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell (\( r > R \)): \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( q = 16 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \), \( r = 0.3 \, \text{m} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{16 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.3)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{16 \times 10^{-6}}{0.09} = 1.6 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 29 cm has a surface charge density of \( 50 \, \mu\text{C/m}^2 \). What is the total charge?
questions.explanation: Surface area: \( A = 4 \pi r^2 = 4 \pi (0.29)^2 = 0.335 \pi \, \text{m}^2 \). Charge: \( q = \sigma A = 50 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.335 \pi = 5.27 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with charges \( +3 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 5 mm is in a field \( 8 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) at 45°. What is the torque?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a = 3 \times 10^{-6} \times 5 \times 10^{-3} = 1.5 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C m} \). Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta = 1.5 \times 10^{-8} \times 8 \times 10^4 \times \sin 45^\circ = 1.2 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 8.48 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with charges \( +5 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 3 mm is in a field of \( 2 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) at 45°. What is the torque?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a = 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 3 \times 10^{-3} = 1.5 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C m} \). Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta = 1.5 \times 10^{-8} \times 2 \times 10^4 \times \sin 45^\circ = 3 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 2.12 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: What property of insulators causes charges to remain localized when applied to their surface?
questions.explanation: Insulators lack free charge carriers (e.g., electrons), preventing charge movement. Applied charges stay where they are placed due to the absence of conductivity, unlike conductors where charges redistribute freely.

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +5 \, \mu\text{C}, -5 \, \mu\text{C}, +2 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1.5 m. What is the force magnitude on \( +5 \, \mu\text{C} \)?
questions.explanation: \( F_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 5 \times 10^{-12}}{(1.5)^2} = 0.1 \, \text{N} \) (attractive). \( F_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 2 \times 10^{-12}}{(1.5)^2} = 0.04 \, \text{N} \) (repulsive).
