Angle 60°. Net \( F = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2 F_1 F_2 \cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{0.1^2 + 0.04^2 + 0.004} = 0.129 \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +5 \, \mu\text{C}, -3 \, \mu\text{C}, +4 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1.5 m. What is the force magnitude on \( +5 \, \mu\text{C} \)?
Two charges \( +8 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 40 cm apart. What is the electric field magnitude at the midpoint?
questions.explanation: Midpoint distance = 20 cm = 0.2 m. \( E_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.2)^2} = 1.8 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \)). \( E_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.2)^2} = 9 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) (towards \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \)). Net \( E = 1.8 \times 10^6 + 9 \times 10^5 = 2.7 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a charged conducting shell remain unaffected by charges placed outside it?
questions.explanation: Gauss’s law shows that the field inside depends only on enclosed charge. External charges induce surface charges on the conductor, but these adjust to cancel the external field inside, leaving it zero regardless of outside charges.

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 13

questions.question_text: What explains why the electric field outside a neutral object can be non-zero when placed in an external field?
questions.explanation: Induced charge separation occurs in a neutral object under an external field, creating dipoles or surface charges. These induced charges produce their own field, which adds to the external field, resulting in a non-zero total field outside.

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 5 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the y-axis. What is the flux through a square of side 40 cm in the xz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = (0.4)^2 = 0.16 \, \text{m}^2 \) along y-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = 5 \times 10^3 \times 0.16 = 800 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: What fundamental principle allows the electric field due to multiple charges to be calculated as the vector sum of the fields due to each charge individually?
questions.explanation: The superposition principle states that the electric field produced by multiple charges is the vector sum of the fields produced by each charge independently. This principle holds because electric forces and fields are linear and unaffected by the presence of other charges.

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 19 cm has an electric field of \( 3 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 38 cm from its center. What is the charge?
Two point charges \( 9 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) and \( -3 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) are 100 cm apart in vacuum. What is the magnitude of the force between them?
A thin spherical shell of radius 25 cm has a charge of \( 15 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 30 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell (\( r > R \)): \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( q = 15 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \), \( r = 0.3 \, \text{m} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{15 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.3)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{15 \times 10^{-6}}{0.09} = 1.5 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 4 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 30° to a field \( E = 6 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque?
questions.explanation: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 4 \times 10^{-9} \times 6 \times 10^4 \times \sin 30^\circ = 24 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.5 = 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 14 cm has a charge of \( 7 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 16 cm from the center?
Why does the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet remain constant with distance from the sheet?
questions.explanation: For an infinite plane sheet, symmetry and Gauss’s law show that the field depends only on surface charge density, not distance. The field lines are parallel and uniform, as contributions from all parts of the infinite sheet balance out distance effects.

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 17 cm has \( q = 13 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 20 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{13 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.2)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{13 \times 10^{-6}}{0.04} = 2.925 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 14

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 2 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the x-axis. What is the flux through a square of side 20 cm in the yz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = 0.04 \, \text{m}^2 \) along x-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = (2 \times 10^4) \times 0.04 = 800 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A uniform field \( E = 5 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the x-axis. What is the flux through a circle of radius 20 cm in the yz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area: \( A = \pi (0.2)^2 = 0.1256 \, \text{m}^2 \). Flux: \( \phi = E A \cos 0^\circ = 5 \times 10^3 \times 0.1256 = 628 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A body acquires a charge of \( -9.6 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \) when rubbed. How many electrons were transferred to it?
questions.explanation: Negative charge indicates electrons gained. \( q = n e \), \( e = -1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{9.6 \times 10^{-8}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 6 \times 10^{11} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 18 cm has a surface charge density of \( 25 \, \mu\text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside its surface?
questions.explanation: For a conductor: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{25 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 2.82 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge produces an electric field of \( 1.8 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at 3 cm. What is its linear charge density?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\lambda}{2 \pi \varepsilon_0 r} \), or \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \). \( 1.8 \times 10^5 = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times \lambda}{0.03} \). \( \lambda = \frac{1.8 \times 10^5 \times 0.03}{18 \times 10^9} = 3 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C/m} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +4 \, \mu\text{C}, -4 \, \mu\text{C}, +2 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1 m. What is the force magnitude on \( +4 \, \mu\text{C} \)?
questions.explanation: \( F_1 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 4 \times 10^{-12}}{1} = 0.144 \, \text{N} \) (attractive). \( F_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 2 \times 10^{-12}}{1} = 0.072 \, \text{N} \) (repulsive). Angle 60°. Net \( F = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2 F_1 F_2 \cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{0.144^2 + 0.072^2 + 0.010368} = 0.187 \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: What ensures that the electric field lines from a positive point charge always point radially outward?
questions.explanation: The positive charge generates a repulsive force on a positive test charge, as per Coulomb’s law. Due to the spherical symmetry of a point charge, the field is directed radially outward, reflecting the repulsion and symmetry of the charge distribution.

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field due to a dipole exhibit a stronger angular dependence compared to a single point charge?
questions.explanation: The dipole’s field arises from two opposite charges, creating a directional dependence. The angle between the dipole axis and the point affects the field’s magnitude and direction more significantly than a point charge’s isotropic \( 1/r^2 \) field.

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field due to a charged conducting sphere remain constant just outside its surface regardless of its radius?
questions.explanation: The field just outside a conductor is \( \sigma/\varepsilon_0 \), where \( \sigma \) is the surface charge density. For a sphere, \( \sigma = Q/(4\pi r^2) \), but the field depends only on \( \sigma \) at the surface, not \( r \), due to equilibrium conditions.

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 15 cm has an electric field of \( 4 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 30 cm from its center. What is the charge?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( 4 \times 10^3 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{q}{(0.3)^2} \). \( q = \frac{4 \times 10^3 \times 0.09}{9 \times 10^9} = 4 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 15

questions.question_text: In an experiment, a charged object is brought near a neutral conductor, causing charge separation. What phenomenon is responsible for this effect?
questions.explanation: Electrostatic induction occurs when a charged object induces a separation of charges in a neutral conductor. The electric field of the charged object attracts opposite charges and repels like charges, redistributing them without direct contact.

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( \lambda = 7 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at 25 cm?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 7 \times 10^{-7}}{0.25} = 5.04 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A uniform field \( E = 9 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the x-axis. What is the flux through a rectangle of 35 cm × 45 cm in the yz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area: \( A = 0.35 \times 0.45 = 0.1575 \, \text{m}^2 \). Flux: \( \phi = E A \cos 0^\circ = 9 \times 10^3 \times 0.1575 = 1417.5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 10 cm has \( q = 8 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 15 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.15)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{0.0225} = 3.2 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( \lambda = 9 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at 30 cm?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 9 \times 10^{-7}}{0.3} = 5.4 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field near a charged surface exhibit a sharp increase in strength compared to regions further away?
questions.explanation: The inverse-square law governs the field from charges on the surface. Near the surface, the distance \( r \) is small, making \( 1/r^2 \) large, resulting in a strong field that weakens rapidly as distance increases.

questions.question_text: Two point charges \( 6 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) and \( 10 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) are 120 cm apart in vacuum. What is the magnitude of the force between them?
A thin spherical shell of radius 28 cm has \( q = 8 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 20 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Inside shell (\( r < R \)): \( E = 0 \) (Gauss’s law).

questions.question_text: What property of the electric field allows it to exert a force on a charge without physical contact?
questions.explanation: The field’s ability to act at a distance is due to its nature as a force mediator. Generated by charges, it extends through space, influencing other charges via the force \( F = qE \), without requiring direct interaction.

questions.question_text: Two point charges \( 7 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) and \( -2 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) are 70 cm apart in vacuum. What is the magnitude of the force between them?

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 16

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( \lambda = 5 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at 10 cm?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 5 \times 10^{-7}}{0.1} = 9 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with charges \( +6 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 2 mm is in a field \( 8 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) at 60°. What is the torque?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a = 6 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 1.2 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C m} \). Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta = 1.2 \times 10^{-8} \times 8 \times 10^4 \times \sin 60^\circ = 9.6 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 8.31 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: What causes the electric field to be discontinuous across a charged surface, such as a thin sheet?
questions.explanation: The surface charge density on the sheet generates a field that changes abruptly. Gauss’s law shows the field on either side is \( \sigma/2\varepsilon_0 \), with opposite directions, resulting in a discontinuity equal to \( \sigma/\varepsilon_0 \) across the surface.

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 19 cm has \( q = 7 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 15 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Inside shell (\( r < R \)): \( E = 0 \) (Gauss’s law).

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 4 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the x-axis. What is the flux through a square of side 70 cm in the yz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = (0.7)^2 = 0.49 \, \text{m}^2 \) along x-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = 4 \times 10^3 \times 0.49 = 1960 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 6 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the z-axis. What is the flux through a square of side 50 cm in the xy-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = (0.5)^2 = 0.25 \, \text{m}^2 \) along z-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = 6 \times 10^3 \times 0.25 = 1500 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: Which property of electric field lines ensures they never intersect, even in complex charge distributions?
questions.explanation: Electric field lines represent the direction of the field at each point. If they intersected, it would imply two different field directions at the same point, which is impossible since the electric field is a unique vector quantity at any given position.

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +6 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 25 cm apart. What is the distance from \( +6 \, \mu\text{C} \) where the electric field is zero?
A dipole with charges \( +6 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) separated by 4 mm is in a field \( 5 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \) at 60°. What is the torque?
questions.explanation: Dipole moment: \( p = q \times 2a = 6 \times 10^{-6} \times 4 \times 10^{-3} = 2.4 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C m} \). Torque: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta = 2.4 \times 10^{-8} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times \sin 60^\circ = 1.2 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 1.04 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 8 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 90° to a field \( E = 6 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque?
questions.explanation: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 8 \times 10^{-9} \times 6 \times 10^4 \times \sin 90^\circ = 48 \times 10^{-5} \times 1 = 4.8 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 17

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field due to a dipole have both radial and tangential components at a general point?
questions.explanation: The dipole’s field results from two opposite charges, creating a complex pattern. At a general point, the field vectors from each charge have different directions, resolving into radial (along the line from the dipole) and tangential (perpendicular) components due to asymmetry.

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( E = 3.6 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at 10 cm. What is \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \). \( 3.6 \times 10^5 = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times \lambda}{0.1} \). \( \lambda = \frac{3.6 \times 10^5 \times 0.1}{18 \times 10^9} = 2 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( q = 5 \, \mu\text{C} \) is placed at the origin. What is the electric field magnitude at a point 2 m away along the x-axis?
questions.explanation: Electric field: \( E = \frac{k |q|}{r^2} \). \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \), \( q = 5 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \), \( r = 2 \, \text{m} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{(2)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{4} = 1.125 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 20 cm has an electric field of \( 3 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 40 cm from its center. What is its charge?
questions.explanation: For a conductor, \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \) outside. \( 3 \times 10^3 = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{q}{(0.4)^2} \). \( q = \frac{3 \times 10^3 \times 0.16}{9 \times 10^9} = 5.33 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A plastic rod gains a charge of \( -1.28 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) when rubbed. How many electrons were transferred to it?
questions.explanation: Negative charge means electrons gained. \( q = n e \), \( e = -1.6 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C} \). \( n = \frac{q}{|e|} = \frac{1.28 \times 10^{-7}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 8 \times 10^{11} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 18 cm has \( q = 12 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 22 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{12 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.22)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{12 \times 10^{-6}}{0.0484} = 2.23 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A spherical shell has a net flux of \( 1.13 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \) through it. What is the charge enclosed?
questions.explanation: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( q = \phi \varepsilon_0 = 1.13 \times 10^5 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} = 1 \, \mu\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: What characteristic of conductors allows charges to distribute uniformly over their surface when placed in an external electric field?
questions.explanation: In conductors, charges (free electrons) can move freely. In an external field, they redistribute until the internal field cancels the external field, achieving equilibrium. This results in charges residing only on the surface, distributed uniformly for a spherical conductor due to symmetry.

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 7 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the x-axis. What is the flux through a rectangle of 25 cm × 40 cm in the yz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = 0.25 \times 0.4 = 0.1 \, \text{m}^2 \) along x-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = 7 \times 10^3 \times 0.1 = 700 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( E = 6.0 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at 3 cm. What is \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \). \( 6.0 \times 10^5 = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times \lambda}{0.03} \). \( \lambda = \frac{6.0 \times 10^5 \times 0.03}{18 \times 10^9} = 1 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 18

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 30 cm has a surface charge density of \( 50 \, \mu\text{C/m}^2 \). What is the total charge on it?
questions.explanation: Surface area: \( A = 4 \pi r^2 = 4 \pi (0.3)^2 = 0.36 \pi \, \text{m}^2 \). Charge: \( q = \sigma A = 50 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.36 \pi = 5.654 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{C} \).

questions.question_text: What explains why the electric field due to a charged object can penetrate an insulator but not a conductor?
questions.explanation: Insulators lack free charges to redistribute and cancel an external field, allowing it to penetrate. Conductors, with mobile charges, redistribute them to create an opposing field, shielding the interior from penetration.

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 12 cm has \( q = 10 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 14 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.14)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{0.0196} = 4.59 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 15 cm has \( q = 6 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 10 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Inside shell (\( r < R \)): \( E = 0 \) (Gauss’s law).

questions.question_text: What ensures that the electric field inside a hollow conductor remains zero even if an external charge is placed nearby?
questions.explanation: Electrostatic shielding occurs as free charges in the conductor redistribute to cancel any external field inside. This adjustment creates an induced field that neutralizes the external influence, maintaining zero field within the hollow region.

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 9 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 90° to a field \( E = 3 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque?
questions.explanation: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 9 \times 10^{-9} \times 3 \times 10^4 \times \sin 90^\circ = 27 \times 10^{-5} \times 1 = 2.7 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: What ensures that electric field lines never cross each other in a static field configuration?
questions.explanation: The electric field has a unique direction at each point, defined by the force on a test charge. Crossing lines would imply multiple directions at one point, which is impossible in a static field where the field vector is well-defined.

questions.question_text: Two point charges \( 6 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) and \( 9 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) are 45 cm apart in air. What is the magnitude of the force between them?
Two point charges \( q_1 = 4 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( q_2 = -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) are placed 20 cm apart in vacuum. What is the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them?
A closed surface has a net flux of \( 7.91 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). What is the charge enclosed?
questions.explanation: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( q = \phi \varepsilon_0 = 7.91 \times 10^5 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} = 7 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} = 7 \, \mu\text{C} \).

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 19

questions.question_text: A plane sheet has \( \sigma = 1.416 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field near it?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{1.416 \times 10^{-10}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 8 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Why does Gauss’s law fail to determine the electric field for a finite charged object without symmetry?
questions.explanation: Gauss’s law requires a Gaussian surface with symmetry matching the charge distribution to simplify field calculation. For finite, asymmetric objects, the field varies in complex ways, making symmetry-based simplification impossible without additional methods.

questions.question_text: A plane sheet has \( \sigma = 7.08 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field near it?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{7.08 \times 10^{-11}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 12 cm has an electric field of \( 6 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 24 cm from its center. What is the charge?
A thin spherical shell of radius 16 cm has a charge of \( 11 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 20 cm from the center?
What property of electric charges explains why two objects with identical charges repel each other?
questions.explanation: The polarity of charge (positive or negative) determines interaction: like charges repel due to the repulsive force described by Coulomb’s law, where the force direction depends on the sign of the charges, causing repulsion for identical signs.

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 9 cm has \( q = 6 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 12 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.12)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-6}}{0.0144} = 3.75 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A net flux of \( 9.04 \times 10^4 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \) passes through a closed surface. What is the charge enclosed?
questions.explanation: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( q = \phi \varepsilon_0 = 9.04 \times 10^4 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} = 8 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} = 0.8 \, \mu\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 25 cm has an electric field of \( 5 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 50 cm from its center. What is the charge?
What characteristic of an electric field ensures that work done in moving a charge along a closed path is zero in electrostatics?
questions.explanation: The conservative nature of the electrostatic field means the work done depends only on the potential difference between points, not the path. For a closed path, the start and end points are the same, so the net work is zero.

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 20

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 10 cm has a charge of \( 8 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 5 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Inside a thin spherical shell (\( r < R \)), \( E = 0 \) (Gauss’s law). Here, \( r = 5 \, \text{cm} < R = 10 \, \text{cm} \), so \( E = 0 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 8 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the x-axis. What is the flux through a rectangle of 20 cm × 30 cm in the yz-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = 0.2 \times 0.3 = 0.06 \, \text{m}^2 \) along x-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = 8 \times 10^3 \times 0.06 = 480 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +2 \, \mu\text{C} \) each are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 2 m. What is the force on one charge?
questions.explanation: Force between two charges: \( F = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{(2 \times 10^{-6})^2}{(2)^2} = 9 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{N} \). Two forces at 60°. Net force: \( F_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{F^2 + F^2 + 2 F^2 \cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{3} \times 9 \times 10^{-3} = 1.56 \times 10^{-2} \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: A closed surface has a net flux of \( 9.04 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). What is the charge enclosed?
questions.explanation: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \). \( q = \phi \varepsilon_0 = 9.04 \times 10^5 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} = 8 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} = 8 \, \mu\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A plane sheet has a surface charge density \( \sigma = 1.77 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field near it?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{1.77 \times 10^{-10}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 10 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +15 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 75 cm apart. What is the distance from \( +15 \, \mu\text{C} \) where the electric field is zero?
An infinite line charge has \( \lambda = 1.5 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \). What is the electric field at 50 cm?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2 \). \( E = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-6}}{0.5} = 5.4 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: What causes electric field lines to emerge perpendicularly from the surface of a charged conductor?
questions.explanation: In equilibrium, the field inside a conductor is zero. Any tangential component outside would drive surface charge motion, violating equilibrium. Thus, the field must be perpendicular to avoid such motion, maintaining static conditions.

questions.question_text: What causes the electric field to be stronger near a sharp point on a charged conductor compared to a flat surface?
questions.explanation: Charge concentrates more at sharp points due to lower surface area, increasing the surface charge density. Since the field just outside a conductor is proportional to this density, the field is stronger near points than on flatter regions.

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field remain constant inside a region where field lines are uniformly spaced and parallel?
questions.explanation: Uniformly spaced, parallel field lines indicate a uniform field, where the field strength and direction do not vary. This occurs in regions like between parallel plates, where the field is constant due to consistent charge distribution.

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 21

questions.question_text: Which characteristic of insulators prevents them from shielding their interior from an external electric field?
questions.explanation: Insulators lack free charges that can move to cancel an external field. Unlike conductors, where mobile electrons redistribute, insulators’ fixed charges allow the field to penetrate, as no shielding mechanism exists.

questions.question_text: A uniform electric field \( E = 4 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) is along the z-axis. What is the flux through a square of side 15 cm in the xy-plane?
questions.explanation: Area vector \( \Delta \mathbf{S} = (0.15)^2 = 0.0225 \, \text{m}^2 \) along z-axis. Flux: \( \phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S} = 4 \times 10^3 \times 0.0225 = 90 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: Two point charges \( 5 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) and \( -7 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \) are 150 cm apart in vacuum. What is the magnitude of the force between them?
Why can’t the electric field inside a charged insulator be zero, unlike in a conductor?
questions.explanation: In insulators, charges are fixed and cannot move to cancel an internal field. If charges are present inside, they generate a field that persists, as there are no free charges to redistribute and neutralize it, unlike in conductors.

questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell of radius 8 cm has \( q = 4 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 10 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.1)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{0.01} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( E = 5.4 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at 6 cm. What is \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \). \( 5.4 \times 10^5 = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times \lambda}{0.06} \). \( \lambda = \frac{5.4 \times 10^5 \times 0.06}{18 \times 10^9} = 1.8 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 6 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is at 60° to a field \( E = 7 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the torque?
questions.explanation: \( \tau = p E \sin \theta \). \( \tau = 6 \times 10^{-9} \times 7 \times 10^4 \times \sin 60^\circ = 42 \times 10^{-5} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3.64 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{N m} \).

questions.question_text: What property of electric charges explains why the smallest observable charge is that of an electron or proton?
questions.explanation: Quantization of charge means that charge exists in discrete units, with the smallest unit being the charge of an electron or proton (\( e \)). All observable charges are integer multiples of this fundamental unit, reflecting this property.

questions.question_text: A metallic sphere of radius 15 cm has a charge of \( 6 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field just outside its surface?
questions.explanation: For a conductor, \( E = \frac{k q}{r^2} \) at surface (\( r = 0.15 \, \text{m} \)). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.15)^2} = 2.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( +9 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) are 45 cm apart. What is the distance from \( +9 \, \mu\text{C} \) where the electric field is zero?

tests.title: Electric Charges and Fields Chapter-Wise Test 22

questions.question_text: What explains why the electric field inside a charged non-conducting sphere is non-zero and varies with position?
questions.explanation: In a non-conductor, charges are fixed and distributed throughout the volume. Gauss’s law shows the field inside depends on the enclosed charge, which increases with radius, leading to a non-zero, position-dependent field.

questions.question_text: An infinite line charge has \( E = 7.2 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at 5 cm. What is \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{2 k \lambda}{r} \). \( 7.2 \times 10^5 = \frac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times \lambda}{0.05} \). \( \lambda = \frac{7.2 \times 10^5 \times 0.05}{18 \times 10^9} = 2 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m} \).

questions.question_text: What allows an electric dipole to experience a net force in a non-uniform electric field but not in a uniform one?
questions.explanation: In a non-uniform field, the field strength varies across the dipole, causing unequal forces on the positive and negative charges. This results in a net force, unlike in a uniform field where equal and opposite forces cancel out.

questions.question_text: What ensures that the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite wire decreases as \( 1/r \) instead of \( 1/r^2 \)?
questions.explanation: The cylindrical symmetry of an infinite wire, when analyzed with Gauss’s law, shows the field depends on the radial distance \( r \) with a \( 1/r \) relationship. This arises because the field spreads over a cylindrical surface, not a spherical one like a point charge.

questions.question_text: Which property of electric charge explains why the total charge of an isolated system remains constant even when objects within it are rubbed together?
questions.explanation: The conservation of electric charge states that the total charge in an isolated system remains constant over time. When objects are rubbed together, charge is transferred from one to another (e.g., electrons move), but no new charge is created or destroyed. This ensures the net charge of the system stays the same.

questions.question_text: A conducting sphere of radius 21 cm has an electric field of \( 8 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \) at 42 cm from its center. What is the charge?
A thin spherical shell of radius 7 cm has \( q = 3 \, \mu\text{C} \). What is the electric field at 4 cm from the center?
questions.explanation: Inside shell (\( r < R \)): \( E = 0 \) (Gauss’s law).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 17 \, \mu\text{C} \) is at the center of a cube of edge 55 cm. What is the flux through one face?
questions.explanation: Total flux: \( \phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{17 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 1.92 \times 10^6 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \). Flux per face (6 faces): \( \phi_{\text{face}} = \frac{1.92 \times 10^6}{6} = 3.2 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^2/\text{C} \).

questions.question_text: A plane sheet has \( \sigma = 1.062 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field near it?
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \). \( E = \frac{1.062 \times 10^{-10}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = 6 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Why can’t electric field lines form closed loops in electrostatics, unlike magnetic field lines?
questions.explanation: Electric field lines begin at positive charges and end at negative charges (or infinity), reflecting the conservative nature of the electrostatic field. Closed loops would imply a non-conservative field, which contradicts Coulomb’s law and Gauss’s law in static conditions.

questions.question_text: A coil of 100 turns experiences a magnetic flux change from 0 to 0.03 Wb in 0.06 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta \Phi = 0.03 \, \text{Wb} \), \( \Delta t = 0.06 \, \text{s} \), \( N = 100 \). \( \varepsilon = 100 \times \frac{0.03}{0.06} = 100 \times 0.5 = 50 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 150 turns and area 0.06 m² is in a 0.14 T field that drops to zero in 0.3 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \Delta \Phi = B A = 0.14 \times 0.06 = 0.0084 \, \text{Wb} \). \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = 150 \times \frac{0.0084}{0.3} = 150 \times 0.028 = 4.2 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A square loop of side 22 cm rotates at 14 rad/s in a 0.15 T field. What is the maximum emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( A = (0.22)^2 = 0.0484 \, \text{m}^2 \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 1 \times 0.15 \times 0.0484 \times 14 = 0.10164 \, \text{V} \approx 0.102 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of 0.38 m × 0.55 m moves out of a 0.65 T field at 0.7 m/s along its shorter side. What is the emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.55 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.65 \times 0.55 \times 0.7 = 0.25025 \, \text{V} \approx 0.25 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of sides 35 cm and 15 cm moves out of a 0.8 T field at 1.5 m/s perpendicular to the shorter side. What is the motional emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.35 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.8 \times 0.35 \times 1.5 = 0.42 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid carries a steady current. A second coil placed nearby experiences an emf only when what happens to the current in the solenoid?
questions.explanation: Emf is induced in the second coil only when the magnetic flux changes, which occurs when the current in the solenoid changes, not when it remains steady.

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 650 turns per meter and area 0.014 m² has a current change from 6 A to 3 A in 0.25 s. What is the self-induced emf? (\( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{H/m} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = \mu_0 n^2 A l \), assume \( l = 1 \, \text{m} \). \( L = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (650)^2 \times 0.014 \times 1 = 0.00744 \, \text{H} \). \( \varepsilon = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 0.00744 \times \frac{3 - 6}{0.25} = 0.00744 \times (-12) = 0.08928 \, \text{V} \approx 0.089 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of 0.22 m × 0.4 m moves out of a 0.35 T field at 0.5 m/s along its shorter side. What is the emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.4 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.35 \times 0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.07 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A circular loop of radius 16 cm is deformed into a straight wire in a 0.12 T field in 0.6 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: Initial flux: \( \Phi = B A = 0.12 \times \pi \times (0.16)^2 = 0.00965 \, \text{Wb} \). Final flux = 0. \( \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = \frac{0.00965}{0.6} = 0.01608 \, \text{V} \approx 0.016 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 60 turns experiences a magnetic flux change from 0 to 0.015 Wb in 0.03 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta \Phi = 0.015 \, \text{Wb} \), \( \Delta t = 0.03 \, \text{s} \), \( N = 60 \). \( \varepsilon = 60 \times \frac{0.015}{0.03} = 60 \times 0.5 = 30 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 500 turns and length 1 m induces an emf of 1.5 V in a nearby coil when its current changes from 0 to 3 A in 0.2 s. What is the mutual inductance?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta I = 3 - 0 = 3 \, \text{A} \), \( \Delta t = 0.2 \, \text{s} \). \( M = \frac{\varepsilon}{\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}} = \frac{1.5}{\frac{3}{0.2}} = \frac{1.5}{15} = 0.1 \, \text{H} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid has 200 turns and length 0.5 m. If the current changes from 2 A to 4 A in 0.2 s in a nearby coil, inducing an emf of 0.5 V, what is the mutual inductance?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta I = 4 - 2 = 2 \, \text{A} \), \( \Delta t = 0.2 \, \text{s} \), \( \varepsilon = 0.5 \, \text{V} \). \( M = \frac{\varepsilon}{\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}} = \frac{0.5}{\frac{2}{0.2}} = \frac{0.5}{10} = 0.05 \, \text{H} \).

questions.question_text: A rod of length 0.9 m moves at 1.2 m/s in a 0.5 T field perpendicular to its length. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v = 0.5 \times 0.9 \times 1.2 = 0.54 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rod of length 0.5 m moves at 3 m/s in a 0.2 T field perpendicular to its length. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v = 0.2 \times 0.5 \times 3 = 0.3 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A magnet is moved towards a coil with its south pole first. The coil’s face nearest the magnet becomes what pole to oppose the motion?
questions.explanation: Lenz’s law dictates that the induced current creates a south pole to repel the approaching south pole, opposing the flux increase.

questions.question_text: A coil is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The area of the coil is 0.04 m², and the angle between the field and the area vector changes from 0° to 90° in 0.2 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: Initial flux: \( \Phi_i = B A \cos 0^\circ = 0.5 \times 0.04 \times 1 = 0.02 \, \text{Wb} \). Final flux: \( \Phi_f = B A \cos 90^\circ = 0.5 \times 0.04 \times 0 = 0 \, \text{Wb} \). \( \Delta \Phi = 0.02 - 0 = 0.02 \, \text{Wb} \), \( \Delta t = 0.2 \, \text{s} \). \( \varepsilon = -\frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = \frac{0.02}{0.2} = 0.1 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 200 turns and area 0.04 m² is rotated at 50 Hz in a 0.1 T field. What is the maximum emf?
questions.explanation: \( \omega = 2\pi v = 2\pi \times 50 = 100\pi \, \text{rad/s} \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 200 \times 0.1 \times 0.04 \times 100\pi = 251.33 \, \text{V} \approx 251.3 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 110 turns and area 0.035 m² is in a field that decreases from 0.09 T to 0 in 0.5 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \Delta \Phi = B A = 0.09 \times 0.035 = 0.00315 \, \text{Wb} \). \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = 110 \times \frac{0.00315}{0.5} = 110 \times 0.0063 = 0.693 \, \text{V} \approx 0.69 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 180 turns rotates at 60 rad/s in a 0.03 T field. If the area is 0.02 m², what is the maximum emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 180 \times 0.03 \times 0.02 \times 60 = 6.48 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A loop of 0.28 m × 0.14 m moves out of a 0.3 T field at 1.4 m/s along its longer side. How long does the emf last?
questions.explanation: Time = distance/velocity, distance = width along motion = 0.14 m. \( t = \frac{0.14}{1.4} = 0.1 \, \text{s} \).

questions.question_text: A rod rotates at 25 rad/s in a 0.5 T field. If the length from the axis to the tip is 0.7 m, what is the emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 \). \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 25 \times (0.7)^2 = 3.0625 \, \text{V} \approx 3.06 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rod rotates at 12 rad/s in a 0.5 T field. If the length from the axis to the tip is 0.9 m, what is the emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 \). \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 12 \times (0.9)^2 = 2.43 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid with mutual inductance 0.4 H has a current change of 3 A/s in the primary coil. What is the induced emf in the secondary coil?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{dI}{dt} = 0.4 \times 3 = 1.2 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rod of length 0.4 m moves at 2 m/s in a 0.3 T field perpendicular to its length. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v = 0.3 \times 0.4 \times 2 = 0.24 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 650 turns and length 1.2 m induces an emf of 2.6 V in a nearby coil when its current changes from 2 A to 6 A in 0.4 s. What is the mutual inductance?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta I = 6 - 2 = 4 \, \text{A} \), \( \Delta t = 0.4 \, \text{s} \). \( M = \frac{\varepsilon}{\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}} = \frac{2.6}{\frac{4}{0.4}} = \frac{2.6}{10} = 0.26 \, \text{H} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 110 turns experiences a magnetic flux change from 0 to 0.05 Wb in 0.1 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta \Phi = 0.05 \, \text{Wb} \), \( \Delta t = 0.1 \, \text{s} \), \( N = 110 \). \( \varepsilon = 110 \times \frac{0.05}{0.1} = 110 \times 0.5 = 55 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting loop is moved into a uniform magnetic field region. During the entry, the induced current flows in a direction determined by what?
questions.explanation: The direction opposes the increase in flux as the loop enters, governed by Lenz’s law, which ensures the current resists the change.

questions.question_text: A coil connected to a DC source shows a slow rise in current when switched on. This delay is primarily due to what effect?
questions.explanation: Self-inductance induces a back emf that opposes the current increase, causing a gradual rise until the steady state is reached.

questions.question_text: A rod of length 0.7 m moves at 2 m/s in a 0.3 T field perpendicular to its length. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v = 0.3 \times 0.7 \times 2 = 0.42 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil with \( L = 0.45 \, \text{H} \) has its current increased from 0 to 8 A in 0.8 s. What is the energy stored?
A loop of 0.25 m × 0.15 m moves out of a 0.2 T field at 1.5 m/s along its longer side. How long does the emf last?
questions.explanation: Time = distance/velocity, distance = width along motion = 0.15 m. \( t = \frac{0.15}{1.5} = 0.1 \, \text{s} \).

questions.question_text: Two coils are placed close to each other. When the current in one coil is changed, an emf is induced in the other. This phenomenon is known as what?
questions.explanation: This is mutual induction, where a changing current in one coil induces an emf in a nearby coil due to the changing magnetic flux linking them.

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of 0.2 m × 0.35 m moves out of a 0.4 T field at 0.8 m/s along its shorter side. What is the emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.35 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.4 \times 0.35 \times 0.8 = 0.112 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A circular loop of radius 18 cm is deformed into a straight wire in a 0.14 T field in 0.7 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: Initial flux: \( \Phi = B A = 0.14 \times \pi \times (0.18)^2 = 0.01425 \, \text{Wb} \). Final flux = 0. \( \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = \frac{0.01425}{0.7} = 0.02036 \, \text{V} \approx 0.02 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 160 turns and area 0.025 m² is rotated at 20 Hz in a 0.09 T field. What is the maximum emf?
questions.explanation: \( \omega = 2\pi v = 2\pi \times 20 = 40\pi \, \text{rad/s} \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 160 \times 0.09 \times 0.025 \times 40\pi = 45.24 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of 0.15 m × 0.25 m moves out of a 0.3 T field at 0.8 m/s along its shorter side. What is the emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.25 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.3 \times 0.25 \times 0.8 = 0.06 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A wheel with 8 spokes of 0.25 m each rotates at 60 rpm in a 0.5 T field. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \omega = 2\pi \times \frac{60}{60} = 2\pi \, \text{rad/s} \). \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 2\pi \times (0.25)^2 = 0.098 \, \text{V} \approx 0.1 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A circular coil of radius 5 cm and 300 turns rotates at 35 rad/s in a 0.05 T field. What is the maximum emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( A = \pi r^2 = 3.14 \times (0.05)^2 = 0.00785 \, \text{m}^2 \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 300 \times 0.05 \times 0.00785 \times 35 = 4.12375 \, \text{V} \approx 4.12 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A loop enters a magnetic field region with its plane perpendicular to the field. The induced current flows to produce a magnetic field opposing what?
questions.explanation: The current opposes the increase in flux as the loop enters the field, creating a field opposite to the external field per Lenz’s law.

questions.question_text: In an AC generator, the emf varies sinusoidally with time. What is the primary reason for this variation?
options: Rotation of the coil in a uniform magnetic field
Change in the magnetic field strength
questions.explanation: The emf varies sinusoidally because the coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field, causing the angle between the magnetic field and the coil’s area vector to change continuously, following a sine function.

questions.question_text: A conducting rod slides along parallel rails in a magnetic field perpendicular to its motion. The emf induced in the circuit is classified as what type?
questions.explanation: This is motional emf, as it arises from the rod’s motion through the magnetic field, cutting flux lines to induce a potential difference.

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 850 turns/m and area 0.01 m² has \( \mu_r = 1 \). What is its self-inductance? (\( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{H/m} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = \mu_r \mu_0 n^2 A l \), assume \( l = 1 \, \text{m} \). \( L = 1 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (850)^2 \times 0.01 \times 1 = 0.00907 \, \text{H} \approx 0.009 \, \text{H} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 90 turns experiences a magnetic flux change from 0 to 0.025 Wb in 0.05 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta \Phi = 0.025 \, \text{Wb} \), \( \Delta t = 0.05 \, \text{s} \), \( N = 90 \). \( \varepsilon = 90 \times \frac{0.025}{0.05} = 90 \times 0.5 = 45 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 950 turns/m and area 0.012 m² has \( \mu_r = 1 \). What is its self-inductance? (\( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{H/m} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = \mu_r \mu_0 n^2 A l \), assume \( l = 1 \, \text{m} \). \( L = 1 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (950)^2 \times 0.012 \times 1 = 0.0136 \, \text{H} \approx 0.014 \, \text{H} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting loop is moved out of a magnetic field region. The induced current flows to oppose what specific change?
questions.explanation: Moving the loop out reduces the magnetic flux through it, and the induced current opposes this decrease by generating a field in the same direction as the original field.

questions.question_text: A flat coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field. The induced emf is zero when the plane of the coil is in which position?
questions.explanation: The emf is zero when the rate of flux change is zero (\( \frac{d\Phi}{dt} = 0 \)), which occurs when the coil is parallel to the field (\( \sin\theta = 0 \)).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of sides 20 cm and 8 cm moves out of a 0.45 T field at 1.2 m/s perpendicular to the shorter side. What is the motional emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.2 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.45 \times 0.2 \times 1.2 = 0.108 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil with a ferromagnetic core has higher self-inductance compared to an air-core coil. This is primarily due to what property of the core?
questions.explanation: The ferromagnetic core increases the magnetic permeability (\( \mu \)), enhancing the magnetic flux linkage and thus increasing self-inductance (\( L = \mu n^2 A l \)).

questions.question_text: A loop of 0.5 m × 0.22 m moves out of a 0.7 T field at 1.4 m/s along its longer side. How long does the emf last?
questions.explanation: Time = distance/velocity, distance = width along motion = 0.22 m. \( t = \frac{0.22}{1.4} = 0.1571 \, \text{s} \approx 0.16 \, \text{s} \).

questions.question_text: A circular loop of radius 9 cm is deformed into a straight wire in a 0.25 T field in 0.4 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: Initial flux: \( \Phi = B A = 0.25 \times \pi \times (0.09)^2 = 0.00636 \, \text{Wb} \). Final flux = 0. \( \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = \frac{0.00636}{0.4} = 0.0159 \, \text{V} \approx 0.016 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Two coils are arranged such that their mutual inductance is maximized. What is the most likely orientation of their axes?
questions.explanation: Mutual inductance is maximized when the magnetic flux from one coil fully links with the other, which occurs when their axes are aligned (coaxial).

questions.question_text: A circular coil of radius 12 cm and 250 turns rotates at 55 rad/s in a 0.025 T field. What is the maximum emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( A = \pi r^2 = 3.14 \times (0.12)^2 = 0.0452 \, \text{m}^2 \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 250 \times 0.025 \times 0.0452 \times 55 = 15.535 \, \text{V} \approx 15.54 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rod of length 0.3 m moves at 4 m/s in a 0.25 T field perpendicular to its length. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v = 0.25 \times 0.3 \times 4 = 0.3 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A metal disc rotates in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its plane. The induced emf between the center and the rim is due to what?
questions.explanation: The rotation causes charges in the disc to move through the magnetic field, experiencing a Lorentz force that separates them radially, inducing an emf from center to rim.

questions.question_text: A coil of 200 turns rotates at 90 rad/s in a 0.04 T field. If the area is 0.015 m², what is the maximum emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 200 \times 0.04 \times 0.015 \times 90 = 10.8 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: In a setup with two coils, if the primary coil’s current is constant DC, what will be the induced emf in the secondary coil?
options: Equal to the primary coil’s emf
questions.explanation: A constant DC current produces a steady magnetic field, resulting in no change in magnetic flux through the secondary coil, so the induced emf is zero.

questions.question_text: A circular coil of radius 6 cm and 200 turns rotates at 30 rad/s in a 0.08 T field. What is the maximum emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( A = \pi r^2 = 3.14 \times (0.06)^2 = 0.0113 \, \text{m}^2 \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 200 \times 0.08 \times 0.0113 \times 30 = 5.424 \, \text{V} \approx 5.42 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil with \( L = 0.15 \, \text{H} \) has its current increased from 0 to 3 A in 0.3 s. What is the energy stored?
A solenoid with mutual inductance 0.35 H has a current change of 4 A/s in the primary coil. What is the induced emf in the secondary coil?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{dI}{dt} = 0.35 \times 4 = 1.4 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of self-inductance 0.7 H has its current increased from 2 A to 5 A in 0.3 s. What is the magnitude of the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta I = 5 - 2 = 3 \, \text{A} \), \( \Delta t = 0.3 \, \text{s} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.7 \times \frac{3}{0.3} = 0.7 \times 10 = 7 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A circular loop is placed in a uniform magnetic field, and the field strength is increased steadily. What determines the magnitude of the induced emf in the loop?
options: Rate of change of magnetic field
questions.explanation: According to Faraday’s law, the induced emf depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux, which increases with the rate at which the magnetic field strength changes.

questions.question_text: A coil of self-inductance 0.9 H has its current increased from 1 A to 4 A in 0.25 s. What is the magnitude of the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta I = 4 - 1 = 3 \, \text{A} \), \( \Delta t = 0.25 \, \text{s} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.9 \times \frac{3}{0.25} = 0.9 \times 12 = 10.8 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of sides 10 cm and 5 cm moves out of a 0.2 T magnetic field at 2 m/s perpendicular to the longer side. What is the motional emf induced?
questions.explanation: For motional emf: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), where \( l \) is the length perpendicular to velocity. Here, \( B = 0.2 \, \text{T} \), \( l = 0.05 \, \text{m} \), \( v = 2 \, \text{m/s} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.2 \times 0.05 \times 2 = 0.02 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 850 turns per meter and area 0.017 m² has a current drop from 10 A to 7 A in 0.25 s. What is the self-induced emf? (\( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{H/m} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = \mu_0 n^2 A l \), assume \( l = 1 \, \text{m} \). \( L = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (850)^2 \times 0.017 \times 1 = 0.01541 \, \text{H} \). \( \varepsilon = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 0.01541 \times \frac{7 - 10}{0.25} = 0.01541 \times (-12) = 0.18492 \, \text{V} \approx 0.185 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting loop is expanded in a uniform magnetic field. The induced emf is caused by what physical process?
options: Change in magnetic flux through the loop
Change in resistance of the loop
Motion of charges due to thermal energy
questions.explanation: Expanding the loop increases the magnetic flux through it, and the rate of this flux change induces an emf as per Faraday’s law.

questions.question_text: A coil is placed in a magnetic field that oscillates rapidly. The induced emf is higher when what property of the field increases?
questions.explanation: The induced emf depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux (\( \varepsilon = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt} \)), which increases with the frequency of oscillation of the magnetic field.

questions.question_text: In an AC generator, increasing the number of turns in the coil affects what aspect of the output?
questions.explanation: The emf (\( \varepsilon = N B A \omega \sin\omega t \)) is directly proportional to the number of turns, so more turns increase the amplitude of the induced emf.

questions.question_text: A wheel with 5 spokes of 0.65 m each rotates at 42 rpm in a 0.7 T field. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \omega = 2\pi \times \frac{42}{60} = 1.4\pi \, \text{rad/s} \). \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.7 \times 1.4\pi \times (0.65)^2 = 0.623 \, \text{V} \approx 0.62 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A circular loop of radius 17 cm is deformed into a straight wire in a 0.15 T field in 0.5 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: Initial flux: \( \Phi = B A = 0.15 \times \pi \times (0.17)^2 = 0.01363 \, \text{Wb} \). Final flux = 0. \( \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = \frac{0.01363}{0.5} = 0.02726 \, \text{V} \approx 0.027 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: In an AC generator, the output voltage reverses direction every half-cycle due to what?
questions.explanation: The coil’s rotation causes the flux to change sign every half-cycle as it passes from one field direction to the opposite, reversing the emf.

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 900 turns/m and area 0.018 m² has \( \mu_r = 1 \). What is its self-inductance? (\( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{H/m} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = \mu_r \mu_0 n^2 A l \), assume \( l = 1 \, \text{m} \). \( L = 1 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (900)^2 \times 0.018 \times 1 = 0.01831 \, \text{H} \approx 0.018 \, \text{H} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 190 turns and area 0.03 m² is rotated at 40 Hz in a 0.09 T field. What is the maximum emf?
questions.explanation: \( \omega = 2\pi v = 2\pi \times 40 = 80\pi \, \text{rad/s} \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 190 \times 0.09 \times 0.03 \times 80\pi = 128.91 \, \text{V} \approx 128.9 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rod rotates at 30 rad/s in a 0.6 T field. If the length from the axis to the tip is 0.8 m, what is the emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 \). \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.6 \times 30 \times (0.8)^2 = 5.76 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rod of length 0.35 m moves at 2.5 m/s in a 0.2 T field perpendicular to its length. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v = 0.2 \times 0.35 \times 2.5 = 0.175 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Two nearby coils are arranged such that a changing current in one induces an emf in the other. The strength of this effect is quantified by what property?
questions.explanation: Mutual inductance measures the emf induced in one coil per unit rate of current change in the other, reflecting the strength of their magnetic coupling.

questions.question_text: A coil with \( L = 0.25 \, \text{H} \) has its current increased from 0 to 4 A in 0.4 s. What is the energy stored?
A solenoid of 400 turns per meter and area 0.015 m² has a current drop from 5 A to 2 A in 0.3 s. What is the self-induced emf? (\( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{H/m} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = \mu_0 n^2 A l \), assume \( l = 1 \, \text{m} \). \( L = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (400)^2 \times 0.015 \times 1 = 0.003016 \, \text{H} \). \( \varepsilon = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 0.003016 \times \frac{2 - 5}{0.3} = 0.003016 \times (-10) = 0.03016 \, \text{V} \approx 0.03 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 100 turns and area 0.03 m² is in a 0.08 T field that drops to zero in 0.2 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \Delta \Phi = B A = 0.08 \times 0.03 = 0.0024 \, \text{Wb} \). \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = 100 \times \frac{0.0024}{0.2} = 100 \times 0.012 = 1.2 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting rod is rotated about one end in a uniform magnetic field. The emf induced between the ends is due to what fundamental effect?
questions.explanation: The rotation causes charges to move through the field, experiencing a magnetic force (Lorentz force) that separates them, inducing an emf along the rod.

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 300 turns and length 0.6 m induces an emf of 0.9 V in a nearby coil when its current changes from 1 A to 3 A in 0.3 s. What is the mutual inductance?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta I = 3 - 1 = 2 \, \text{A} \), \( \Delta t = 0.3 \, \text{s} \). \( M = \frac{\varepsilon}{\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}} = \frac{0.9}{\frac{2}{0.3}} = \frac{0.9}{6.67} \approx 0.135 \, \text{H} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 950 turns/m and area 0.016 m² has \( \mu_r = 1 \). What is its self-inductance? (\( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{H/m} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = \mu_r \mu_0 n^2 A l \), assume \( l = 1 \, \text{m} \). \( L = 1 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (950)^2 \times 0.016 \times 1 = 0.01815 \, \text{H} \approx 0.018 \, \text{H} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of sides 45 cm and 25 cm moves out of a 1.0 T field at 0.8 m/s perpendicular to the longer side. What is the motional emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.25 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 1.0 \times 0.25 \times 0.8 = 0.2 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of sides 12 cm and 4 cm moves out of a 0.35 T field at 2 m/s perpendicular to the longer side. What is the motional emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.04 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.35 \times 0.04 \times 2 = 0.028 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid with mutual inductance 0.18 H has a current change of 5 A/s in the primary coil. What is the induced emf in the secondary coil?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{dI}{dt} = 0.18 \times 5 = 0.9 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of self-inductance 1.5 H has its current decreased from 7 A to 4 A in 0.3 s. What is the magnitude of the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta I = 4 - 7 = -3 \, \text{A} \), \( \Delta t = 0.3 \, \text{s} \). \( \varepsilon = 1.5 \times \frac{-3}{0.3} = 1.5 \times (-10) = -15 \, \text{V} \), magnitude = 15 V.

questions.question_text: A conducting rod moves parallel to its length in a uniform magnetic field. Why is no emf induced across its ends?
options: Due to low magnetic field strength
questions.explanation: Motional emf requires the rod to move perpendicular to the magnetic field to cut flux lines. Moving parallel to its length does not change the flux through any area, so no emf is induced.

questions.question_text: A loop moves into a 0.3 T field at 1 m/s. If the length perpendicular to velocity is 0.1 m, how long does the emf last?
questions.explanation: Time = distance/velocity, where distance = width of loop along motion. Assume width = 0.1 m (typical NEET assumption). \( t = \frac{0.1}{1} = 0.1 \, \text{s} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid with mutual inductance 0.3 H has a current change of 6 A/s in the primary coil. What is the induced emf in the secondary coil?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{dI}{dt} = 0.3 \times 6 = 1.8 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil is placed in a time-varying magnetic field. The direction of the induced current is determined by which principle?
questions.explanation: Lenz’s law dictates that the induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux, determining its direction based on the field’s variation.

questions.question_text: A bar magnet is pushed towards a coil with its north pole first, then pulled back. The direction of the induced current in the coil during withdrawal is opposite to that during approach due to what?
questions.explanation: Lenz’s law causes the current to oppose the flux change: it creates a north pole to repel the approaching magnet and a south pole to attract it during withdrawal, reversing the direction.

questions.question_text: A rod of length 0.25 m moves at 3 m/s in a 0.4 T field perpendicular to its length. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v = 0.4 \times 0.25 \times 3 = 0.3 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 120 turns and area 0.025 m² is in a field that decreases from 0.08 T to 0 in 0.4 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \Delta \Phi = B A = 0.08 \times 0.025 = 0.002 \, \text{Wb} \). \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = 120 \times \frac{0.002}{0.4} = 120 \times 0.005 = 0.6 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 140 turns and area 0.05 m² is in a 0.1 T field that drops to zero in 0.25 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \Delta \Phi = B A = 0.1 \times 0.05 = 0.005 \, \text{Wb} \). \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = 140 \times \frac{0.005}{0.25} = 140 \times 0.02 = 2.8 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of 0.18 m × 0.3 m moves out of a 0.25 T field at 1 m/s along its shorter side. What is the emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.3 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.25 \times 0.3 \times 1 = 0.075 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: In an AC generator, the frequency of the output voltage depends on which factor?
questions.explanation: The frequency equals the rotational speed of the coil in revolutions per second, as each full rotation produces one cycle of emf (\( f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} \)).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of sides 25 cm and 10 cm moves out of a 0.5 T field at 1.5 m/s perpendicular to the longer side. What is the motional emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.1 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.5 \times 0.1 \times 1.5 = 0.075 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil with \( L = 0.35 \, \text{H} \) has its current increased from 0 to 5 A in 0.5 s. What is the energy stored?
A coil with a high self-inductance is connected to a battery. Why does the current take time to reach its maximum value?
options: Due to resistance of the coil
Due to back emf opposing current change
questions.explanation: High self-inductance induces a back emf that opposes the increase in current, slowing the rate at which the current builds up to its steady-state value.

questions.question_text: A solenoid with mutual inductance 0.15 H has a current change of 8 A/s in the primary coil. What is the induced emf in the secondary coil?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{dI}{dt} = 0.15 \times 8 = 1.2 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A square loop of side 24 cm rotates at 15 rad/s in a 0.25 T field. What is the maximum emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( A = (0.24)^2 = 0.0576 \, \text{m}^2 \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 1 \times 0.25 \times 0.0576 \times 15 = 0.216 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A metal plate swings like a pendulum through a magnetic field. The slowing of its motion is primarily due to what?
questions.explanation: The motion induces currents in the plate, which produce an opposing magnetic field, exerting a force that resists the motion (Lenz’s law), slowing it down.

questions.question_text: A rod rotates at 22 rad/s in a 0.4 T field. If the length from the axis to the tip is 0.6 m, what is the emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 \). \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.4 \times 22 \times (0.6)^2 = 1.584 \, \text{V} \approx 1.58 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil is connected to a DC source via a switch. When the switch is opened, a spark is observed. This is due to what phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Opening the switch causes a rapid decrease in current, inducing a high back emf due to self-inductance, which can cause a spark as the energy dissipates.

questions.question_text: A coil of 120 turns experiences a magnetic flux change from 0 to 0.04 Wb in 0.08 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta \Phi = 0.04 \, \text{Wb} \), \( \Delta t = 0.08 \, \text{s} \), \( N = 120 \). \( \varepsilon = 120 \times \frac{0.04}{0.08} = 120 \times 0.5 = 60 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of 0.26 m × 0.42 m moves out of a 0.45 T field at 0.7 m/s along its shorter side. What is the emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.42 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.45 \times 0.42 \times 0.7 = 0.1323 \, \text{V} \approx 0.132 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 180 turns and area 0.09 m² is in a field that decreases from 0.11 T to 0 in 0.6 s. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \Delta \Phi = B A = 0.11 \times 0.09 = 0.0099 \, \text{Wb} \). \( \varepsilon = N \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = 180 \times \frac{0.0099}{0.6} = 180 \times 0.0165 = 2.97 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rod rotates at 16 rad/s in a 0.6 T field. If the length from the axis to the tip is 0.5 m, what is the emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 \). \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.6 \times 16 \times (0.5)^2 = 1.2 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A magnet is oscillated near a coil. The induced emf in the coil alternates because of what characteristic of the magnet’s motion?
questions.explanation: The oscillatory motion causes the magnetic flux to alternately increase and decrease, inducing an alternating emf as the flux change direction reverses.

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of sides 28 cm and 14 cm moves out of a 0.7 T field at 1.2 m/s perpendicular to the longer side. What is the motional emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.14 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.7 \times 0.14 \times 1.2 = 0.1176 \, \text{V} \approx 0.118 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rod rotates at 18 rad/s in a 0.4 T field. If the length from the axis to the tip is 0.7 m, what is the emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 \). \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.4 \times 18 \times (0.7)^2 = 1.764 \, \text{V} \approx 1.76 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 250 turns rotates at 80 rad/s in a 0.04 T field. If the area is 0.015 m², what is the maximum emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 250 \times 0.04 \times 0.015 \times 80 = 12 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A loop of 0.4 m × 0.18 m moves out of a 0.5 T field at 1.8 m/s along its longer side. How long does the emf last?
questions.explanation: Time = distance/velocity, distance = width along motion = 0.18 m. \( t = \frac{0.18}{1.8} = 0.1 \, \text{s} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of 140 turns and area 0.02 m² is rotated at 25 Hz in a 0.07 T field. What is the maximum emf?
questions.explanation: \( \omega = 2\pi v = 2\pi \times 25 = 50\pi \, \text{rad/s} \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 140 \times 0.07 \times 0.02 \times 50\pi = 30.79 \, \text{V} \approx 30.8 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid of 500 turns per meter and area 0.02 m² has a current drop from 6 A to 3 A in 0.25 s. What is the self-induced emf? (\( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{H/m} \))
questions.explanation: \( L = \mu_0 n^2 A l \), assume \( l = 1 \, \text{m} \). \( L = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (500)^2 \times 0.02 \times 1 = 0.00628 \, \text{H} \). \( \varepsilon = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 0.00628 \times \frac{3 - 6}{0.25} = 0.00628 \times (-12) = 0.07536 \, \text{V} \approx 0.075 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A flat coil is placed in a magnetic field that decreases with time. The direction of the induced current is such that it produces a magnetic field in which direction?
questions.explanation: Lenz’s law dictates that the induced current opposes the decrease in flux by producing a magnetic field in the same direction as the original field.

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of 0.24 m × 0.38 m moves out of a 0.3 T field at 0.6 m/s along its shorter side. What is the emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.38 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.3 \times 0.38 \times 0.6 = 0.0684 \, \text{V} \approx 0.068 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A coil of self-inductance 0.4 H has its current decreased from 5 A to 2 A in 0.1 s. What is the magnitude of the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = -L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \). \( \Delta I = 2 - 5 = -3 \, \text{A} \), \( \Delta t = 0.1 \, \text{s} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.4 \times \frac{-3}{0.1} = 0.4 \times (-30) = -12 \, \text{V} \). Magnitude = 12 V.

questions.question_text: A wheel with 10 spokes of 0.7 m each rotates at 60 rpm in a 0.5 T field. What is the induced emf?
questions.explanation: \( \omega = 2\pi \times \frac{60}{60} = 2\pi \, \text{rad/s} \). \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 2\pi \times (0.7)^2 = 0.7697 \, \text{V} \approx 0.77 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A conducting loop is shrunk in a uniform magnetic field. The induced current flows in a direction to oppose what change?
questions.explanation: Shrinking the loop decreases the magnetic flux through it. Lenz’s law states the induced current opposes this decrease by creating a field in the same direction as the original field.

questions.question_text: A square loop of side 26 cm rotates at 12 rad/s in a 0.3 T field. What is the maximum emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( A = (0.26)^2 = 0.0676 \, \text{m}^2 \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 1 \times 0.3 \times 0.0676 \times 12 = 0.24336 \, \text{V} \approx 0.243 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid with mutual inductance 0.25 H has a current change of 6 A/s in the primary coil. What is the induced emf in the secondary coil?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = M \frac{dI}{dt} = 0.25 \times 6 = 1.5 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A rectangular loop of 0.36 m × 0.5 m moves out of a 0.55 T field at 0.8 m/s along its shorter side. What is the emf?
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon = B l v \), \( l = 0.5 \, \text{m} \). \( \varepsilon = 0.55 \times 0.5 \times 0.8 = 0.22 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A solenoid’s current is increased, and the energy stored in its magnetic field increases. This energy is analogous to what mechanical quantity?
questions.explanation: The energy (\( \frac{1}{2} L I^2 \)) is analogous to kinetic energy (\( \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \)), with inductance acting like mass and current like velocity.

questions.question_text: A loop of 0.35 m × 0.1 m moves out of a 0.25 T field at 2.5 m/s along its longer side. How long does the emf last?
questions.explanation: Time = distance/velocity, distance = width along motion = 0.1 m. \( t = \frac{0.1}{2.5} = 0.04 \, \text{s} \).

questions.question_text: A loop of 0.32 m × 0.16 m moves out of a 0.35 T field at 2 m/s along its longer side. How long does the emf last?
questions.explanation: Time = distance/velocity, distance = width along motion = 0.16 m. \( t = \frac{0.16}{2} = 0.08 \, \text{s} \).

questions.question_text: A circular coil of radius 4 cm and 250 turns rotates at 40 rad/s in a 0.06 T field. What is the maximum emf induced?
questions.explanation: \( A = \pi r^2 = 3.14 \times (0.04)^2 = 0.005024 \, \text{m}^2 \). \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega = 250 \times 0.06 \times 0.005024 \times 40 = 3.0144 \, \text{V} \approx 3.01 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: In an AC generator, the maximum emf occurs when the coil is in which orientation relative to the magnetic field?
questions.explanation: The maximum emf occurs when the rate of flux change is greatest, which happens when the coil is perpendicular to the field (\( \sin\theta = 1 \)).

questions.question_text: A magnet is moved away from a coil, and the induced current flows clockwise as viewed from the magnet. What is the polarity of the coil’s face towards the magnet?
questions.explanation: By Lenz’s law, the clockwise current opposes the decreasing flux by producing a south pole facing the receding north pole of the magnet, creating an attractive force.
