questions.question_text: In a system of two parallel plate capacitors with different dielectrics connected in parallel, why does the capacitor with a higher dielectric constant store more energy for the same applied voltage?
options: It stores more energy due to larger capacitance
The voltage across it is higher
questions.explanation: In parallel, both capacitors have the same voltage \( V \). Capacitance is \( C = \frac{K \varepsilon_0 A}{d} \), where \( K \) is the dielectric constant. A higher \( K \) increases \( C \). Energy stored is \( U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 \), so a larger \( C \) (due to higher \( K \)) leads to more energy stored for the same \( V \). The higher \( K \) allows more charge (\( Q = C V \)) to be stored, increasing energy without changing \( V \).

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 4 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) lies along the x-axis. What is the potential at \( (-2, 0, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Along the dipole axis (\( \theta = 180^\circ \)): \( V = -\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{p}{r^2} \). \( V = -9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-9}}{2^2} = -9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-9}}{4} = -9 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: What is the work done in moving a \( 5 \, \mu\text{C} \) charge from infinity to a point where the potential is \( 2000 \, \text{V} \)?
questions.explanation: Work done = Potential energy = \( q V \). \( W = 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 2000 = 10^{-2} \, \text{J} = 0.01 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 12 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 30 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 12 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the final potential difference?
questions.explanation: Initial charge: \( Q = 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 30 = 3.6 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total capacitance: \( 12 + 12 = 24 \, \mu\text{F} \). Final voltage: \( V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{3.6 \times 10^{-4}}{24 \times 10^{-6}} = 15 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +6 \, \mu\text{C} \), \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \), and \( +1 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (0, 0, 0) \), \( (6, 0, 0) \), and \( (0, 6, 0) \, \text{m} \). What is the potential at \( (6, 6, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).

A conductor has a surface charge density of \( 2.5 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside it? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{2.5 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 2.82 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A conductor has a surface charge density of \( 5 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside it? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{5 \times 10^{-7}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 5.65 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 24 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -12 \, \mu\text{C} \) are placed 24 cm apart. What is the potential energy of the system? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{24 \times 10^{-6} \times (-12 \times 10^{-6})}{0.24} \). \( U = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{-288 \times 10^{-12}}{0.24} = -10.8 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A conductor has a surface charge density of \( 3 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside it? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 3.39 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with capacitance \( 100 \, \text{pF} \) has a dielectric (\( K = 3 \), thickness \( d/3 \)) inserted. What is the new capacitance? (Original separation \( d \)).
questions.explanation: Potential difference: \( V = E_0 \left( \frac{2d}{3} \right) + \frac{E_0}{K} \left( \frac{d}{3} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3 \times 3} \right) \). \( V = E_0 d \left( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{9} \right) = E_0 d \times \frac{7}{9} \). \( C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{\frac{7}{9} V_0} = \frac{9}{7} \times 100 \approx 128.57 \, \text{pF} \).

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 7

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +8 \, \mu\text{C} \), \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \), and \( +3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (0, 0, 0) \), \( (8, 0, 0) \), and \( (0, 8, 0) \, \text{m} \). What is the potential at \( (8, 8, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
In an isolated system of two capacitors initially charged and then connected in parallel with opposite polarities, what happens to the final energy of the system compared to the initial energy?
options: Final energy is less than initial energy due to heat loss
Final energy equals initial energy as charge is conserved
Final energy is greater due to increased potential
Final energy becomes zero as charges cancel out
questions.explanation: When two capacitors are connected in parallel with opposite polarities, charges redistribute such that the net charge on the positive plates (and negative plates) adjusts to a new equilibrium. The initial energy stored in the capacitors (\( U_i = \frac{1}{2} C_1 V_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} C_2 V_2^2 \)) is greater than the final energy after connection due to energy losses during charge redistribution. Some energy is lost as heat or electromagnetic radiation during the transient current flow, so the final energy is less than the initial energy.

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 10 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -2 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (8, 0, 0) \) and \( (-8, 0, 0) \, \text{cm} \). What is the potential at midpoint? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Distance to midpoint = 0.08 m. \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \left( \frac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{0.08} + \frac{-2 \times 10^{-6}}{0.08} \right) = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{0.08} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{0.08} = 9 \times 10^5 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field increase when rotated from alignment (\( \theta = 0^\circ \)) to perpendicular (\( \theta = 90^\circ \))?
options: Work is done against the aligning torque
questions.explanation: The potential energy of a dipole is \( U = -p E \cos \theta \). At \( \theta = 0^\circ \), \( \cos 0 = 1 \), \( U = -p E \), the minimum. At \( \theta = 90^\circ \), \( \cos 90 = 0 \), \( U = 0 \). From \( \theta = 0^\circ \) to \( 90^\circ \), \( U \) increases from \( -p E \) to 0 (less negative to zero), as the dipole moves against the torque (\( \tau = p E \sin \theta \)) aligning with the field, requiring external work that increases the system's energy.

questions.question_text: A \( 16 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 10 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 16 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the final potential difference?
questions.explanation: Initial charge: \( Q = 16 \times 10^{-6} \times 10 = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total capacitance: \( 16 + 16 = 32 \, \mu\text{F} \). Final voltage: \( V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-4}}{32 \times 10^{-6}} = 5 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 6 cm has a charge of \( 6 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the potential at its surface? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential at the surface: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{R} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-8}}{0.06} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-6} = 9000 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A charged conductor is surrounded by a thin concentric hollow conducting shell. If the shell is grounded, what happens to the charge on the inner conductor?
options: It induces an equal charge on the shell
It transfers entirely to the shell
questions.explanation: When the outer shell is grounded (potential \( V = 0 \)), the potential on the inner conductor adjusts due to charge redistribution. If the inner conductor has charge \( Q \), the inner surface of the shell induces \( -Q \), and since the shell's potential is zero, the outer surface of the shell acquires \( +Q \). The charge on the inner conductor remains \( Q \), as grounding the shell does not change the charge on the inner conductor but affects the potential and charge distribution on the shell.

questions.question_text: Three capacitors \( 10 \, \text{pF} \), \( 20 \, \text{pF} \), and \( 40 \, \text{pF} \) are in parallel. What is the total capacitance?
In a parallel plate capacitor with a partially inserted dielectric slab while maintaining constant charge, why does the capacitance decrease as the slab is withdrawn?
options: The charge on the plates decreases
questions.explanation: Capacitance \( C = \frac{Q}{V} \). With constant charge \( Q \), inserting a dielectric (\( K > 1 \)) increases \( C \) by reducing \( V \) (\( C = \frac{K \varepsilon_0 A}{d} \)). As the slab is withdrawn, the effective dielectric constant decreases (less area has \( K \)), lowering \( C \). Since \( Q \) is constant, \( V \) increases (\( V = \frac{Q}{C} \)), reflecting the reduced capacitance due to less dielectric influence.

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 8 \, \mu\text{C} \) is moved from infinity to a point where the potential is \( 50 \, \text{V} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done = Potential energy = \( q V \). \( W = 8 \times 10^{-6} \times 50 = 4 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} = 0.4 \, \text{mJ} \).

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 8

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +5 \, \mu\text{C} \), \( -2 \, \mu\text{C} \), and \( +3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (0, 0, 0) \), \( (5, 0, 0) \), and \( (0, 5, 0) \, \text{m} \). What is the potential at \( (5, 5, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
Why does the potential energy of a system of two opposite charges increase when their separation decreases?
questions.explanation: For two opposite charges \( +q \) and \( -q \), the potential energy is \( U = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = -\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q^2}{r} \), negative due to attraction. Decreasing \( r \) makes \( U \) more negative (e.g., from \( -1/r_1 \) to \( -1/r_2 \), \( r_2 < r_1 \), \( U \) decreases). However, the question interprets "increase" as increasing in magnitude (more negative), as the attractive energy becomes stronger, lowering the system's energy state.

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 30 cm has a charge of \( 12 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the electric field at 70 cm from the center? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: For \( r = 0.7 \, \text{m} > R = 0.3 \, \text{m} \), \( E = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{12 \times 10^{-8}}{(0.7)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{12 \times 10^{-8}}{0.49} \approx 2.204 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area \( 0.02 \, \text{m}^2 \) separated by 2 mm in air. What is its capacitance? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \frac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.02}{2 \times 10^{-3}} = 8.85 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{F} = 88.5 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor increase when a dielectric slab is inserted between the plates while keeping the plates connected to a battery?
options: The plates attract more charge due to increased voltage
The dielectric increases the plate area
The dielectric allows more charge storage for the same voltage
The dielectric reduces the plate separation
questions.explanation: When a dielectric slab (with \( K > 1 \)) is inserted while the capacitor remains connected to a battery (constant voltage \( V \)), the electric field decreases due to polarization (\( E = E_0/K \)), and the capacitance increases (\( C' = K C \)). This happens because the dielectric reduces the field, allowing more charge to be stored on the plates (\( Q = C V \), so \( Q' = K C V \)) for the same voltage, effectively increasing the capacitance as \( C = \frac{Q}{V} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 10 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are placed 20 cm apart. What is the potential energy of the system? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{10 \times 10^{-6} \times (-5 \times 10^{-6})}{0.2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{-50 \times 10^{-12}}{0.2} = -2.25 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 8 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (6, 0, 0) \) and \( (-6, 0, 0) \, \text{cm} \). What is the potential at midpoint? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Distance to midpoint = 0.06 m. \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \left( \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{0.06} + \frac{-4 \times 10^{-6}}{0.06} \right) = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{0.06} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{0.06} = 6 \times 10^5 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with \( C = 100 \, \text{pF} \) in air has a dielectric (\( K = 10 \)) inserted fully between plates. What is the new capacitance?
A metal sphere is placed inside a uniform electric field \( E \). What is the electric field inside the sphere after it reaches electrostatic equilibrium?
options: It depends on the strength of the external field
It is zero due to charge redistribution
It is equal to the external field
It is non-uniform and depends on the sphere's radius
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero. When a metal sphere is placed in a uniform electric field, charges redistribute on its surface such that the induced field inside cancels the external field. This results in a net electric field of zero inside the sphere, regardless of the external field strength, as conductors allow free movement of charges to achieve this equilibrium.

questions.question_text: A point charge \( Q = 8 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C} \) is placed at the origin. Calculate the potential at a point 4 m away from the charge. (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential due to a point charge: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r} \). Substitute: \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-9}}{4} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-9} = 18 \, \text{V} \).

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 9

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with capacitance \( 120 \, \text{pF} \) has a dielectric (\( K = 4 \), thickness \( d/4 \)) inserted. What is the new capacitance? (Original separation \( d \)).
questions.explanation: Potential difference: \( V = E_0 \left( \frac{3d}{4} \right) + \frac{E_0}{K} \left( \frac{d}{4} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{4 \times 4} \right) \). \( V = E_0 d \left( \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{16} \right) = E_0 d \times \frac{13}{16} \). \( C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{\frac{13}{16} V_0} = \frac{16}{13} \times 120 \approx 147.69 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( Q = 24 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C} \) is placed at the origin. Calculate the potential at a point 8 m away from the charge. (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential due to a point charge: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r} \). Substitute: \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{24 \times 10^{-9}}{8} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 3 \times 10^{-9} = 27 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 25 cm has a charge of \( 10 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the electric field at 60 cm from the center? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: For \( r = 0.6 \, \text{m} > R = 0.25 \, \text{m} \), \( E = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{10 \times 10^{-8}}{(0.6)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{10 \times 10^{-8}}{0.36} = 2.5 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A capacitor of \( 5 \, \mu\text{F} \) is charged to \( 100 \, \text{V} \). What is the energy stored in it?
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \times (100)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^4 = 0.025 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 6 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{C m} \) lies along the x-axis. What is the potential at \( (5, 0, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Along the dipole axis (\( \theta = 0^\circ \)): \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{p}{r^2} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-10}}{5^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-10}}{25} = 2.16 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 6 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) makes an angle of \( 45^\circ \) with a uniform field \( E = 5 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: \( U = -p E \cos \theta = -6 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times \cos 45^\circ \). \( \cos 45^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707 \), so \( U = -6 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times 0.707 = -2.121 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the potential energy of an electric dipole in a uniform electric field become minimum when the dipole aligns with the field?
options: The dipole moment cancels the field
The torque is zero at alignment
questions.explanation: The potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field is \( U = -p E \cos \theta \), where \( p \) is the dipole moment, \( E \) is the field strength, and \( \theta \) is the angle between \( p \) and \( E \). The energy is minimum when \( \cos \theta = 1 \), i.e., \( \theta = 0^\circ \), meaning the dipole aligns with the field. At this position, the torque (\( \tau = p E \sin \theta \)) is zero, and the system is in stable equilibrium, minimizing the potential energy.

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with capacitance \( 60 \, \text{pF} \) has a dielectric (\( K = 4 \), thickness \( d/4 \)) inserted. What is the new capacitance? (Original separation \( d \)).
questions.explanation: Potential difference: \( V = E_0 \left( \frac{3d}{4} \right) + \frac{E_0}{K} \left( \frac{d}{4} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{4 \times 4} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{16} \right) = E_0 d \times \frac{13}{16} \). \( C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{\frac{13}{16} V_0} = \frac{16}{13} \times 60 \approx 73.85 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: Two capacitors of \( 60 \, \text{pF} \) and \( 120 \, \text{pF} \) are connected in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?
A dipole with \( p = 3 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{C m} \) makes an angle of \( 90^\circ \) with a uniform field \( E = 2 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: \( U = -p E \cos \theta = -3 \times 10^{-10} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times \cos 90^\circ = 0 \, \text{J} \).

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 10

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 6 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) lies along the z-axis. What is the potential at \( (0, 0, -2) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Along the dipole axis (\( \theta = 180^\circ \)): \( V = -\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{p}{r^2} \). \( V = -9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-9}}{2^2} = -9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-9}}{4} = -13.5 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: In a system of two capacitors connected in series across a battery, why does the capacitor with smaller capacitance store more energy compared to the one with larger capacitance?
options: It has a larger voltage across it
questions.explanation: In series, the charge \( Q \) on each capacitor is the same. Energy stored in a capacitor is \( U = \frac{Q^2}{2C} \). For a smaller capacitance \( C \), the denominator \( 2C \) is smaller, so \( U \) is larger compared to a capacitor with larger \( C \). Alternatively, since \( V = \frac{Q}{C} \), the smaller capacitor has a larger voltage \( V \), and energy \( U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 \) increases with \( V^2 \), leading to more energy in the smaller capacitor.

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a uniformly charged spherical shell remain zero even if the shell is placed in an external uniform electric field?
options: The external field penetrates the shell
Charge redistribution cancels the internal field
The shell's charge neutralizes the field
The field lines bend around the shell
questions.explanation: For a uniformly charged spherical shell in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside is zero regardless of external fields due to electrostatic shielding. Applying Gauss’s law inside the shell (no charge enclosed within the cavity), \( E = 0 \). The external field induces charge redistribution on the shell's outer surface, but this does not affect the interior, as the induced charges ensure the internal field cancels out, maintaining \( E = 0 \) inside the cavity.

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 5 cm has a charge of \( 5 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the potential at its surface? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential at the surface: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{R} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-8}}{0.05} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-6} = 9000 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: In a series combination of capacitors with different dielectric materials between their plates, why do capacitors with higher dielectric constants have lower potential differences?
questions.explanation: In series, the charge \( Q \) on each capacitor is the same. Capacitance is \( C = \frac{K \varepsilon_0 A}{d} \), where \( K \) is the dielectric constant. A higher \( K \) increases \( C \). Since \( V = \frac{Q}{C} \), a larger \( C \) (due to higher \( K \)) results in a smaller \( V \). Thus, capacitors with higher dielectric constants have lower potential differences because their capacitance is larger for the same \( Q \), distributing the voltage inversely with capacitance.

questions.question_text: Why does the total energy stored in a system of capacitors connected in series decrease if one of the capacitors is removed and the battery remains connected?
questions.explanation: In series, the equivalent capacitance \( C_{\text{eq}} \) decreases when a capacitor is removed (\( \frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \sum \frac{1}{C_i} \)). With a battery maintaining constant voltage \( V \), the energy stored is \( U = \frac{1}{2} C_{\text{eq}} V^2 \). A smaller \( C_{\text{eq}} \) reduces \( U \), as energy is directly proportional to capacitance under constant \( V \). Additionally, removing a capacitor redistributes charges, potentially dissipating energy during the process, further reducing total energy.

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 10 cm has a charge of \( 5 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the electric field at 25 cm from the center? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: For \( r = 0.25 \, \text{m} > R = 0.1 \, \text{m} \), \( E = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-8}}{(0.25)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-8}}{0.0625} = 7.2 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +7 \, \mu\text{C} \), \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \), and \( +2 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (0, 0, 0) \), \( (7, 0, 0) \), and \( (0, 7, 0) \, \text{m} \). What is the potential at \( (7, 7, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
A charged particle is released from rest near a large charged conducting sheet. Why does the particle initially accelerate toward or away from the sheet?
options: Due to induced charges on the particle
Due to the uniform electric field of the sheet
questions.explanation: A large charged conducting sheet creates a uniform electric field near its surface (\( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \)). If the sheet is positively charged, the field points away from it; if negatively charged, it points toward it. A charged particle experiences a force \( F = q E \). Depending on the particle's charge (same or opposite to the sheet), it accelerates toward (opposite charges) or away (like charges) due to this force, as the field exerts an attractive or repulsive force.

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 5 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) lies along the y-axis. What is the potential at \( (0, 3, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Along the dipole axis (\( \theta = 0^\circ \)): \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{p}{r^2} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-9}}{3^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-9}}{9} = 5 \, \text{V} \).

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 11

questions.question_text: Why does the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor increase when the plates are moved closer while maintaining the same dielectric?
options: The charge on the plates increases
questions.explanation: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor is \( C = \frac{K \varepsilon_0 A}{d} \), where \( d \) is the separation between plates, \( A \) is the area, and \( K \) is the dielectric constant. When the plates are moved closer, \( d \) decreases, and since \( C \propto \frac{1}{d} \), the capacitance increases. A smaller \( d \) means a stronger field for the same charge (\( E = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 A} \)), allowing more charge storage for the same voltage, thus increasing \( C \).

questions.question_text: A dipole \( p = 3 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is rotated from \( \theta = 0^\circ \) to \( 180^\circ \) in a field \( E = 4 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done: \( W = p E (\cos \theta_0 - \cos \theta_1) = 3 \times 10^{-9} \times 4 \times 10^5 \times (\cos 0^\circ - \cos 180^\circ) \). \( W = 3 \times 10^{-9} \times 4 \times 10^5 \times (1 - (-1)) = 3 \times 10^{-9} \times 4 \times 10^5 \times 2 = 2.4 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside the dielectric of a parallel plate capacitor decrease when the dielectric is inserted while keeping the plates disconnected?
options: Due to increased charge on the plates
Due to polarization opposing the applied field
questions.explanation: When a dielectric (\( K > 1 \)) is inserted into a disconnected capacitor, the charge \( Q \) remains constant. The dielectric polarizes, creating an induced field opposing the applied field. The effective field inside the dielectric becomes \( E = \frac{E_0}{K} \), where \( E_0 = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \) is the field without the dielectric (\( \sigma = Q/A \)). Since \( K > 1 \), the field decreases due to the polarization reducing the net field between the plates.

questions.question_text: Four capacitors of \( 25 \, \mu\text{F} \) each are in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?
A \( 7 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 400 \, \text{V} \). What is the energy stored in it?
A parallel plate capacitor with \( C = 50 \, \text{pF} \) in air has a dielectric (\( K = 4 \)) inserted fully between plates. What is the new capacitance?
questions.explanation: \( C' = K C = 4 \times 50 = 200 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 15 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are placed 12 cm apart. What is the potential energy of the system? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{15 \times 10^{-6} \times (-5 \times 10^{-6})}{0.12} \). \( U = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{-75 \times 10^{-12}}{0.12} = -5.625 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 10 cm has a charge of \( 2 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{C} \). What is the electric field at a point 15 cm from its center? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: For \( r = 0.15 \, \text{m} > R = 0.1 \, \text{m} \), \( E = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{2 \times 10^{-7}}{(0.15)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{2 \times 10^{-7}}{0.0225} = 8 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Two capacitors of \( 20 \, \text{pF} \) and \( 30 \, \text{pF} \) are connected in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?
In a system where a charged conductor is placed inside a larger uncharged hollow conductor, why does the inner conductor induce charges on both the inner and outer surfaces of the outer conductor?
options: Due to the dielectric properties of the conductor
To minimize the electric field outside
To satisfy charge conservation and equilibrium
questions.explanation: When a charged conductor (charge \( Q \)) is placed inside a larger uncharged hollow conductor, the electric field from the inner charge induces \( -Q \) on the inner surface of the hollow conductor to ensure the field inside the conductor's material is zero. Since the hollow conductor is initially uncharged, its total charge must remain zero, so \( +Q \) appears on its outer surface to balance the induced \( -Q \), maintaining charge conservation and equilibrium.

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 12

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field between two large parallel plates with opposite charges remain uniform even if one plate has a dielectric coating on its inner surface?
options: The coating increases the charge on the plates
The field depends on free charge density
questions.explanation: For large parallel plates with charges \( +\sigma \) and \( -\sigma \), the field between them is \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \), uniform due to symmetry. A dielectric coating on one plate polarizes, inducing bound charges, but does not alter the free charge on the plates. The net field between the plates remains determined by the free charge density \( \sigma \), and the uniformity is preserved by the geometry, though the effective field in the dielectric region adjusts locally. For ideal plates, the field remains uniform in the air gap.

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 4 cm has a charge of \( 4 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the potential at its surface? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential at the surface: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{R} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-8}}{0.04} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-6} = 9000 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: In a charged parallel plate capacitor, why does the electric field remain uniform between the plates even when a dielectric slab is partially inserted?
options: Due to increased charge on the plates
Due to the dielectric's non-uniform polarization
Due to the geometry of parallel plates
Due to the dielectric's high conductivity
questions.explanation: The electric field between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is ideally uniform (\( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \)) in air. When a dielectric slab is partially inserted, the field in the air region remains \( E_0 = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \), and in the dielectric region, it reduces to \( E = \frac{E_0}{K} \). However, within each region (air or dielectric), the field remains uniform because the plates are large and parallel, maintaining a constant field perpendicular to the plates despite the dielectric's presence.

questions.question_text: A conductor has a surface charge density of \( 3.5 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside it? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{3.5 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 3.955 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 2 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 500 \, \text{V} \). What is the energy stored in it?
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times (500)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 25 \times 10^4 = 0.25 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a dielectric material decrease when placed in an external field, compared to the field in free space?
options: The field lines bend around the dielectric
Polarization creates an opposing internal field
The dielectric increases the external field
questions.explanation: When a dielectric is placed in an external field \( E_0 \), it polarizes, creating bound charges that produce an internal field \( E_{\text{induced}} \) opposing \( E_0 \). The net field inside the dielectric is \( E = \frac{E_0}{K} \), where \( K > 1 \) is the dielectric constant. For linear dielectrics, \( K > 1 \), so \( E < E_0 \), as the polarization reduces the effective field by aligning dipoles to counteract the external field.

questions.question_text: A charged particle moves along a path between two points in an electric field where the potential difference is zero. What can be inferred about the path taken?
options: The path is a straight line
The path lies on an equipotential surface
The path is parallel to the field lines
questions.explanation: If the potential difference between two points is zero, they lie on the same equipotential surface. The path taken by the particle must lie entirely on this equipotential surface (where \( V \) is constant), as any deviation would imply a potential difference. Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to the electric field, so the particle moves perpendicular to the field direction, doing no work against the field along this path.

questions.question_text: A conductor has a surface charge density of \( 1 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside it? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{1 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 1.13 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 6 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) makes an angle of \( 45^\circ \) with a uniform field \( E = 2 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: \( U = -p E \cos \theta = -6 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times \cos 45^\circ \). \( \cos 45^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707 \), so \( U = -6 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times 0.707 = -8.48 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field just outside a charged conductor depend only on the surface charge density and not on the total charge of the conductor?
options: It is determined by the local surface charge density
The total charge cancels out at the surface
The field inside the conductor shields the total charge
The conductor's shape alters the field distribution
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, the field just outside a conductor is given by \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \), where \( \sigma \) is the local surface charge density. This relation arises from Gauss's law applied to a small Gaussian surface at the conductor's surface. The field depends on the charge enclosed per unit area (\( \sigma \)), not the total charge, because the field is determined locally by the surface charge density at that point, regardless of how much charge resides elsewhere on the conductor.

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 13

questions.question_text: Two capacitors of \( 70 \, \text{pF} \) and \( 140 \, \text{pF} \) are connected in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?

Two charges \( 12 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (5, 0, 0) \) and \( (-5, 0, 0) \, \text{cm} \). What is the potential at midpoint? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Distance to midpoint = 0.05 m. \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \left( \frac{12 \times 10^{-6}}{0.05} + \frac{-3 \times 10^{-6}}{0.05} \right) = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{0.05} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{0.05} = 1.62 \times 10^6 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 5 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) makes an angle of \( 30^\circ \) with a uniform field \( E = 3 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: \( U = -p E \cos \theta = -5 \times 10^{-9} \times 3 \times 10^5 \times \cos 30^\circ \). \( \cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866 \), so \( U = -5 \times 10^{-9} \times 3 \times 10^5 \times 0.866 = -1.299 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole \( p = 8 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is rotated from \( \theta = 0^\circ \) to \( 180^\circ \) in a field \( E = 1 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done: \( W = p E (\cos \theta_0 - \cos \theta_1) = 8 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 10^5 \times (\cos 0^\circ - \cos 180^\circ) \). \( W = 8 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 10^5 \times (1 - (-1)) = 8 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 10^5 \times 2 = 1.6 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the potential difference between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor remain constant when a dielectric slab is inserted while the capacitor is connected to a battery?
options: The dielectric reduces the electric field
The battery maintains a fixed voltage
The charge on the plates remains constant
questions.explanation: When a capacitor is connected to a battery, the potential difference \( V \) across its plates is fixed by the battery. Inserting a dielectric slab (with \( K > 1 \)) increases the capacitance (\( C' = K C \)), but the battery maintains \( V \). To keep \( V \) constant (\( Q = C V \)), the charge \( Q \) on the plates increases (\( Q' = C' V = K C V \)), as the battery supplies additional charge. Thus, the potential difference remains constant because the battery ensures it.

questions.question_text: An isolated charged capacitor is connected across a resistor momentarily. Why does the energy stored in the capacitor decrease to zero after a long time?
options: The charge dissipates as heat in the resistor
The resistor absorbs the electric field
questions.explanation: When a charged capacitor is connected across a resistor, it discharges through the resistor, forming an RC circuit. The charge \( Q \) on the capacitor decreases exponentially (\( Q(t) = Q_0 e^{-t/RC} \)). After a long time (\( t \to \infty \)), \( Q \to 0 \), so the energy \( U = \frac{Q^2}{2C} \to 0 \). The energy is dissipated as heat in the resistor during discharge, leaving no energy stored in the capacitor.

questions.question_text: Three capacitors \( 4 \, \text{pF} \), \( 8 \, \text{pF} \), and \( 16 \, \text{pF} \) are in parallel. What is the total capacitance?
A \( 6 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 100 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 18 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the energy lost?
questions.explanation: Initial energy: \( U_i = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 10^{-6} \times (100)^2 = 0.03 \, \text{J} \). Charge: \( Q = 6 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 = 6 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total \( C = 6 + 18 = 24 \, \mu\text{F} \), \( V = \frac{6 \times 10^{-4}}{24 \times 10^{-6}} = 25 \, \text{V} \). Final energy: \( U_f = \frac{1}{2} \times 24 \times 10^{-6} \times (25)^2 = 0.0075 \, \text{J} \). Loss: \( U_i - U_f = 0.03 - 0.0075 = 0.0225 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Three capacitors \( 10 \, \text{pF} \), \( 20 \, \text{pF} \), and \( 40 \, \text{pF} \) are in parallel. What is the total capacitance?

Two charges \( 18 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -9 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (2, 0, 0) \) and \( (-2, 0, 0) \, \text{cm} \). What is the potential at midpoint? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Distance to midpoint = 0.02 m. \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \left( \frac{18 \times 10^{-6}}{0.02} + \frac{-9 \times 10^{-6}}{0.02} \right) = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{0.02} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-6}}{0.02} = 4.05 \times 10^6 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 20 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -10 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (1, 0, 0) \) and \( (-1, 0, 0) \, \text{cm} \). What is the potential at midpoint? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Distance to midpoint = 0.01 m. \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \left( \frac{20 \times 10^{-6}}{0.01} + \frac{-10 \times 10^{-6}}{0.01} \right) = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{0.01} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{0.01} = 9 \times 10^6 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A charged particle is placed in a region where the electric potential is constant everywhere. What can be inferred about the motion of the particle if it is released from rest?
options: It moves in a circular path
questions.explanation: If the electric potential \( V \) is constant everywhere, the electric field \( E = -\frac{dV}{dx} = 0 \), since the gradient of a constant potential is zero. With no electric field, there is no electrostatic force (\( F = qE \)) acting on the charged particle. If released from rest, the particle experiences no acceleration due to the electric field and thus remains at rest, assuming no other forces (like gravity) are considered.

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with capacitance \( 50 \, \text{pF} \) has a dielectric (\( K = 2 \), thickness \( d/3 \)) inserted. What is the new capacitance? (Original separation \( d \)).
questions.explanation: Potential difference: \( V = E_0 \left( \frac{2d}{3} \right) + \frac{E_0}{K} \left( \frac{d}{3} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3 \times 2} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{6} \right) = E_0 d \times \frac{5}{6} \). \( C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{\frac{5}{6} V_0} = \frac{6}{5} \times 50 = 60 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole \( p = 4 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{C m} \) is in a uniform field \( E = 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \) at \( 60^\circ \). What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: \( U = -\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{E} = -p E \cos \theta = -4 \times 10^{-10} \times 10^5 \times \cos 60^\circ = -4 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.5 = -2 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 3 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) makes an angle of \( 60^\circ \) with a uniform field \( E = 2 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: \( U = -p E \cos \theta = -3 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times \cos 60^\circ \). \( \cos 60^\circ = 0.5 \), so \( U = -3 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times 0.5 = -3 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a conductor vanish in electrostatic equilibrium, even if the conductor is irregularly shaped?
options: Charges redistribute to cancel the internal field
The conductor absorbs the external field
The field accumulates on the surface only
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, free charges in a conductor redistribute to cancel any internal electric field. If there were a field inside, it would exert a force on the free charges, causing them to move until the field becomes zero everywhere inside. This principle holds regardless of shape because conductors allow charge mobility, and equilibrium requires \( E = 0 \) inside, with all excess charge residing on the surface, adjusting to the geometry.

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with capacitance \( 150 \, \text{pF} \) has a dielectric (\( K = 6 \), thickness \( d/5 \)) inserted. What is the new capacitance? (Original separation \( d \)).
questions.explanation: Potential difference: \( V = E_0 \left( \frac{4d}{5} \right) + \frac{E_0}{K} \left( \frac{d}{5} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{4}{5} + \frac{1}{5 \times 6} \right) \). \( V = E_0 d \left( \frac{4}{5} + \frac{1}{30} \right) = E_0 d \times \frac{25}{30} = E_0 d \times \frac{5}{6} \). \( C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{\frac{5}{6} V_0} = \frac{6}{5} \times 150 = 180 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: In an electrostatic shielding scenario, a cavity inside a conductor contains a charge. What can be said about the electric field outside the conductor?
options: It is zero due to shielding
It depends only on the conductor's shape
It depends on the net charge on the conductor
It is zero regardless of the charge on the conductor
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, a conductor with a cavity shields the external region from charges inside the cavity. The charge inside induces an equal and opposite charge on the inner surface of the cavity, and the conductor adjusts its outer surface charge distribution to ensure the field inside the conductor (outside the cavity) is zero. The field outside depends only on the net charge on the conductor's outer surface, which includes the induced charges due to the internal charge but is not shielded, so the field outside is non-zero and unaffected by the cavity's internal configuration.

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 18 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) are placed 18 cm apart. What is the potential energy of the system? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{18 \times 10^{-6} \times (-6 \times 10^{-6})}{0.18} \). \( U = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{-108 \times 10^{-12}}{0.18} = -5.4 \, \text{J} \).

questions.explanation: Potential due to a point charge: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r} \). Substitute: \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{12 \times 10^{-9}}{6} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-9} = 18 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Why can't the electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium have a tangential component along its surface?
options: It would cause charges to move along the surface, violating equilibrium
It would create a potential difference inside the conductor
It would lead to infinite energy storage
It would make the field inside non-zero
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero, and charges reside on the surface. If the electric field had a tangential component along the surface, it would exert a force on the free charges, causing them to move along the surface. This movement would contradict the condition of equilibrium where no net motion of charges occurs. Therefore, the field must be normal to the surface, ensuring no tangential component exists to drive charge motion.

questions.question_text: A conductor has a surface charge density of \( 4 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside it? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 4.52 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 10 \, \mu\text{C} \) is moved from infinity to a point where the potential is \( 30 \, \text{V} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done = Potential energy = \( q V \). \( W = 10 \times 10^{-6} \times 30 = 3 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} = 0.3 \, \text{mJ} \).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with capacitance \( 80 \, \text{pF} \) has a dielectric (\( K = 5 \), thickness \( d/5 \)) inserted. What is the new capacitance? (Original separation \( d \)).
questions.explanation: Potential difference: \( V = E_0 \left( \frac{4d}{5} \right) + \frac{E_0}{K} \left( \frac{d}{5} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{4}{5} + \frac{1}{5 \times 5} \right) \). \( V = E_0 d \left( \frac{4}{5} + \frac{1}{25} \right) = E_0 d \times \frac{21}{25} \). \( C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{\frac{21}{25} V_0} = \frac{25}{21} \times 80 \approx 95.24 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 8 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) makes an angle of \( 60^\circ \) with a uniform field \( E = 1 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: \( U = -p E \cos \theta = -8 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 10^5 \times \cos 60^\circ \). \( \cos 60^\circ = 0.5 \), so \( U = -8 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 10^5 \times 0.5 = -4 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 10 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 40 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 10 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the final potential difference?
questions.explanation: Initial charge: \( Q = 10 \times 10^{-6} \times 40 = 4 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total capacitance: \( 10 + 10 = 20 \, \mu\text{F} \). Final voltage: \( V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{4 \times 10^{-4}}{20 \times 10^{-6}} = 20 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A capacitor with \( C = 10 \, \text{pF} \) in air has a dielectric (\( K = 4 \), thickness \( d/2 \)) inserted. What is the new capacitance if \( d \) is the original separation? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 A/d = 10 \, \text{pF} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential difference: \( V = E_0 \left( \frac{d}{2} \right) + \frac{E_0}{K} \left( \frac{d}{2} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2 \times 4} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{8} \right) = \frac{5}{8} E_0 d \). \( C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{\frac{5}{8} V_0} = \frac{8}{5} \times \frac{Q}{V_0} = \frac{8}{5} \times 10 = 16 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 15 cm has a charge of \( 9 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the electric field at 20 cm from the center? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: For \( r = 0.2 \, \text{m} > R = 0.15 \, \text{m} \), \( E = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-8}}{(0.2)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-8}}{0.04} = 2.025 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( Q = 15 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C} \) is placed at the origin. Calculate the potential at a point 5 m away from the charge. (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential due to a point charge: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r} \). Substitute: \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{15 \times 10^{-9}}{5} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 3 \times 10^{-9} = 27 \, \text{V} \).

questions.explanation: Work done = Potential energy = \( q V \). \( W = 6 \times 10^{-6} \times 150 = 9 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} = 0.9 \, \text{mJ} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 3 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 300 \, \text{V} \). What is the energy stored in it?
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 10^{-6} \times (300)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 10^{-6} \times 9 \times 10^4 = 0.135 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +3 \, \mu\text{C} \), \( -2 \, \mu\text{C} \), and \( +4 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (0, 0, 0) \), \( (3, 0, 0) \), and \( (0, 4, 0) \, \text{m} \). questions.explanation: Work done: \( W = p E (\cos \theta_0 - \cos \theta_1) = 7 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times (\cos 90^\circ - \cos 0^\circ) \). \( W = 7 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times (0 - 1) = -1.4 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 5 \, \mu\text{C} \) is moved from infinity to a point where the potential is \( 300 \, \text{V} \). What is the work done?

questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-6} \times (-3 \times 10^{-6})}{0.12} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{-18 \times 10^{-12}}{0.12} = -1.35 \, \text{J} \).
