questions.explanation: \( C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \frac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.06}{0.3 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.77 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{F} = 1770 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a conductor remain zero when a non-symmetric external field is applied?
options: The field cancels due to symmetry
Charge redistribution cancels the field inside
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor must be zero, regardless of the external field’s symmetry. Free charges redistribute on the conductor’s surface to cancel the external field inside. For a non-symmetric field, the surface charge distribution adjusts accordingly—more charges where the field is stronger and fewer where weaker—ensuring the net field inside is zero, as any internal field would cause charge motion, contradicting equilibrium.

questions.question_text: A \( 8 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 50 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 8 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the final potential difference?
questions.explanation: Initial charge: \( Q = 8 \times 10^{-6} \times 50 = 4 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total capacitance: \( 8 + 8 = 16 \, \mu\text{F} \). Final voltage: \( V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{4 \times 10^{-4}}{16 \times 10^{-6}} = 25 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 8 cm has a charge of \( 4 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the electric field at 12 cm from the center? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: For \( r = 0.12 \, \text{m} > R = 0.08 \, \text{m} \), \( E = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-8}}{(0.12)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{4 \times 10^{-8}}{0.0144} = 2.5 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the potential at the surface of a charged conductor vary if the conductor has an irregular shape?
options: Due to varying electric field strength
It stays constant to maintain equilibrium
questions.explanation: For a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, the potential is constant throughout its volume and surface because \( E = 0 \) inside, so no work is done moving a charge within. However, for an irregular shape, the surface charge density \( \sigma \) varies (higher at sharper regions due to higher curvature), affecting the field just outside (\( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \)). Despite this, the potential \( V \) on the surface remains constant across the entire surface, as any variation would cause charge flow, contradicting equilibrium. The question may imply field variation, but potential is constant.

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 2 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) lies along the z-axis. What is the potential at \( (0, 0, 4) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Along the dipole axis (\( \theta = 0^\circ \)): \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{p}{r^2} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{2 \times 10^{-9}}{4^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{2 \times 10^{-9}}{16} = 1.125 \, \text{V} \).

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 18

questions.question_text: In a system where a positively charged sphere is enclosed by an uncharged conducting shell, why does the outer surface of the shell acquire a negative charge if a negative charge is brought near it?
options: Due to the shell's dielectric properties
Due to repulsion by the external negative charge
Due to the inner sphere's positive charge
Due to grounding of the shell
questions.explanation: The positively charged sphere induces a negative charge on the inner surface of the shell and a positive charge on its outer surface to maintain zero field inside the conductor. When a negative charge is brought near the shell, it repels negative charges to the far side of the shell and attracts positive charges closer, altering the charge distribution. The shell, being uncharged initially, redistributes charges so the outer surface gains a net negative charge to balance the influence of the external negative charge while maintaining equilibrium.

questions.question_text: A conductor has a surface charge density of \( 1.5 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside it? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 1.695 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 2 \, \mu\text{C} \) is moved from infinity to a point with potential \( 500 \, \text{V} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done = Potential energy = \( q V \). \( W = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 500 = 10^{-3} \, \text{J} = 1 \, \text{mJ} \).

questions.question_text: Two capacitors of \( 30 \, \text{pF} \) and \( 60 \, \text{pF} \) are connected in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?

Two charges \( 14 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -6 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (3, 0, 0) \) and \( (-3, 0, 0) \, \text{cm} \). What is the potential at midpoint? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Distance to midpoint = 0.03 m. \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \left( \frac{14 \times 10^{-6}}{0.03} + \frac{-6 \times 10^{-6}}{0.03} \right) = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{0.03} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{0.03} = 2.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A conductor has a surface charge density of \( 4.5 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C/m}^2 \). What is the electric field just outside it? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{4.5 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 5.085 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 3 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 200 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 9 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the energy lost?
questions.explanation: Initial energy: \( U_i = \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 10^{-6} \times (200)^2 = 0.06 \, \text{J} \). Charge: \( Q = 3 \times 10^{-6} \times 200 = 6 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total \( C = 3 + 9 = 12 \, \mu\text{F} \), \( V = \frac{6 \times 10^{-4}}{12 \times 10^{-6}} = 50 \, \text{V} \). Final energy: \( U_f = \frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 10^{-6} \times (50)^2 = 0.015 \, \text{J} \). Loss: \( U_i - U_f = 0.06 - 0.015 = 0.045 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: When a charged conductor is placed in contact with an uncharged conductor of smaller size, why does the smaller conductor acquire a higher surface charge density upon reaching equilibrium?
options: It has a larger surface area
It has a smaller radius, increasing density
questions.explanation: When two conductors reach equilibrium, they share charge and attain the same potential. Potential on a conductor's surface is \( V = \frac{Q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R} \) for a sphere (or similar for other shapes). For equal \( V \), \( \frac{Q_1}{R_1} = \frac{Q_2}{R_2} \), so \( Q \propto R \). Surface charge density \( \sigma = \frac{Q}{4 \pi R^2} \), so \( \sigma \propto \frac{Q}{R^2} \propto \frac{R}{R^2} = \frac{1}{R} \). The smaller conductor (smaller \( R \)) has higher \( \sigma \) because \( \sigma \) is inversely proportional to radius.

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 2 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{C m} \) is at the origin, aligned along the x-axis. What is the potential at \( (0, 2, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Position vector \( \mathbf{r} = (0, 2, 0) \), \( r = 2 \, \text{m} \), \( \hat{\mathbf{r}} = (0, 1, 0) \). Dipole moment \( \mathbf{p} = (2 \times 10^{-10}, 0, 0) \). \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{\mathbf{p} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}}}{r^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{(2 \times 10^{-10}) \cdot (0)}{2^2} = 0 \, \text{V} \) (since \( \cos \theta = 0 \), equatorial plane).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area \( 0.05 \, \text{m}^2 \) and separation 0.25 mm in air. What is its capacitance? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \frac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.05}{0.25 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.77 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{F} = 1770 \, \text{pF} \).

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 19

questions.question_text: A dipole \( p = 10 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is rotated from \( \theta = 0^\circ \) to \( 90^\circ \) in a field \( E = 4 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done: \( W = p E (\cos \theta_0 - \cos \theta_1) = 10 \times 10^{-9} \times 4 \times 10^5 \times (\cos 0^\circ - \cos 90^\circ) \). \( W = 10 \times 10^{-9} \times 4 \times 10^5 \times (1 - 0) = 4 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 5 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 120 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 15 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the energy lost?
questions.explanation: Initial energy: \( U_i = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \times (120)^2 = 0.036 \, \text{J} \). Charge: \( Q = 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 120 = 6 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total \( C = 5 + 15 = 20 \, \mu\text{F} \), \( V = \frac{6 \times 10^{-4}}{20 \times 10^{-6}} = 30 \, \text{V} \). Final energy: \( U_f = \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 10^{-6} \times (30)^2 = 0.009 \, \text{J} \). Loss: \( U_i - U_f = 0.036 - 0.009 = 0.027 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field inside a uniformly charged spherical shell vary linearly with distance from the center if a point charge is placed at the center?
options: Due to the shell's charge distribution
Due to the shell's dielectric properties
Due to the point charge's field variation
questions.explanation: Without the point charge, the field inside a uniformly charged spherical shell is zero (Gauss’s law). With a point charge \( Q \) at the center, the field inside the shell is due to the point charge only (\( E = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \)), which varies as \( \frac{1}{r^2} \), not linearly. The question may imply a misunderstanding; in standard electrostatics (per the PDF), the shell contributes no field inside, and the point charge's field does not vary linearly. Thus, \( E \propto \frac{1}{r^2} \), correcting the premise to standard interpretation.

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with \( C = 20 \, \text{pF} \) in air has a dielectric (\( K = 3 \)) inserted fully between plates. What is the new capacitance?
questions.explanation: \( C' = K C = 3 \times 20 = 60 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 4 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 50 \, \text{V} \) and then connected to an uncharged \( 2 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the final energy?
questions.explanation: Initial charge: \( Q = 4 \times 10^{-6} \times 50 = 2 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total capacitance: \( 4 + 2 = 6 \, \mu\text{F} \). Final voltage: \( V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-4}}{6 \times 10^{-6}} = 33.33 \, \text{V} \). Final energy: \( U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 10^{-6} \times (33.33)^2 = 3.33 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: In a system where a charged particle moves along a curved path between two points with different potentials, what can be inferred about the work done by the electric field?
options: It depends on the length of the path
It varies with the curvature of the path
It depends only on the potential difference
It is zero due to the curved trajectory
questions.explanation: The work done by the electric field on a charge \( q \) moving between two points is \( W = q (V_{\text{final}} - V_{\text{initial}}) \), where \( V \) is the potential. Since the electrostatic field is conservative, this work depends only on the potential difference between the points and not on the path taken (straight or curved). Thus, the work done is path-independent and determined solely by the potential difference, regardless of the curved trajectory.

questions.question_text: A dipole \( p = 5 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is rotated from \( \theta = 90^\circ \) to \( 180^\circ \) in a field \( E = 2 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done: \( W = p E (\cos \theta_0 - \cos \theta_1) = 5 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times (\cos 90^\circ - \cos 180^\circ) \). \( W = 5 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times (0 - (-1)) = 5 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^5 \times 1 = 10^{-3} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Four capacitors of \( 20 \, \mu\text{F} \) each are in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?

A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area \( 0.07 \, \text{m}^2 \) and separation 0.35 mm in air. What is its capacitance? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \frac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.07}{0.35 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.77 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{F} = 1770 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 14 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 20 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 14 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the final potential difference?
questions.explanation: Initial charge: \( Q = 14 \times 10^{-6} \times 20 = 2.8 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total capacitance: \( 14 + 14 = 28 \, \mu\text{F} \). Final voltage: \( V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{2.8 \times 10^{-4}}{28 \times 10^{-6}} = 10 \, \text{V} \).

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 20

questions.question_text: A dipole \( p = 9 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is rotated from \( \theta = 90^\circ \) to \( 180^\circ \) in a field \( E = 5 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done: \( W = p E (\cos \theta_0 - \cos \theta_1) = 9 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times (\cos 90^\circ - \cos 180^\circ) \). \( W = 9 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times (0 - (-1)) = 9 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times 1 = 4.5 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 5 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are placed 10 cm apart. What is the potential energy of the system? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-6} \times (-5 \times 10^{-6})}{0.1} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{-25 \times 10^{-12}}{0.1} = -2.25 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 3 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) lies along the x-axis. What is the potential at \( (0, 5, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: In the equatorial plane (\( \theta = 90^\circ \)): \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{p \cos \theta}{r^2} \). Since \( \cos 90^\circ = 0 \), \( V = 0 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A charged particle is placed in a region where the electric potential varies linearly with distance. What can be said about the electric field in that region?
questions.explanation: The electric field \( E \) is related to potential \( V \) by \( E = -\frac{dV}{dx} \). If \( V \) varies linearly with distance (\( V = kx + c \)), then \( \frac{dV}{dx} = k \), a constant. Thus, \( E = -k \), meaning the electric field is uniform (constant magnitude and direction) in the direction opposite to the gradient of \( V \), consistent with a linear potential gradient creating a constant field.

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 3 cm has a charge of \( 3 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the potential at its surface? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential at the surface: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{R} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{3 \times 10^{-8}}{0.03} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-6} = 9000 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 7 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) lies along the x-axis. What is the potential at \( (4, 0, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Along the dipole axis (\( \theta = 0^\circ \)): \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{p}{r^2} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{7 \times 10^{-9}}{4^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{7 \times 10^{-9}}{16} = 3.9375 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with \( C = 80 \, \text{pF} \) in air has a dielectric (\( K = 8 \)) inserted fully between plates. What is the new capacitance?
questions.explanation: \( C' = K C = 8 \times 80 = 640 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 5 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 200 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 5 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the final potential difference?
questions.explanation: Initial charge: \( Q = 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 200 = 10^{-3} \, \text{C} \). Total capacitance: \( 5 + 5 = 10 \, \mu\text{F} \). Final voltage: \( V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{10^{-3}}{10 \times 10^{-6}} = 100 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 4 cm has a charge of \( 8 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the potential at its surface? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential at the surface: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{R} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-8}}{0.04} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-6} = 18000 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with capacitance \( 300 \, \text{pF} \) has a dielectric (\( K = 3 \), thickness \( d/8 \)) inserted. What is the new capacitance? (Original separation \( d \)).
questions.explanation: Potential difference: \( V = E_0 \left( \frac{7d}{8} \right) + \frac{E_0}{K} \left( \frac{d}{8} \right) = E_0 d \left( \frac{7}{8} + \frac{1}{8 \times 3} \right) \). \( V = E_0 d \left( \frac{7}{8} + \frac{1}{24} \right) = E_0 d \times \frac{22}{24} = E_0 d \times \frac{11}{12} \). \( C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{Q}{\frac{11}{12} V_0} = \frac{12}{11} \times 300 \approx 327.27 \, \text{pF} \).

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 21

questions.question_text: A \( 8 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 500 \, \text{V} \). What is the energy stored in it?
A \( 1 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 400 \, \text{V} \). What is the energy stored in it?
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 10^{-6} \times (400)^2 \). \( U = \frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 10^{-6} \times 16 \times 10^4 = 0.08 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Three capacitors \( 6 \, \text{pF} \), \( 12 \, \text{pF} \), and \( 4 \, \text{pF} \) are in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?
A \( 2 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 200 \, \text{V} \) loses how much energy when connected to an uncharged \( 3 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor?
questions.explanation: Initial energy: \( U_i = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times (200)^2 = 0.04 \, \text{J} \). Charge: \( Q = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 200 = 4 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total \( C = 2 + 3 = 5 \, \mu\text{F} \), \( V = \frac{4 \times 10^{-4}}{5 \times 10^{-6}} = 80 \, \text{V} \). Final energy: \( U_f = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \times (80)^2 = 0.016 \, \text{J} \). Loss: \( 0.04 - 0.016 = 0.024 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +10 \, \mu\text{C} \), \( -7 \, \mu\text{C} \), and \( +5 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (0, 0, 0) \), \( (10, 0, 0) \), and \( (0, 10, 0) \, \text{m} \). What is the potential at \( (10, 10, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).

Two charges \( 6 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -3 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (10, 0, 0) \) and \( (-10, 0, 0) \, \text{cm} \). What is the potential at midpoint? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Distance to midpoint = 0.1 m. \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \left( \frac{6 \times 10^{-6}}{0.1} + \frac{-3 \times 10^{-6}}{0.1} \right) = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{0.1} = 2.7 \times 10^5 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: When a dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of a charged parallel plate capacitor (disconnected from the battery), what happens to the energy stored in the capacitor?
options: It increases due to higher capacitance
It decreases due to reduced potential difference
It remains the same due to constant charge
It becomes zero as the field vanishes
questions.explanation: When a dielectric slab (with \( K > 1 \)) is inserted into a disconnected capacitor, the charge \( Q \) remains constant. The capacitance increases (\( C' = K C \)), and the potential difference decreases (\( V' = V/K \)). The energy stored is given by \( U = \frac{Q^2}{2C} \), so with increased \( C \), the energy decreases (\( U' = \frac{Q^2}{2 K C} \)), as \( K > 1 \). The energy decrease occurs because work is done by the electric field to polarize the dielectric.

questions.question_text: Why does the potential energy of a system of two charges depend only on their separation and not on their orientation in space?
options: Due to the charges' alignment with the field
Due to the field's directional dependence
Due to the charges' orbital motion
Due to the isotropic nature of Coulomb's law
questions.explanation: The potential energy between two point charges is \( U = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} \), where \( r \) is the distance between them. This expression depends only on the magnitude of the separation \( r \), not on the direction or orientation of the line joining the charges in space, because the Coulomb force is isotropic (depends only on distance) and the potential is a scalar quantity derived from integrating the force over distance, independent of spatial orientation.

questions.question_text: Three capacitors \( 8 \, \text{pF} \), \( 16 \, \text{pF} \), and \( 32 \, \text{pF} \) are in parallel. What is the total capacitance?
Why does the electric field inside a charged spherical shell vary linearly with distance from the center when a uniform dielectric fills the interior?
options: Due to the field's inverse square law
Due to the shell's non-uniform charge
It does not vary, field is zero inside
questions.explanation: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance typically assumes no charge inside a spherical shell, leading to \( E = 0 \). However, if misinterpreted as a charged dielectric sphere (common in advanced contexts but not in the PDF), the field varies as \( E \propto r \). Since the PDF context implies an empty shell or uniform shell charge, \( E = 0 \). Assuming a misinterpretation, the correct context is \( E = 0 \), but for a filled dielectric with uniform charge (not in PDF), \( E \) varies linearly. Here, we clarify: \( E = 0 \) inside a shell, so no variation.

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 22

questions.question_text: A point charge \( Q = 18 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C} \) is placed at the origin. Calculate the potential at a point 6 m away from the charge. (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential due to a point charge: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r} \). Substitute: \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{18 \times 10^{-9}}{6} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 3 \times 10^{-9} = 27 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with \( C = 70 \, \text{pF} \) in air has a dielectric (\( K = 5 \)) inserted fully between plates. What is the new capacitance?
questions.explanation: \( C' = K C = 5 \times 70 = 350 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( Q = 9 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C} \) is placed at the origin. Calculate the potential at a point 3 m away from the charge. (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential due to a point charge: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r} \). Substitute: \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{9 \times 10^{-9}}{3} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 3 \times 10^{-9} = 27 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Three charges \( +11 \, \mu\text{C} \), \( -8 \, \mu\text{C} \), and \( +6 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (0, 0, 0) \), \( (11, 0, 0) \), and \( (0, 11, 0) \, \text{m} \). What is the potential at \( (11, 11, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
Three capacitors \( 5 \, \text{pF} \), \( 10 \, \text{pF} \), and \( 20 \, \text{pF} \) are in parallel. What is the total capacitance?

A dielectric slab is partially inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor while maintaining a constant voltage across the plates. What happens to the electric field between the plates in the region where the dielectric is present?
options: It decreases due to the dielectric's polarization
It increases due to increased charge on the plates
It remains unchanged due to constant voltage
It becomes zero inside the dielectric
questions.explanation: When a dielectric slab (with dielectric constant \( K > 1 \)) is inserted between the plates of a capacitor with constant voltage \( V \), the electric field \( E \) in the dielectric region decreases. The electric field in a dielectric is given by \( E = \frac{E_0}{K} \), where \( E_0 = \frac{V}{d} \) is the field without the dielectric (\( d \) is the plate separation). Since \( K > 1 \), \( E \) is reduced in the dielectric region compared to the air region, as the dielectric polarizes and induces charges that oppose the applied field.

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 4 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) makes an angle of \( 30^\circ \) with a uniform field \( E = 5 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: \( U = -p E \cos \theta = -4 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times \cos 30^\circ \). \( \cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866 \), so \( U = -4 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^4 \times 0.866 = -1.732 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Five capacitors of \( 20 \, \mu\text{F} \) each are in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?
A dipole \( p = 2 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) is rotated from \( \theta = 90^\circ \) to \( 0^\circ \) in a field \( E = 5 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done: \( W = p E (\cos \theta_0 - \cos \theta_1) = 2 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^5 \times (\cos 90^\circ - \cos 0^\circ) = 2 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^5 \times (0 - 1) = -10^{-3} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: In a system of two identical conductors initially charged differently and then connected by a wire, why does the final energy of the system decrease?
options: The conductors lose charge to ground
Energy is lost during charge redistribution
questions.explanation: Initially, the conductors have charges \( Q_1 \) and \( Q_2 \), with energy \( U_i = \frac{Q_1^2}{2C} + \frac{Q_2^2}{2C} \). Upon connection, charge redistributes to equal potentials, total charge \( Q_1 + Q_2 \) splits equally (\( \frac{Q_1 + Q_2}{2} \) each), so final energy \( U_f = 2 \times \frac{\left(\frac{Q_1 + Q_2}{2}\right)^2}{2C} = \frac{(Q_1 + Q_2)^2}{4C} \). Typically, \( (Q_1 + Q_2)^2 < Q_1^2 + Q_2^2 \) unless \( Q_1 = Q_2 \), so \( U_f < U_i \), with energy lost as heat or radiation during charge flow.

tests.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance Chapter-Wise Test 23

questions.question_text: Four capacitors of \( 5 \, \mu\text{F} \) each are in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?
When a dielectric slab fills only half the space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor (connected to a battery), why does the electric field differ in the dielectric and air regions?
options: Due to polarization reducing the field in the dielectric
Due to increased capacitance in the air region
questions.explanation: With a constant voltage \( V \) across the plates, the electric field \( E \) varies between regions. In the air region, \( E_{\text{air}} = \frac{V}{d} \), where \( d \) is the plate separation. In the dielectric region (\( K > 1 \)), polarization reduces the field: \( E_{\text{dielectric}} = \frac{E_{\text{air}}}{K} = \frac{V}{K d} \). Since \( K > 1 \), \( E_{\text{dielectric}} < E_{\text{air}} \). The field differs because the dielectric polarizes, creating an opposing field that reduces the net field within it, while the air region experiences the full field.

questions.question_text: A dipole \( p = 8 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{C m} \) is rotated from \( \theta = 0^\circ \) to \( 90^\circ \) in a field \( E = 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done: \( W = p E (\cos \theta_0 - \cos \theta_1) = 8 \times 10^{-10} \times 10^6 \times (\cos 0^\circ - \cos 90^\circ) = 8 \times 10^{-4} \times (1 - 0) = 8 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) lies along the y-axis. What is the potential at \( (0, 3, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Along the dipole axis (\( \theta = 0^\circ \)): \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{p}{r^2} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{10^{-9}}{3^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{10^{-9}}{9} = 1 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A dipole with \( p = 5 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) makes an angle of \( 30^\circ \) with a uniform field \( E = 3 \times 10^4 \, \text{N/C} \). What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: \( U = -p E \cos \theta = -5 \times 10^{-9} \times 3 \times 10^4 \times \cos 30^\circ \). \( \cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866 \), so \( U = -5 \times 10^{-9} \times 3 \times 10^4 \times 0.866 = -1.3 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 5 cm has a charge of \( 5 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the potential at its surface? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential at the surface: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{R} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-8}}{0.05} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-6} = 9000 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 6 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 150 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 9 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the energy lost?
questions.explanation: Initial energy: \( U_i = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 10^{-6} \times (150)^2 = 0.0675 \, \text{J} \). Charge: \( Q = 6 \times 10^{-6} \times 150 = 9 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total \( C = 6 + 9 = 15 \, \mu\text{F} \), \( V = \frac{9 \times 10^{-4}}{15 \times 10^{-6}} = 60 \, \text{V} \). Final energy: \( U_f = \frac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 10^{-6} \times (60)^2 = 0.027 \, \text{J} \). Loss: \( U_i - U_f = 0.0675 - 0.027 = 0.0405 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with \( A = 0.01 \, \text{m}^2 \), \( d = 1 \, \text{mm} \) has a dielectric (\( K = 5 \)). What is its capacitance? (Take \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 K A}{d} = \frac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 5 \times 0.01}{10^{-3}} = 4.425 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{F} = 442.5 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the potential due to an electric dipole fall off as \( 1/r^2 \) at large distances, unlike the potential of a point charge which falls off as \( 1/r \)?
options: The dipole has a larger charge magnitude
The dipole's charges cancel out more rapidly with distance
The dipole's field is always zero at large distances
The dipole has a larger separation between charges
questions.explanation: The potential due to a point charge falls as \( 1/r \) because it behaves as a single source of charge. An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance, so their potentials partially cancel out at large distances. The net potential depends on the dipole moment and the angle between the position vector and dipole axis, leading to a \( 1/r^2 \) dependence, as derived from the superposition of potentials from the two charges, with higher-order terms becoming negligible at large \( r \).

questions.question_text: When two identical capacitors, one charged and one uncharged, are connected in parallel, why does the total energy decrease even though charge is conserved?
options: The capacitors mutually cancel their energies
Energy is lost as heat during charge redistribution
The total charge halves, reducing energy
questions.explanation: When a charged capacitor (\( C \), charge \( Q \), voltage \( V \)) is connected in parallel with an uncharged capacitor (\( C \)), the total capacitance becomes \( 2C \), and the charge redistributes to a final voltage \( V' = Q/(2C) = V/2 \). Initial energy is \( U_i = \frac{Q^2}{2C} \), while final energy is \( U_f = \frac{(Q)^2}{2 \times 2C} = \frac{Q^2}{4C} \), which is half the initial energy. The decrease occurs because energy is lost as heat or radiation during the transient current flow when charges redistribute, even though charge is conserved.

questions.question_text: A spherical conductor of radius 20 cm has a charge of \( 8 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{C} \). What is the electric field at 50 cm from the center? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: For \( r = 0.5 \, \text{m} > R = 0.2 \, \text{m} \), \( E = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \). \( E = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-8}}{(0.5)^2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-8}}{0.25} = 2.88 \times 10^3 \, \text{N/C} \).

questions.question_text: Two capacitors of \( 15 \, \text{pF} \) each are connected in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?
A \( 5 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 200 \, \text{V} \). What is the energy stored in it?
In an electrostatic field, if a positive charge is moved along an equipotential surface, what can be said about the work done by the electric field?
options: It depends on the path taken
It is proportional to the distance moved
questions.explanation: An equipotential surface has a constant potential at all points. The work done by the electric field when a charge moves along such a surface is zero because the potential difference between any two points on the surface is zero (\( W = q \Delta V \), and \( \Delta V = 0 \)). Additionally, the electric field is always perpendicular to an equipotential surface, so there is no component of the field along the direction of motion, confirming that no work is done.

questions.question_text: A point charge \( Q = 6 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C} \) is placed at the origin. Calculate the potential at a point 2 m away from the charge. (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential due to a point charge: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r} \). Substitute: \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{6 \times 10^{-9}}{2} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 3 \times 10^{-9} = 27 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( Q = 21 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C} \) is placed at the origin. Calculate the potential at a point 7 m away from the charge. (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential due to a point charge: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r} \). Substitute: \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{21 \times 10^{-9}}{7} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 3 \times 10^{-9} = 27 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field due to an infinite charged sheet remain constant with distance from the sheet?
options: The field depends only on surface charge density
The field decreases inversely with distance
The sheet's charge varies with distance
The field cancels out at large distances
questions.explanation: Using Gauss’s law for an infinite charged sheet with surface charge density \( \sigma \), a Gaussian surface (e.g., a cylinder perpendicular to the sheet) shows that the electric field \( E \) is perpendicular to the sheet and constant. The flux through the cylinder's end caps is \( E \cdot 2A \), and the enclosed charge is \( \sigma A \), so \( E \cdot 2A = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \), giving \( E = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \). Since no distance term appears, \( E \) is independent of distance from the sheet.

questions.question_text: When a conductor is placed in an external electric field, why does the potential throughout its volume become constant in electrostatic equilibrium?
options: Because the electric field inside is zero
Because charges accumulate only inside the conductor
Because the external field penetrates the conductor
Because the potential varies linearly inside
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero because free charges rearrange to cancel any internal field. Since the electric field is the negative gradient of potential (\( E = -\frac{dV}{dr} \)), if \( E = 0 \), the potential gradient must be zero, implying the potential \( V \) is constant throughout the conductor's volume. Any potential difference would drive charge movement, contradicting the equilibrium state.

questions.question_text: An electric dipole with moment \( p = 8 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C m} \) lies along the y-axis. What is the potential at \( (0, -4, 0) \, \text{m} \)? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Along the dipole axis (\( \theta = 180^\circ \)): \( V = -\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{p}{r^2} \). \( V = -9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-9}}{4^2} = -9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-9}}{16} = -4.5 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 2 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 400 \, \text{V} \) is connected to an uncharged \( 6 \, \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. What is the energy lost?
questions.explanation: Initial energy: \( U_i = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times (400)^2 = 0.16 \, \text{J} \). Charge: \( Q = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 400 = 8 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{C} \). Total \( C = 2 + 6 = 8 \, \mu\text{F} \), \( V = \frac{8 \times 10^{-4}}{8 \times 10^{-6}} = 100 \, \text{V} \). Final energy: \( U_f = \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 10^{-6} \times (100)^2 = 0.04 \, \text{J} \). Loss: \( U_i - U_f = 0.16 - 0.04 = 0.12 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the energy density in an electric field depend on the square of the field strength?
options: Due to the field's linear variation
Due to the permittivity's dependence on \( E \)
Due to the quadratic nature of energy storage
Due to the inverse square law of fields
questions.explanation: The energy density in an electric field is given by \( u = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E^2 \). This arises from the energy stored in a capacitor (\( U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 \)), scaled over the volume. For a parallel plate capacitor, \( E = \frac{V}{d} \), \( C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} \), so \( U = \frac{1}{2} \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} (E d)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E^2 (A d) \), where \( A d \) is the volume. Thus, energy density \( u = \frac{U}{A d} = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E^2 \), showing the \( E^2 \) dependence due to the quadratic relation between energy and field.

questions.question_text: Why does the electric field near the edge of a charged conducting plate differ from the field at the center of the plate?
options: Charge density is uniform across the plate
The field lines are denser at the center
The plate's thickness varies at the edges
Field lines fringe outward at the edges
questions.explanation: Near the center of a large charged conducting plate, the field is approximately uniform (\( E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \)), as the plate behaves like an infinite sheet. At the edges, the field lines fringe outward due to the finite size of the plate, leading to a non-uniform field. The charge density \( \sigma \) may also increase near edges due to higher curvature or boundary effects, causing the field to be stronger and non-perpendicular, differing from the uniform field at the center.

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 16 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (4, 0, 0) \) and \( (-4, 0, 0) \, \text{cm} \). What is the potential at midpoint? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Distance to midpoint = 0.04 m. \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \left( \frac{16 \times 10^{-6}}{0.04} + \frac{-4 \times 10^{-6}}{0.04} \right) = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{12 \times 10^{-6}}{0.04} \). \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{12 \times 10^{-6}}{0.04} = 2.7 \times 10^6 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 32 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -16 \, \mu\text{C} \) are placed 32 cm apart. What is the potential energy of the system? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: \( U = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{32 \times 10^{-6} \times (-16 \times 10^{-6})}{0.32} \). \( U = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{-512 \times 10^{-12}}{0.32} = -14.4 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Two charges \( 8 \, \mu\text{C} \) and \( -4 \, \mu\text{C} \) are at \( (-6, 0, 0) \) and \( (6, 0, 0) \, \text{cm} \) in an external field \( E = 10^5/r^2 \, \text{N/C} \). What is the total potential energy? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Mutual energy: \( U_{12} = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{8 \times 10^{-6} \times (-4 \times 10^{-6})}{0.12} = -2.4 \, \text{J} \). External potential: \( V(r) = \frac{10^5}{r} \), at \( r = 0.06 \, \text{m} \), \( V = \frac{10^5}{0.06} = 1.67 \times 10^6 \, \text{V} \). External energy: \( 8 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.67 \times 10^6 + (-4 \times 10^{-6}) \times 1.67 \times 10^6 = 13.36 - 6.68 = 6.68 \, \text{J} \). Total: \( -2.4 + 6.68 = 4.28 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with \( C = 90 \, \text{pF} \) in air has a dielectric (\( K = 9 \)) inserted fully between plates. What is the new capacitance?
questions.explanation: \( C' = K C = 9 \times 90 = 810 \, \text{pF} \).

questions.question_text: A charge of \( 7 \, \mu\text{C} \) is moved from infinity to a point where the potential is \( 100 \, \text{V} \). What is the work done?
questions.explanation: Work done = Potential energy = \( q V \). \( W = 7 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 = 7 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{J} = 0.7 \, \text{mJ} \).

questions.question_text: A point charge \( Q = 5 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{C} \) is placed at the origin. What is the potential at a point 10 m away from the charge? (Take \( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{Nm}^2 \text{C}^{-2} \)).
questions.explanation: Potential due to a point charge: \( V = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r} \). Substitute: \( V = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-9}}{10} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-9} = 4.5 \, \text{V} \).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct about the gravitational force between two masses?
options: It is zero at all distances
questions.explanation: \( F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2} \) is always attractive, as masses are positive and the force vector points toward each other, making option 1 correct.

questions.question_text: A satellite orbits a planet at \( 7 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \) from its center with a period of 18 hours. What is the planet’s mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))

Two masses \( 8 \, \text{kg} \) and \( 16 \, \text{kg} \) are \( 16 \, \text{m} \) apart. What is the gravitational potential at a point \( 7 \, \text{m} \) from the \( 8 \, \text{kg} \) mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
A planet orbits the Sun with a period of 3 years. If Earth’s orbital radius is \( 1.5 \times 10^{11} \, \text{m} \), what is its semi-major axis?
Which property of gravitational force allows us to define a potential energy?
questions.explanation: Gravitational force is a conservative force, meaning the work done is path-independent and depends only on the initial and final positions. This property allows a potential energy function to be defined, as the work done equals the negative change in potential energy.

questions.question_text: A body experiences \( g = 7.35 \, \text{m/s}^2 \) at a certain height above Earth. What is the height? (\( g_0 = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
What is the escape speed from a planet with mass \( 2.7 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 4.5 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \)? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 2.7 \times 10^{24}}{4.5 \times 10^6}} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{8.001 \times 10^7} \approx 8.94 \times 10^3 \, \text{m/s} \approx 8.9 \, \text{km/s} \).

questions.question_text: What is the kinetic energy of a \( 700 \, \text{kg} \) satellite at \( 9 R_E \) from Earth’s center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
A projectile is launched at \( 6 \, \text{km/s} \) from Earth’s surface. What is its maximum distance from the center? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
What does the inverse-square nature of gravitational force imply about its range?
questions.explanation: \( F \propto 1/r^2 \) means the force decreases with distance but never reaches zero, implying an infinite range, as it extends indefinitely, though it weakens rapidly.

questions.question_text: A satellite’s period near Earth’s surface is 88 minutes. What is its period at \( h = 4 R_E \)? (\( R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
A body is launched from Earth at \( 14.5 \, \text{km/s} \). What is its speed at infinity? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s} \))

Two masses \( 6 \, \text{kg} \) and \( 12 \, \text{kg} \) are \( 12 \, \text{m} \) apart. What is the gravitational potential at a point \( 5 \, \text{m} \) from the \( 6 \, \text{kg} \) mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
Four masses of \( 2 \, \text{kg} \) each are at the vertices of a square with side \( 4 \, \text{m} \). What is the net force on one mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Force from adjacent: \( F_1 = G \frac{m^2}{r^2} = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \frac{2 \times 2}{4^2} = 1.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N} \) (2 forces at 90°). Force from diagonal: \( F_2 = G \frac{m^2}{(4\sqrt{2})^2} = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \frac{4}{32} = 8.34 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{N} \). Resultant of two \( F_1 \): \( F_R = \sqrt{2} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-11} \approx 2.36 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N} \). Net force: \( F = \sqrt{(2.36 \times 10^{-11})^2 + (8.34 \times 10^{-12})^2} \approx 2.50 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about gravitational force?
options: It can be zero at some points
It decreases with the square of distance
questions.explanation: Gravitational force is always attractive (option 2 is correct), follows the inverse-square law (option 3 is correct), and acts between all masses (option 4 is correct). Option 1 is incorrect as it can be zero inside a shell.

questions.question_text: What is the gravitational potential due to Earth at \( 2.56 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \) from its center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))

Two masses \( 7 \, \text{kg} \) and \( 14 \, \text{kg} \) are \( 14 \, \text{m} \) apart. What is the gravitational potential at a point \( 6 \, \text{m} \) from the \( 7 \, \text{kg} \) mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
A body weighs \( 98 \, \text{N} \) on Earth’s surface. What is its weight at a height \( h = 2 R_E/3 \)? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
Four \( 3 \, \text{kg} \) masses form a square of side \( 3 \, \text{m} \). What is the potential energy of the system? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
A satellite orbits Earth at \( 13 R_E \) from the center. What is its orbital speed? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: \( v = \sqrt{\frac{g R_E^2}{r}} \). \( r = 13 R_E \), \( v = \sqrt{\frac{9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6}{13}} \). \( v = \sqrt{4.826 \times 10^6} \approx 2.20 \times 10^3 \, \text{m/s} \).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about a satellite in orbit?
options: Total energy is negative in circular orbit
Kinetic energy varies in elliptical orbit
Gravitational force keeps it in orbit
questions.explanation: otal energy is negative (option 1 correct), kinetic energy varies in elliptical orbits (option 2 correct), and gravity provides centripetal force (option 3 correct). Option 4 is incorrect as speed decreases with altitude.

questions.question_text: Why does the acceleration due to gravity decrease both above and below Earth’s surface?
options: Due to distance and mass contribution effects
questions.explanation: Above the surface, \( g \) decreases as \( g(h) \propto 1/(R_E + h)^2 \). Below the surface, only the mass inside a radius \( r < R_E \) contributes, reducing \( g \) linearly as \( g(d) = g (1 - d/R_E) \). Thus, \( g \) is maximum at the surface and decreases in both directions.

questions.question_text: A satellite orbits a planet at \( 5 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \) from its center with a period of 12 hours. What is the planet’s mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
A satellite near Earth has a period of 83 minutes. What is its period at \( h = 8 R_E \)? (\( R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))

A \( 400 \, \text{kg} \) satellite orbits Earth at \( 5 R_E \) from the center. What is its total energy? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( E = -\frac{G M_E m}{2 r} \). \( r = 5 R_E = 3.2 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \). \( E = -\frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 400}{2 \times 3.2 \times 10^7} \). \( E = -\frac{1.601 \times 10^{17}}{6.4 \times 10^7} \approx -2.5 \times 10^9 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A projectile is launched from Earth’s surface with speed \( 8 \, \text{km/s} \). How far from the center does it reach? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))

A \( 6 \, \text{kg} \) mass is moved from \( 6 R_E \) to \( 12 R_E \) from Earth’s center. What is the change in potential energy? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta V = -G M_E m \left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) \). \( r_1 = 3.84 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \), \( r_2 = 7.68 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \). \( \Delta V = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 6 \left(\frac{1}{7.68 \times 10^7} - \frac{1}{3.84 \times 10^7}\right) \). \( \Delta V = -2.401 \times 10^{15} (-1.302 \times 10^{-8}) \approx 3.13 \times 10^7 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A projectile is launched at \( 4 \, \text{km/s} \) from Earth’s surface. What is its maximum distance from the center? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))

A \( 4 \, \text{kg} \) mass is moved from \( 3 R_E \) to \( 6 R_E \) from Earth’s center. What is the change in potential energy? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta V = -G M_E m \left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) \). \( r_1 = 1.92 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \), \( r_2 = 3.84 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \). \( \Delta V = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 4 \left(\frac{1}{3.84 \times 10^7} - \frac{1}{1.92 \times 10^7}\right) \). \( \Delta V = -1.601 \times 10^{15} (-2.604 \times 10^{-8}) \approx 4.17 \times 10^7 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: What happens to the acceleration due to gravity at Earth’s center?
questions.explanation: At Earth’s center (\( r = 0 \)), the gravitational force from all surrounding mass cancels out due to symmetry, reducing \( g \) to zero, as \( g(d) = g (1 - d/R_E) \) becomes zero when \( d = R_E \).

questions.question_text: A \( 3 \, \text{kg} \) mass is moved from \( 4 R_E \) to \( 8 R_E \) from Earth’s center. What is the change in potential energy? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta V = -G M_E m \left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) \). \( r_1 = 2.56 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \), \( r_2 = 5.12 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \). \( \Delta V = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 3 \left(\frac{1}{5.12 \times 10^7} - \frac{1}{2.56 \times 10^7}\right) \). \( \Delta V = -1.201 \times 10^{15} (-1.953 \times 10^{-8}) \approx 2.34 \times 10^7 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A satellite orbits a planet at \( 2 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \) from its center with a period of 2 hours. What is the planet’s mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
What ensures that the area swept by a planet’s orbit is constant over equal time intervals?
questions.explanation: (\( L = m r v \)), which remains constant for a central force like gravity, ensuring \( \Delta A / \Delta t = L/(2m) \) is constant.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct about a satellite in circular orbit?
questions.explanation: The gravitational force provides the centripetal force (\( \frac{G M_E m}{r^2} = \frac{m v^2}{r} \)), making option 2 correct.

questions.question_text: At what depth below Earth’s surface is \( g \) reduced to \( 5.39 \, \text{m/s}^2 \)? (\( g_0 = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
Why does the Moon have no atmosphere compared to Earth?
options: It is closer to the Sun
questions.explanation: The Moon’s escape speed (2.3 km/s) is much lower than Earth’s (11.2 km/s) due to its smaller mass and radius. Gas molecules with speeds exceeding this low escape speed can easily escape the Moon’s gravitational pull.

questions.question_text: A satellite orbits Earth at \( 15 R_E \) from the center. What is its orbital speed? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: \( v = \sqrt{\frac{g R_E^2}{r}} \). \( r = 15 R_E \), \( v = \sqrt{\frac{9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6}{15}} \). \( v = \sqrt{4.181 \times 10^6} \approx 2.04 \times 10^3 \, \text{m/s} \).

questions.question_text: What happens to a satellite’s orbital speed if its altitude increases?
questions.explanation: \( v = \sqrt{\frac{G M_E}{r}} \). As altitude increases, \( r \) (distance from Earth’s center) increases, reducing \( v \) since \( v \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}} \). Thus, orbital speed decreases.

questions.question_text: What happens to the time period of a satellite if its orbital radius is doubled?
questions.explanation: \( T^2 \propto r^3 \) (Kepler’s third law for satellites). If \( r \) is doubled (\( r' = 2r \)), then \( T'^2 = (2r)^3 = 8r^3 \), so \( T' = T \sqrt{8} = T \times 2\sqrt{2} \), meaning the period increases by a factor of \( 2\sqrt{2} \).

questions.question_text: What is the gravitational potential due to Earth at a distance of \( 1.6 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \) from its center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))

A \( 1000 \, \text{kg} \) satellite orbits Earth at \( 1.5 R_E \) from the center. What is its potential energy? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
Why is the gravitational force considered a conservative force?
questions.explanation: The work done by gravity is independent of the path taken and depends only on the initial and final positions. This path independence defines a conservative force, allowing a potential energy function to be defined.

questions.question_text: A body is launched from Earth at \( 14 \, \text{km/s} \). What is its speed at infinity? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s} \))
What is the minimum speed to escape from \( 6 R_E \) from Earth’s center? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 g R_E^2}{6 R_E}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6}{6}} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{2.09 \times 10^7} \approx 4.57 \times 10^3 \, \text{m/s} \approx 4.6 \, \text{km/s} \).

questions.question_text: What does the zero gravitational potential at infinity imply about gravitational systems?
questions.explanation: \( V = 0 \) at \( r \to \infty \) as a convention, implying that all bound systems (e.g., orbits) have negative potential energy, requiring external work to unbind them to infinity.

questions.question_text: A planet orbits the Sun with a period of 9 years. If Earth’s orbital radius is \( 1.5 \times 10^{11} \, \text{m} \), what is its semi-major axis?
A planet’s orbital period around the Sun is 8 years. If Earth’s orbital radius is \( 1.5 \times 10^{11} \, \text{m} \), what is its semi-major axis?

A satellite’s orbit changes from \( 2 R_E \) to \( 4 R_E \) from Earth’s center. What is the change in its potential energy? (\( m = 200 \, \text{kg}, M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta V = -G M_E m \left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) \). \( r_1 = 2 R_E = 1.28 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \), \( r_2 = 4 R_E = 2.56 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \). \( \Delta V = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 200 \left(\frac{1}{2.56 \times 10^7} - \frac{1}{1.28 \times 10^7}\right) \). \( \Delta V = -8.004 \times 10^{16} (-3.906 \times 10^{-8}) \approx 3.13 \times 10^9 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A body weighs \( 98 \, \text{N} \) on Earth’s surface. What is its weight at a depth of \( R_E/2 \)? (\( R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( g(d) = g \left(1 - \frac{d}{R_E}\right) \). At \( d = R_E/2 \), \( g(d) = 9.8 \left(1 - \frac{R_E/2}{R_E}\right) = 9.8 \times 0.5 = 4.9 \, \text{m/s}^2 \). Mass: \( m = \frac{W}{g} = \frac{98}{9.8} = 10 \, \text{kg} \). Weight at depth: \( W = m g(d) = 10 \times 4.9 = 49 \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: A body weighs \( 196 \, \text{N} \) on Earth’s surface. What is its weight at a depth \( d = R_E/4 \)? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2 \))
What is the escape speed from a planet with mass \( 1.2 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 3 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \)? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.2 \times 10^{24}}{3 \times 10^6}} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{5.336 \times 10^7} \approx 7.3 \times 10^3 \, \text{m/s} = 7.3 \, \text{km/s} \).

questions.question_text: What is the gravitational force on a \( 10 \, \text{kg} \) mass outside a spherical shell of mass \( 500 \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 2 \, \text{m} \), at \( 3 \, \text{m} \) from the center? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Outside a shell, \( F = \frac{G M m}{r^2} \). \( F = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 500 \times 10}{3^2} \). \( F = \frac{3.335 \times 10^{-7}}{9} \approx 3.71 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: What is the minimum speed to escape from \( 4 R_E \) from Earth’s center? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 g R_E^2}{4 R_E}} = \sqrt{\frac{9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6}{2}} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{3.136 \times 10^7} \approx 5.6 \times 10^3 \, \text{m/s} = 5.6 \, \text{km/s} \).

questions.question_text: A satellite near Earth has a period of 81 minutes. What is its period at \( h = 10 R_E \)? (\( R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
What is the minimum speed to escape from \( 9 R_E \) from Earth’s center? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 g R_E^2}{9 R_E}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6}{9}} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{1.395 \times 10^7} \approx 3.73 \times 10^3 \, \text{m/s} \approx 3.7 \, \text{km/s} \).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct about Kepler’s first law?
options: The Sun is at the center of circular orbits
Orbits are elliptical with varying speeds
Orbits are circular with the Sun at the center
questions.explanation: Kepler’s first law (law of orbits) describes planetary orbits as ellipses with the Sun at one focus, not circles, contradicting option 4.

questions.question_text: What is the gravitational force on a \( 11 \, \text{kg} \) mass \( 9 \, \text{m} \) from the center of a spherical shell of mass \( 500 \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 7 \, \text{m} \)? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( F = \frac{G M m}{r^2} \). \( F = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 500 \times 11}{9^2} \). \( F = \frac{3.6685 \times 10^{-8}}{81} \approx 4.53 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: Why is the gravitational potential energy of a system of multiple masses the sum of pairwise interactions?
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential energy follows the superposition principle, where the total energy is the sum of the potential energies of all possible pairs (\( V = -\frac{G m_1 m_2}{r} \)) due to the linear nature of gravitational force.

questions.question_text: What is the kinetic energy of a \( 400 \, \text{kg} \) satellite at \( 6 R_E \) from Earth’s center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( K = \frac{G M_E m}{2 r} \). \( r = 6 R_E = 3.84 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \). \( K = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 400}{2 \times 3.84 \times 10^7} \). \( K = \frac{1.601 \times 10^{17}}{7.68 \times 10^7} \approx 2.08 \times 10^9 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A satellite’s period is 100 minutes at \( h = 0 \). What is its period at \( h = 2 R_E \)? (\( R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))

Two masses \( 9 \, \text{kg} \) and \( 18 \, \text{kg} \) are \( 18 \, \text{m} \) apart. What is the gravitational potential at a point \( 8 \, \text{m} \) from the \( 9 \, \text{kg} \) mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))

What is the gravitational force on a \( 9 \, \text{kg} \) mass \( 7 \, \text{m} \) from the center of a spherical shell of mass \( 350 \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 5 \, \text{m} \)? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( F = \frac{G M m}{r^2} \). \( F = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 350 \times 9}{7^2} \). \( F = \frac{2.101 \times 10^{-8}}{49} \approx 4.29 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: What is the kinetic energy of a \( 600 \, \text{kg} \) satellite at \( 8 R_E \) from Earth’s center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
At what depth below Earth’s surface is \( g \) reduced to \( 7.35 \, \text{m/s}^2 \)? (\( g_0 = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
A satellite orbits Earth at \( 9 R_E \) from the center. What is its orbital speed? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: \( v = \sqrt{\frac{g R_E^2}{r}} \). \( r = 9 R_E \), \( v = \sqrt{\frac{9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6}{9}} \). \( v = \sqrt{6.964 \times 10^6} \approx 2.64 \times 10^3 \, \text{m/s} \).

questions.question_text: Two masses \( 11 \, \text{kg} \) and \( 22 \, \text{kg} \) are \( 22 \, \text{m} \) apart. What is the gravitational potential at a point \( 10 \, \text{m} \) from the \( 11 \, \text{kg} \) mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
A satellite near Earth has a period of 87 minutes. What is its period at \( h = 6 R_E \)? (\( R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))

What is the gravitational potential due to Earth at \( 3.2 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \) from its center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
Why does the gravitational force act as if all mass is at the center for a uniform sphere?
options: Mass is concentrated at the center
questions.explanation: For a uniform sphere, symmetry ensures that the net gravitational force on an external point is equivalent to that of a point mass at the center, as forces from all parts combine accordingly.

questions.question_text: A body weighs \( 343 \, \text{N} \) on Earth’s surface. What is its weight at a height \( h = R_E/5 \)? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2 \))
A projectile is launched at \( 3 \, \text{km/s} \) from Earth’s surface. What is its maximum distance from the center? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
Which of the following statements is correct about gravitational potential energy?
options: It becomes more negative as objects approach
It is zero at Earth’s surface
questions.explanation: \( V = -\frac{G M m}{r} \), which is negative for bound systems and decreases (becomes more negative) as \( r \) decreases, making option 3 correct.

questions.question_text: Three \( 6 \, \text{kg} \) masses form an equilateral triangle of side \( 8 \, \text{m} \). What is the potential energy of the system? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
What determines whether an object can escape Earth’s gravitational influence?
questions.explanation: An object escapes if its total mechanical energy (\( E = KE + PE \)) is zero or positive. This occurs when its initial speed equals or exceeds the escape speed (\( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}} \)), making energy the key factor.

questions.question_text: Three masses of \( 10 \, \text{kg} \) each form an equilateral triangle with side \( 7 \, \text{m} \). What is the net force on one mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Force between two masses: \( F = G \frac{m^2}{r^2} = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \frac{10 \times 10}{7^2} = 1.36 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{N} \). Two forces at 60°: \( F_R = \sqrt{F^2 + F^2 + 2 F^2 \cos 60^\circ} \). \( F_R = \sqrt{(1.36 \times 10^{-10})^2 (1 + 1 + 1)} = 1.36 \times 10^{-10} \sqrt{3} \). \( F_R \approx 2.36 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: Minimum speed to escape from \( 2 R_E \) from Earth’s center is? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
questions.explanation: \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 g R_E^2}{2 R_E}} = \sqrt{g R_E} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6} = \sqrt{6.272 \times 10^7} \). \( v_e \approx 7.92 \times 10^3 \, \text{m/s} \approx 7.9 \, \text{km/s} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the Moon’s orbital period relate to Earth’s mass?
questions.explanation: Kepler’s third law (\( T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{G M_E} r^3 \)) to satellites like the Moon, where the period \( T \) depends on Earth’s mass \( M_E \), the central body, determining the gravitational force strength.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about gravitational potential energy?
options: It is negative for bound systems
It is zero at infinite separation
It is positive when objects are close
It depends on the inverse of distance
questions.explanation: \( V = -\frac{G M m}{r} \), which is negative (option 1 correct), zero at infinity (option 2 correct), and decreases as \( r \) decreases (option 4 correct). Option 3 is incorrect as it is not positive when bound.

questions.question_text: Two masses \( 2 \, \text{kg} \) and \( 8 \, \text{kg} \) are separated by \( 4 \, \text{m} \). What is the gravitational potential at the midpoint? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Distance to midpoint: \( r = 2 \, \text{m} \). \( U = -\frac{G m_1}{r} - \frac{G m_2}{r} \). \( U = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \left(\frac{2}{2} + \frac{8}{2}\right) \). \( U = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times (1 + 4) = -3.335 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{J/kg} \).

questions.question_text: At what depth below Earth’s surface is \( g \) reduced to \( 8.33 \, \text{m/s}^2 \)? (\( g_0 = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
What is the escape speed from a planet with mass \( 3 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \)? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 3 \times 10^{24}}{4 \times 10^6}} \). \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{4.002 \times 10^{14}}{4 \times 10^6}} = \sqrt{1.001 \times 10^8} \). \( v_e \approx 1.0 \times 10^4 \, \text{m/s} = 10 \, \text{km/s} \).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about Kepler’s second law?
options: Area swept is constant over time
questions.explanation: Kepler’s second law (equal areas in equal times) implies varying speed (faster at perihelion, slower at aphelion) due to angular momentum conservation. Option 2 is incorrect as speed is not constant.

questions.question_text: A projectile is launched at \( 7 \, \text{km/s} \) from Earth’s surface. What is its maximum distance from the center? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
Why does Newton’s law of gravitation apply universally to all objects?
questions.explanation: Newton’s law (\( F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2} \)) is universal because it depends only on mass and distance, properties common to all objects, and \( G \) is a universal constant, applicable everywhere.

questions.question_text: What is the gravitational force on a \( 8 \, \text{kg} \) mass \( 5 \, \text{m} \) from the center of a spherical shell of mass \( 400 \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 3 \, \text{m} \)? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( F = \frac{G M m}{r^2} \). \( F = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 400 \times 8}{5^2} \). \( F = \frac{2.135 \times 10^{-8}}{25} \approx 8.54 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 9 \, \text{kg} \) mass is moved from \( 9 R_E \) to \( 18 R_E \) from Earth’s center. What is the change in potential energy? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta V = -G M_E m \left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) \). \( r_1 = 5.76 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \), \( r_2 = 1.152 \times 10^8 \, \text{m} \). \( \Delta V = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 9 \left(\frac{1}{1.152 \times 10^8} - \frac{1}{5.76 \times 10^7}\right) \). \( \Delta V = -3.602 \times 10^{15} (-8.681 \times 10^{-9}) \approx 3.13 \times 10^7 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A projectile is launched at \( 2 \, \text{km/s} \) from Earth’s surface. What is its maximum distance from the center? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
Why does the gravitational force on a body inside Earth decrease linearly with depth?
questions.explanation: Inside a uniform Earth, only the mass within radius \( r < R_E \) contributes to gravity, and this mass decreases with \( r^3 \), while the force depends on \( 1/r^2 \). The net effect is a linear decrease: \( g(d) = g (1 - d/R_E) \).

questions.question_text: A satellite orbits a planet at \( 6 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \) from its center with a period of 15 hours. What is the planet’s mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
What does the constant \( k \) in Kepler’s third law (\( T^2 = k r^3 \)) depend on for satellites?
questions.explanation: \( T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{G M_E} r^3 \) for satellites, where \( k = \frac{4\pi^2}{G M_E} \). Thus, \( k \) depends on the mass of the central body (Earth) and universal constants, not the satellite’s mass.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct about escape speed?
options: It depends on the object’s mass
questions.explanation: \( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}} \) decreases with altitude as \( R + h \) increases, making option 4 correct.

questions.question_text: A body weighs \( 392 \, \text{N} \) on Earth’s surface. What is its weight at a height \( h = R_E/6 \)? (\( g = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2 \))

How much energy is required to move a \( 400 \, \text{kg} \) satellite from \( 8 R_E \) to \( 16 R_E \) from Earth’s center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta E = -G M_E m \left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) \). \( r_1 = 5.12 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \), \( r_2 = 1.024 \times 10^8 \, \text{m} \). \( \Delta E = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 400 \left(\frac{1}{1.024 \times 10^8} - \frac{1}{5.12 \times 10^7}\right) \). \( \Delta E = -1.601 \times 10^{17} (-9.766 \times 10^{-9}) \approx 1.56 \times 10^9 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: At what depth below Earth’s surface is \( g \) reduced to \( 6.86 \, \text{m/s}^2 \)? (\( g_0 = 9.8 \, \text{m/s}^2, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m} \))
Three \( 5 \, \text{kg} \) masses form an equilateral triangle of side \( 4 \, \text{m} \). What is the potential energy of the system? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))

How much energy is required to move a \( 200 \, \text{kg} \) satellite from \( 6 R_E \) to \( 12 R_E \) from Earth’s center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta E = -G M_E m \left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) \). \( r_1 = 3.84 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \), \( r_2 = 7.68 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \). \( \Delta E = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 200 \left(\frac{1}{7.68 \times 10^7} - \frac{1}{3.84 \times 10^7}\right) \). \( \Delta E = -8.004 \times 10^{16} (-1.302 \times 10^{-8}) \approx 1.04 \times 10^9 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: Three masses of \( 6 \, \text{kg} \) each form an equilateral triangle with side \( 5 \, \text{m} \). What is the net force on one mass? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Force between two masses: \( F = G \frac{m^2}{r^2} = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \frac{6 \times 6}{5^2} = 9.61 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N} \). Two forces at 60°: \( F_R = \sqrt{F^2 + F^2 + 2 F^2 \cos 60^\circ} \). \( F_R = \sqrt{(9.61 \times 10^{-11})^2 (1 + 1 + 1)} = 9.61 \times 10^{-11} \sqrt{3} \). \( F_R \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: What is the gravitational potential due to Earth at \( 4.48 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \) from its center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))

What is the gravitational force on a \( 5 \, \text{kg} \) mass \( 4 \, \text{m} \) from the center of a spherical shell of mass \( 200 \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 3 \, \text{m} \)? (\( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: Outside shell: \( F = \frac{G M m}{r^2} \). \( F = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 200 \times 5}{4^2} \). \( F = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-9}}{16} \approx 4.17 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: Why does an object need a minimum speed to escape Earth’s gravity?
options: To balance kinetic and potential energy
questions.explanation: Escape speed (\( v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}} \)) is the minimum speed where kinetic energy equals the gravitational potential energy’s magnitude, ensuring total energy is zero, allowing escape to infinity.

questions.question_text: A body is launched from Earth at \( 11.8 \, \text{km/s} \). What is its speed at infinity? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s} \))
What is the gravitational force on a \( 2 \, \text{kg} \) mass inside a hollow spherical shell of mass \( 1000 \, \text{kg} \) and radius \( 1 \, \text{m} \)?
questions.explanation: Inside a hollow spherical shell, the gravitational force is zero due to symmetry (as per the shell theorem). \( F = 0 \, \text{N} \).

questions.question_text: A \( 800 \, \text{kg} \) satellite orbits Earth at \( 12 R_E \) from the center. What is its total energy? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))

How much energy is required to move a \( 500 \, \text{kg} \) satellite from \( 9 R_E \) to \( 18 R_E \) from Earth’s center? (\( M_E = 6 \times 10^{24} \, \text{kg}, R_E = 6.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{m}, G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2 \))
questions.explanation: \( \Delta E = -G M_E m \left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) \). \( r_1 = 5.76 \times 10^7 \, \text{m} \), \( r_2 = 1.152 \times 10^8 \, \text{m} \). \( \Delta E = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 500 \left(\frac{1}{1.152 \times 10^8} - \frac{1}{5.76 \times 10^7}\right) \). \( \Delta E = -2.001 \times 10^{17} (-8.681 \times 10^{-9}) \approx 1.74 \times 10^9 \, \text{J} \).

questions.question_text: A body is launched from Earth at \( 13.5 \, \text{km/s} \). What is its speed at infinity? (Escape speed = \( 11.2 \, \text{km/s} \))
Why does the gravitational force provide the necessary centripetal force for a circular orbit?
options: It balances the required inward force
It depends on satellite mass only
questions.explanation: In a circular orbit, the gravitational force (\( \frac{G M_E m}{r^2} \)) equals the centripetal force (\( \frac{m v^2}{r} \)), providing the inward force needed to maintain circular motion.
