questions.question_text: Why does a plane mirror not produce magnification greater than unity?
options: Because image size equals object size
Because it forms a real image
questions.explanation: A plane mirror reflects light such that the image distance equals the object distance, and the image is formed by direct reflection without convergence or divergence. This results in an image of the same size as the object, with a magnification of 1, as there’s no mechanism to alter the apparent size.

questions.question_text: A prism of angle \( 45^\circ \) has a refractive index of \( 1.5 \). What is the angle of minimum deviation?
A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 160 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 8 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
questions.explanation: Magnifying power: \( m = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \). \( f_o = 160 \, \text{cm} \), \( f_e = 8 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{160}{8} = 20 \).

questions.question_text: An object is at a depth of \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) in water (\( n = 1.5 \)). What is the apparent depth?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = \( \frac{\text{real depth}}{n} \). Real depth = \( 15 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.5 \). Apparent depth = \( \frac{15}{1.5} = 10 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 2.5 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 20 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?
questions.explanation: Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{20}{2.5} = 8 \). Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{5} = 5 \). Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 8 \times 5 = 40 \).

questions.question_text: A glass slab (\( n = 1.5 \)) of thickness \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) is placed over a point. What is the apparent shift?
questions.explanation: Shift = \( t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{n} \right) \). \( t = 6 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.5 \). Shift = \( 6 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1.5} \right) = 6 \left( 1 - \frac{2}{3} \right) = 6 \times \frac{1}{3} = 2 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: An object is placed \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 8 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -8 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -20 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-20} = \frac{1}{-8} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-8} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{-5 + 2}{40} = \frac{-3}{40} \). \( v = -\frac{40}{3} \approx -13.33 \, \text{cm} \) (real image).

questions.question_text: A convex lens of focal length \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) forms a real image at \( 60 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 20 \, \text{cm} \). Image distance: \( v = 60 \, \text{cm} \) (real image). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{60} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{20} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{60} - \frac{1}{20} = \frac{1 - 3}{60} = \frac{-2}{60} = \frac{-1}{30} \). \( u = -30 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A concave mirror has a focal length of \( 12 \, \text{cm} \). An object is placed \( 18 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -12 \, \text{cm} \) (concave mirror). Object distance: \( u = -18 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-18} = \frac{1}{-12} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-12} + \frac{1}{18} = \frac{-3 + 2}{36} = \frac{-1}{36} \). \( v = -36 \, \text{cm} \) (real image).

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from air to crown glass (\( n = 1.52 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 60^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Air (\( n_1 = 1 \)), glass (\( n_2 = 1.52 \)), \( i = 60^\circ \). \( 1 \times \sin 60^\circ = 1.52 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 60^\circ = 0.866 \Rightarrow 0.866 = 1.52 \sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \frac{0.866}{1.52} \approx 0.57 \). \( r = \sin^{-1}(0.57) \approx 34.8^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A convex lens of focal length \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 24 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 12 \, \text{cm} \). Image distance: \( v = 24 \, \text{cm} \) (real image). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{24} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{12} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{24} - \frac{1}{12} = \frac{1 - 2}{24} = \frac{-1}{24} \). \( u = -24 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A lens has a power of \( -5 \, \text{D} \). What is its focal length?
questions.explanation: Power: \( P = \frac{1}{f} \) (in meters). \( P = -5 \, \text{D} \Rightarrow -5 = \frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow f = -\frac{1}{5} = -0.2 \, \text{m} = -20 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A glass slab (\( n = 1.5 \)) of thickness \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) is placed over a mark. What is the apparent shift?
questions.explanation: Shift = \( t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{n} \right) \). \( t = 12 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.5 \). Shift = \( 12 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1.5} \right) = 12 \left( 1 - \frac{2}{3} \right) = 12 \times \frac{1}{3} = 4 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A concave mirror of focal length \( 9 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 18 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -9 \, \text{cm} \) (concave mirror). Object distance: \( u = -18 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-18} = \frac{1}{-9} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-9} + \frac{1}{18} = \frac{-2 + 1}{18} = \frac{-1}{18} \). \( v = -18 \, \text{cm} \) (real image).

questions.question_text: A prism of refracting angle \( 40^\circ \) has a minimum deviation of \( 24^\circ \). What is the refractive index?
questions.explanation: Refractive index: \( n = \frac{\sin \left( \frac{A + D_m}{2} \right)}{\sin \left( \frac{A}{2} \right)} \). \( A = 40^\circ \), \( D_m = 24^\circ \). \( n = \frac{\sin \left( \frac{40 + 24}{2} \right)}{\sin \left( \frac{40}{2} \right)} = \frac{\sin 32^\circ}{\sin 20^\circ} \). \( \sin 32^\circ \approx 0.530 \), \( \sin 20^\circ \approx 0.342 \). \( n = \frac{0.530}{0.342} \approx 1.55 \).

questions.question_text: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 2 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 4 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 16 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?
questions.explanation: Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{16}{2} = 8 \). Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{4} = 6.25 \). Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 8 \times 6.25 = 50 \).

questions.question_text: A convex lens of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 15 \, \text{cm} \). Image distance: \( v = 30 \, \text{cm} \) (real image). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{30} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{15} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{30} - \frac{1}{15} = \frac{1 - 2}{30} = \frac{-1}{30} \). \( u = -30 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A glass slab (\( n = 1.62 \)) of thickness \( 8.1 \, \text{cm} \) is placed over a dot. What is the apparent shift?
questions.explanation: Shift = \( t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{n} \right) \). \( t = 8.1 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.62 \). Shift = \( 8.1 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1.62} \right) = 8.1 \left( 1 - 0.617 \right) = 8.1 \times 0.383 \approx 3.1 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 100 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
questions.explanation: Magnifying power: \( m = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \). \( f_o = 100 \, \text{cm} \), \( f_e = 5 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{100}{5} = 20 \).

questions.question_text: In a reflecting telescope, why is a concave mirror preferred over a convex lens as the objective?
questions.explanation: A concave mirror avoids chromatic aberration (color distortion) that occurs in lenses due to different wavelengths refracting differently. Mirrors reflect all wavelengths uniformly, providing clearer images, and are easier to support mechanically for large apertures, enhancing light-gathering power.

questions.question_text: A converging beam meets a concave lens (\( f = 10 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 4 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?
questions.explanation: Object distance: \( u = -4 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual object), \( f = -10 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-4} = \frac{1}{-10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{-10} \). \( \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-10} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{-2 - 5}{20} = \frac{-7}{20} \). \( v = -\frac{20}{7} \approx -2.86 \, \text{cm} \) (2.86 cm to the left).

questions.question_text: A convex mirror of radius of curvature \( 36 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 27 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = \frac{R}{2} = \frac{36}{2} = 18 \, \text{cm} \) (convex mirror). Object distance: \( u = -27 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-27} = \frac{1}{18} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{18} + \frac{1}{27} = \frac{3 + 2}{54} = \frac{5}{54} \). \( v = \frac{54}{5} = 10.8 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image).

questions.question_text: A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.6 \) has radii of curvature \( 25 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -25 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 1.2 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 18 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?
questions.explanation: Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{18}{1.2} = 15 \). Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{6} \approx 4.17 \). Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 15 \times 4.17 \approx 62.55 \approx 63 \).

questions.question_text: What happens to the power of a convex lens when its surrounding medium’s refractive index increases?
options: Increases due to shorter focal length
Decreases due to increased focal length
questions.explanation: The power of a convex lens (P = 1/f) decreases as the surrounding medium’s refractive index increases. This is because the focal length increases due to a reduced difference in refractive indices between the lens and the medium, lowering the lens’s ability to converge light.

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from air (\( n = 1 \)) to dense flint glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 45^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Air (\( n_1 = 1 \)), glass (\( n_2 = 1.62 \)), \( i = 45^\circ \). \( 1 \times \sin 45^\circ = 1.62 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 45^\circ = 0.707 \Rightarrow 0.707 = 1.62 \sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \frac{0.707}{1.62} \approx 0.436 \). \( r = \sin^{-1}(0.436) \approx 25.8^\circ \).

questions.question_text: What is the critical angle for a water (\( n = 1.33 \)) to air interface?
questions.explanation: Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \). Water (\( n_1 = 1.33 \)), air (\( n_2 = 1 \)). \( \sin i_c = \frac{1}{1.33} \approx 0.752 \). \( i_c = \sin^{-1}(0.752) \approx 48.75^\circ \).

questions.question_text: In a prism, what causes the emergent ray to deviate from the incident ray’s path?
options: Absorption of light within the prism
questions.explanation: The deviation in a prism occurs because light refracts at both the entry and exit faces, bending toward the normal when entering (denser medium) and away from the normal when exiting (rarer medium). The prism’s geometry and refractive index determine the total deviation angle.

questions.question_text: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 2 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 18 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?
questions.explanation: Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{18}{2} = 9 \). Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{5} = 5 \). Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 9 \times 5 = 45 \).

questions.question_text: A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 4 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at infinity. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Magnification at infinity: \( m = \frac{D}{f} \). \( D = 25 \, \text{cm} \), \( f = 4 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{25}{4} = 6.25 \).

questions.question_text: A coin lies at the bottom of a water tank (\( n = 1.33 \)) with a depth of \( 13.3 \, \text{cm} \). What is its apparent depth?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = \( \frac{\text{real depth}}{n} \). Real depth = \( 13.3 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.33 \). Apparent depth = \( \frac{13.3}{1.33} = 10 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: In a compound microscope, what limits the maximum magnification achievable with a single lens?
questions.explanation: The maximum magnification of a single lens (simple microscope) is limited by its focal length. A shorter focal length increases magnification (m = 1 + D/f), but practical constraints like lens aberrations and the minimum focal length achievable restrict it to around 9-10x, necessitating a compound system.

questions.question_text: A concave lens of focal length \( 18 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 36 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -18 \, \text{cm} \) (concave lens). Object distance: \( u = -36 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-36} = \frac{1}{-18} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{36} = \frac{1}{-18} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-18} - \frac{1}{36} = \frac{-2 - 1}{36} = \frac{-3}{36} = \frac{-1}{12} \). \( v = -12 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image).

questions.question_text: A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 25 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Magnification: \( m = 1 + \frac{D}{f} \). \( D = 25 \, \text{cm} \), \( f = 6 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = 1 + \frac{25}{6} \approx 1 + 4.167 = 5.167 \approx 5.17 \).

questions.question_text: A prism of refracting angle \( 60^\circ \) in air has a refractive index of \( 1.6 \). What is its angle of minimum deviation?
questions.explanation: \( n = \frac{\sin \left( \frac{A + D_m}{2} \right)}{\sin \left( \frac{A}{2} \right)} \). \( A = 60^\circ \), \( n = 1.6 \). \( 1.6 = \frac{\sin \left( \frac{60 + D_m}{2} \right)}{\sin 30^\circ} \Rightarrow 1.6 \times 0.5 = \sin \left( \frac{60 + D_m}{2} \right) \). \( 0.8 = \sin \left( \frac{60 + D_m}{2} \right) \Rightarrow \frac{60 + D_m}{2} = \sin^{-1}(0.8) \approx 53.13^\circ \). \( 60 + D_m = 106.26^\circ \Rightarrow D_m = 106.26 - 60 \approx 46.26^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 1.5 \, \text{cm} \) and tube length \( 18 \, \text{cm} \). If the eyepiece focal length is \( 6 \, \text{cm} \), what is the total magnification at infinity?
questions.explanation: Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{18}{1.5} = 12 \). Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{6} \approx 4.17 \). Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 12 \times 4.17 \approx 50 \).

questions.question_text: A telescope has an objective focal length of \( 150 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece focal length of \( 5 \, \text{cm} \). What is the length of the telescope tube?
questions.explanation: Tube length = \( f_o + f_e \). \( f_o = 150 \, \text{cm} \), \( f_e = 5 \, \text{cm} \). Tube length = \( 150 + 5 = 155 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A converging beam meets a convex lens (\( f = 12 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?
questions.explanation: Object distance: \( u = -6 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual object), \( f = 12 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-6} = \frac{1}{12} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12} \). \( \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{12} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1 - 2}{12} = \frac{-1}{12} \). \( v = -12 \, \text{cm} \) (12 cm to the left).

questions.question_text: A prism of angle \( 30^\circ \) has a minimum deviation of \( 20^\circ \). What is the refractive index?
questions.explanation: Refractive index: \( n = \frac{\sin \left( \frac{A + D_m}{2} \right)}{\sin \left( \frac{A}{2} \right)} \). \( A = 30^\circ \), \( D_m = 20^\circ \). \( n = \frac{\sin \left( \frac{30 + 20}{2} \right)}{\sin \left( \frac{30}{2} \right)} = \frac{\sin 25^\circ}{\sin 15^\circ} \). \( \sin 25^\circ \approx 0.423 \), \( \sin 15^\circ \approx 0.259 \). \( n = \frac{0.423}{0.259} \approx 1.63 \).

questions.question_text: Why does a convex lens fail to form a sharp image when used with white light unless corrected?
questions.explanation: A convex lens exhibits chromatic aberration with white light because different wavelengths refract by varying amounts due to the lens’s material having a wavelength-dependent refractive index. This causes colored fringes as focal points differ for each color, blurring the image.

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) to water (\( n = 1.33 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 50^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Glass (\( n_1 = 1.62 \)), water (\( n_2 = 1.33 \)), \( i = 50^\circ \). \( 1.62 \times \sin 50^\circ = 1.33 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 50^\circ \approx 0.766 \Rightarrow 1.62 \times 0.766 \approx 1.241 \Rightarrow 1.33 \sin r = 1.241 \). \( \sin r = \frac{1.241}{1.33} \approx 0.933 \Rightarrow r = \sin^{-1}(0.933) \approx 68.9^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from air (\( n = 1 \)) to water (\( n = 1.33 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 50^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Air (\( n_1 = 1 \)), water (\( n_2 = 1.33 \)), \( i = 50^\circ \). \( 1 \times \sin 50^\circ = 1.33 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 50^\circ \approx 0.766 \Rightarrow 0.766 = 1.33 \sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \frac{0.766}{1.33} \approx 0.576 \). \( r = \sin^{-1}(0.576) \approx 35.1^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 25 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification?
A convex lens (\( f = 50 \, \text{cm} \)) and a concave lens (\( f = 25 \, \text{cm} \)) are in contact. What is the effective focal length?
An object is placed \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 6 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -6 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -12 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-12} = \frac{1}{-6} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-6} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{-2 + 1}{12} = \frac{-1}{12} \). \( v = -12 \, \text{cm} \) (real image).

questions.question_text: Why does a convex lens submerged in a liquid with the same refractive index as the lens not form an image?
options: Due to no refraction at the interfaces
questions.explanation: When a convex lens is in a medium with the same refractive index, there is no difference in refractive indices between the lens and the medium. Without this difference, light does not bend at the interfaces, and the lens acts like a flat plate, failing to converge or diverge rays to form an image.

questions.question_text: A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.55 \) has radii of curvature \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -30 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 1.5 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 20 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?
questions.explanation: Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{20}{1.5} \approx 13.33 \). Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{5} = 5 \). Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 13.33 \times 5 \approx 66.65 \approx 67 \).

questions.question_text: A convex lens of power \( +4 \, \text{D} \) is used. What is its focal length?
questions.explanation: Power: \( P = \frac{1}{f} \) (in meters). \( P = +4 \, \text{D} \Rightarrow 4 = \frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow f = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25 \, \text{m} = 25 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.5 \) has radii of curvature \( 40 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -40 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?
In a convex lens submerged in a medium of higher refractive index, what happens to its ability to focus light?
options: It behaves as a diverging lens
questions.explanation: When a convex lens is in a medium with a higher refractive index than the lens material, the refractive index difference reverses (medium > lens), causing the lens to diverge light instead of converging it. This occurs because the rays bend away from the normal at the interfaces.

questions.question_text: An object of height \( 2 \, \text{cm} \) is placed \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \). What is the height of the image?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -5 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -10 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-10} = \frac{1}{-5} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-5} + \frac{1}{10} = \frac{-2 + 1}{10} = \frac{-1}{10} \). \( v = -10 \, \text{cm} \). Magnification: \( m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-10}{-10} = -1 \). Image height: \( h' = m \times h = -1 \times 2 = -2 \, \text{cm} \) (inverted). Magnitude = \( 2 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: An object is placed \( 14 \, \text{cm} \) from a convex mirror of focal length \( 28 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 28 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -14 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-14} = \frac{1}{28} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{28} + \frac{1}{14} = \frac{1 + 2}{28} = \frac{3}{28} \). \( v = \frac{28}{3} \approx 9.33 \, \text{cm} \). Magnification: \( m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{9.33}{-14} \approx 0.666 \).

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from air (\( n = 1 \)) to water (\( n = 1.33 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 35^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Air (\( n_1 = 1 \)), water (\( n_2 = 1.33 \)), \( i = 35^\circ \). \( 1 \times \sin 35^\circ = 1.33 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 35^\circ \approx 0.574 \Rightarrow 0.574 = 1.33 \sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \frac{0.574}{1.33} \approx 0.432 \). \( r = \sin^{-1}(0.432) \approx 25.6^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A concave lens has a focal length of \( 20 \, \text{cm} \). Where should an object be placed to get an image half the size of the object?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -20 \, \text{cm} \) (negative for concave lens). Magnification: \( m = \frac{h'}{h} = 0.5 \) (virtual, diminished). \( m = \frac{v}{u} \Rightarrow 0.5 = \frac{v}{u} \Rightarrow v = 0.5u \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{0.5u} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-20} \Rightarrow \frac{2}{u} - \frac{1}{u} = -\frac{1}{20} \). \( \frac{1}{u} = -\frac{1}{20} \Rightarrow u = -20 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: What optical property of a prism allows it to be used in binoculars to invert images?
questions.explanation: Prisms in binoculars use total internal reflection to invert and revert images. By reflecting light multiple times within the prism (e.g., in a Porro prism), the image orientation is corrected from the inverted form produced by the objective lens, maintaining the same size.

questions.question_text: A lens has a power of \( -3 \, \text{D} \). What is its focal length?
questions.explanation: Power: \( P = \frac{1}{f} \) (in meters). \( P = -3 \, \text{D} \Rightarrow -3 = \frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow f = -\frac{1}{3} \approx -0.333 \, \text{m} \approx -33.3 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: What is the critical angle for a diamond-air interface if the refractive index of diamond is \( 2.42 \)?
questions.explanation: Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \). Diamond (\( n_1 = 2.42 \)), air (\( n_2 = 1 \)). \( \sin i_c = \frac{1}{2.42} \approx 0.413 \). \( i_c = \sin^{-1}(0.413) \approx 24.4^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A simple microscope uses a convex lens of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification when the image is at \( 25 \, \text{cm} \)?
An object is at a depth of \( 24 \, \text{cm} \) in a medium with refractive index \( 1.6 \). What is the apparent depth?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = \( \frac{\text{real depth}}{n} \). Real depth = \( 24 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.6 \). Apparent depth = \( \frac{24}{1.6} = 15 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A convex mirror of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image of an object placed \( 45 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the magnification of the image?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 15 \, \text{cm} \) (positive for convex mirror). Object distance: \( u = -45 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-45} = \frac{1}{15} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{45} = \frac{3 + 1}{45} = \frac{4}{45} \). \( v = \frac{45}{4} = 11.25 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image). Magnification: \( m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{11.25}{-45} = 0.25 \).

questions.question_text: An object is placed \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) in front of a concave mirror of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \). Where is the image formed?
What happens to light rays when they strike a convex mirror at an angle parallel to its principal axis?
options: They converge at the focal point
They reflect back along the same path
They appear to diverge from the focal point behind the mirror
They pass through the center of curvature
questions.explanation: In a convex mirror, rays parallel to the principal axis diverge after reflection. When traced backward, these diverging rays appear to originate from the focal point behind the mirror, which is why the focal point is virtual and located on the opposite side of the incident light.

questions.question_text: A concave lens of focal length \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 24 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -12 \, \text{cm} \) (concave lens). Object distance: \( u = -24 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-24} = \frac{1}{-12} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{24} = \frac{1}{-12} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-12} - \frac{1}{24} = \frac{-2 - 1}{24} = \frac{-3}{24} = \frac{-1}{8} \). \( v = -8 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image).

questions.question_text: A glass slab (\( n = 1.5 \)) of thickness \( 9 \, \text{cm} \) is placed over a mark. What is the apparent shift?
questions.explanation: Shift = \( t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{n} \right) \). \( t = 9 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.5 \). Shift = \( 9 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1.5} \right) = 9 \left( 1 - \frac{2}{3} \right) = 9 \times \frac{1}{3} = 3 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A convex mirror of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) behind the mirror. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 10 \, \text{cm} \) (convex mirror). Image distance: \( v = 5 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{5} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{1 - 2}{10} = \frac{-1}{10} \). \( u = -10 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A convex lens (\( f = 25 \, \text{cm} \)) and a concave lens (\( f = 50 \, \text{cm} \)) are in contact. What is the effective focal length?
A concave mirror of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) from the mirror. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -10 \, \text{cm} \) (concave mirror). Image distance: \( v = -20 \, \text{cm} \) (real image, same side as object). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{-20} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-10} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{-2 + 1}{20} = \frac{-1}{20} \). \( u = -20 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: An object is placed \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) from a convex mirror of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 15 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -10 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-10} = \frac{1}{15} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{10} = \frac{2 + 3}{30} = \frac{5}{30} = \frac{1}{6} \). \( v = 6 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image).

questions.question_text: A ray of light is incident from air (\( n = 1 \)) into glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) at \( 30^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Air (\( n_1 = 1 \)), glass (\( n_2 = 1.5 \)), \( i = 30^\circ \). \( 1 \times \sin 30^\circ = 1.5 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 30^\circ = 0.5 \Rightarrow 0.5 = 1.5 \sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \frac{0.5}{1.5} = 0.333 \). \( r = \sin^{-1}(0.333) \approx 19.5^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A glass slab (\( n = 1.52 \)) of thickness \( 7.6 \, \text{cm} \) is placed over a dot. What is the apparent shift?
questions.explanation: Shift = \( t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{n} \right) \). \( t = 7.6 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.52 \). Shift = \( 7.6 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1.52} \right) = 7.6 \left( 1 - 0.658 \right) = 7.6 \times 0.342 \approx 2.6 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A glass slab (\( n = 1.5 \)) of thickness \( 7.5 \, \text{cm} \) is placed over a point. What is the apparent shift?
questions.explanation: Shift = \( t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{n} \right) \). \( t = 7.5 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.5 \). Shift = \( 7.5 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1.5} \right) = 7.5 \left( 1 - \frac{2}{3} \right) = 7.5 \times \frac{1}{3} = 2.5 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A fish is at a depth of \( 40 \, \text{cm} \) in water (\( n = 1.33 \)). What is its apparent depth when viewed from above?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = \( \frac{\text{real depth}}{n} \). Real depth = \( 40 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.33 \). Apparent depth = \( \frac{40}{1.33} \approx 30.08 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: An object is placed \( 24 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 12 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -12 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -24 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-24} = \frac{1}{-12} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-12} + \frac{1}{24} = \frac{-2 + 1}{24} = \frac{-1}{24} \). \( v = -24 \, \text{cm} \) (real image).

questions.question_text: A concave mirror of focal length \( 8 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 16 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -8 \, \text{cm} \) (concave mirror). Object distance: \( u = -16 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-16} = \frac{1}{-8} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-8} + \frac{1}{16} = \frac{-2 + 1}{16} = \frac{-1}{16} \). \( v = -16 \, \text{cm} \) (real image).

questions.question_text: A glass slab (\( n = 1.5 \)) of thickness \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) is placed over a pin. By how much does the pin appear raised?
questions.explanation: Shift = \( t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{n} \right) \). \( t = 15 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.5 \). Shift = \( 15 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1.5} \right) = 15 \left( 1 - \frac{2}{3} \right) = 15 \times \frac{1}{3} = 5 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A lens has a power of \( -4 \, \text{D} \). What is its focal length?
questions.explanation: Power: \( P = \frac{1}{f} \) (in meters). \( P = -4 \, \text{D} \Rightarrow -4 = \frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow f = -\frac{1}{4} = -0.25 \, \text{m} = -25 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A convex lens of focal length \( 25 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image of an object placed \( 50 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 25 \, \text{cm} \). Object distance: \( u = -50 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-50} = \frac{1}{25} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{50} = \frac{1}{25} \). \( \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{25} - \frac{1}{50} = \frac{2 - 1}{50} = \frac{1}{50} \). \( v = 50 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: In a concave mirror, what prevents the formation of an image when the object is placed at the focal point?
options: Convergence of rays at the pole
Parallel reflected rays forming image at infinity
Divergence of rays behind the mirror
Absorption of light by the mirror
questions.explanation: When the object is at the focal point of a concave mirror, the reflected rays become parallel and do not converge to a point. This results in the image being formed at infinity, meaning no distinct image forms at a finite distance.

questions.question_text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 180 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 6 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
questions.explanation: Magnifying power: \( m = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \). \( f_o = 180 \, \text{cm} \), \( f_e = 6 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{180}{6} = 30 \).

questions.question_text: Why does a prism disperse white light into a spectrum of colors?
options: Due to equal refraction of all wavelengths
Due to different refractive indices for different wavelengths
Due to reflection at the prism surfaces
questions.explanation: A prism disperses white light because different wavelengths (colors) of light have different refractive indices in the prism material. Shorter wavelengths (e.g., violet) refract more than longer wavelengths (e.g., red), causing the light to split into a spectrum as it exits the prism.

questions.question_text: A convex mirror of focal length \( 18 \, \text{cm} \) produces an image \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) behind the mirror. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 18 \, \text{cm} \) (convex mirror). Image distance: \( v = 6 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{18} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{18} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1 - 3}{18} = \frac{-2}{18} = \frac{-1}{9} \). \( u = -9 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: What characteristic of a convex mirror makes it suitable for use as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
options: Provides a wide field of view with a diminished image
Produces an inverted image for better clarity
Converges light to a single point
questions.explanation: A convex mirror always produces a virtual, erect, and diminished image, regardless of the object’s position. This provides a wide field of view, allowing drivers to see a larger area behind the vehicle, making it ideal for rear-view mirrors despite the reduced image size.

questions.question_text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 120 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 4 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
questions.explanation: Magnifying power: \( m = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \). \( f_o = 120 \, \text{cm} \), \( f_e = 4 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{120}{4} = 30 \).

questions.question_text: An object is at a depth of \( 16 \, \text{cm} \) in water (\( n = 1.33 \)). What is the apparent depth?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = \( \frac{\text{real depth}}{n} \). Real depth = \( 16 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.33 \). Apparent depth = \( \frac{16}{1.33} \approx 12.03 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: What is the primary reason optical fibers are bent without losing light transmission efficiency?
options: Due to sustained total internal reflection
questions.explanation: Optical fibers maintain light transmission when bent because the angle of incidence at the core-cladding interface remains greater than the critical angle, ensuring total internal reflection. This allows light to follow the bend without escaping into the cladding.

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) to air at an angle of incidence of \( 40^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Glass (\( n_1 = 1.5 \)), air (\( n_2 = 1 \)), \( i = 40^\circ \). \( 1.5 \times \sin 40^\circ = 1 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 40^\circ \approx 0.643 \Rightarrow 1.5 \times 0.643 \approx 0.964 \Rightarrow \sin r = 0.964 \). \( r = \sin^{-1}(0.964) \approx 74.6^\circ \). Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{1}{1.5} \approx 0.667 \), \( \sin 40^\circ < 0.667 \), so refraction occurs.

questions.question_text: In a convex lens, why does the image transition from virtual to real as the object moves from inside to outside the focal point?
options: Due to change from divergence to convergence
Due to reflection within the lens
questions.explanation: Inside the focal point, a convex lens diverges rays, forming a virtual image on the same side. Beyond the focal point, the lens converges rays to a point on the opposite side, forming a real image. This transition occurs as the object crosses the focal point, changing the ray behavior.

questions.question_text: In a prism, what condition results in the minimum deviation of light?
options: Angle of incidence equals angle of emergence
Angle of incidence equals the prism angle
questions.explanation: In a prism, minimum deviation occurs when the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence. This symmetry ensures the refracted ray inside the prism is parallel to the base, minimizing the deviation angle.

questions.question_text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 200 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
questions.explanation: Magnifying power: \( m = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \). \( f_o = 200 \, \text{cm} \), \( f_e = 10 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{200}{10} = 20 \).

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) to air at an angle of incidence equal to the critical angle. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{1}{1.62} \approx 0.617 \). \( i_c = \sin^{-1}(0.617) \approx 38.1^\circ \). At critical angle, angle of refraction = \( 90^\circ \).

questions.question_text: Why does a reflecting telescope often use a secondary mirror in its design?
options: To redirect light to the eyepiece
questions.explanation: In a reflecting telescope (e.g., Cassegrain design), a secondary mirror redirects the light focused by the primary concave mirror through a hole in the primary mirror to the eyepiece. This allows a compact design with a long focal length, improving magnification and convenience of observation.

questions.question_text: A concave lens of focal length \( 25 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 50 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -25 \, \text{cm} \) (concave lens). Object distance: \( u = -50 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-50} = \frac{1}{-25} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{50} = \frac{1}{-25} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-25} - \frac{1}{50} = \frac{-2 - 1}{50} = \frac{-3}{50} \). \( v = -\frac{50}{3} \approx -16.67 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image).

questions.question_text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 100 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
questions.explanation: Magnifying power: \( m = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \). \( f_o = 100 \, \text{cm} \), \( f_e = 5 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{100}{5} = 20 \).

questions.question_text: A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.5 \) has radii of curvature \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -15 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?
In a convex mirror, what is the significance of the focal point being behind the mirror?
options: It indicates the mirror’s converging power
It shows where real images form
It is the point where diverging rays appear to originate
It marks the center of curvature
questions.explanation: The focal point of a convex mirror is virtual and behind the mirror because reflected rays diverge and appear to originate from this point when traced backward. This indicates the mirror’s diverging nature, ensuring all images are virtual, erect, and diminished.

questions.question_text: What is the key optical principle behind the working of a periscope?
questions.explanation: A periscope uses total internal reflection in prisms (or plane mirror reflection) to redirect light. Prisms reflect light internally at angles greater than the critical angle, allowing the viewer to see objects from a different height or direction without direct line-of-sight.

questions.question_text: A lens has a power of \( +4 \, \text{D} \). What is its focal length in centimeters?
questions.explanation: Power: \( P = \frac{1}{f} \) (in meters). \( P = +4 \, \text{D} \Rightarrow 4 = \frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow f = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25 \, \text{m} = 25 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A converging beam of light meets a concave lens of focal length \( 25 \, \text{cm} \) at \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new convergence distance from the lens?

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 1 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 15 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?
questions.explanation: Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{15}{1} = 15 \). Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{5} = 5 \). Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 15 \times 5 = 75 \).

questions.question_text: A prism of angle \( 60^\circ \) and refractive index \( 1.5 \) produces a minimum deviation of \( 30^\circ \). What is the angle of incidence?
questions.explanation: At minimum deviation: \( i = \frac{A + D_m}{2} \). \( A = 60^\circ \), \( D_m = 30^\circ \). \( i = \frac{60 + 30}{2} = \frac{90}{2} = 45^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A concave mirror of focal length \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -6 \, \text{cm} \) (concave mirror). Object distance: \( u = -12 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-12} = \frac{1}{-6} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-6} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{-2 + 1}{12} = \frac{-1}{12} \). \( v = -12 \, \text{cm} \) (real image).

questions.question_text: What is the critical angle for a glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) to water (\( n = 1.33 \)) interface?
questions.explanation: Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \). Glass (\( n_1 = 1.5 \)), water (\( n_2 = 1.33 \)). \( \sin i_c = \frac{1.33}{1.5} \approx 0.887 \). \( i_c = \sin^{-1}(0.887) \approx 62.5^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A concave lens of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -15 \, \text{cm} \) (concave lens). Object distance: \( u = -30 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-30} = \frac{1}{-15} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{-15} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-15} - \frac{1}{30} = \frac{-2 - 1}{30} = \frac{-3}{30} = \frac{-1}{10} \). \( v = -10 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image).

questions.question_text: A convex lens (\( f = 30 \, \text{cm} \)) and a concave lens (\( f = 60 \, \text{cm} \)) are in contact. What is the effective focal length?
A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 8 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at infinity. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Magnification at infinity: \( m = \frac{D}{f} \). \( D = 25 \, \text{cm} \), \( f = 8 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{25}{8} = 3.125 \).

questions.question_text: A converging beam meets a concave lens (\( f = 20 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 8 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?
questions.explanation: Object distance: \( u = -8 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual object), \( f = -20 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-8} = \frac{1}{-20} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{-20} \). \( \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-20} - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{-2 - 5}{40} = \frac{-7}{40} \). \( v = -\frac{40}{7} \approx -5.71 \, \text{cm} \) (5.71 cm to the left).

questions.question_text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 140 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 7 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
questions.explanation: Magnifying power: \( m = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \). \( f_o = 140 \, \text{cm} \), \( f_e = 7 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{140}{7} = 20 \).

questions.question_text: What is the primary optical phenomenon responsible for the mirage effect observed on hot roads?
questions.explanation: The mirage effect on hot roads results from total internal reflection. Hot air near the ground has a lower refractive index than cooler air above, causing light from the sky to bend upward when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, creating an illusion of water.

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from air (\( n = 1 \)) to glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 40^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Air (\( n_1 = 1 \)), glass (\( n_2 = 1.5 \)), \( i = 40^\circ \). \( 1 \times \sin 40^\circ = 1.5 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 40^\circ \approx 0.643 \Rightarrow 0.643 = 1.5 \sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \frac{0.643}{1.5} \approx 0.429 \). \( r = \sin^{-1}(0.429) \approx 25.4^\circ \).

questions.question_text: What is the significance of the critical angle in the context of total internal reflection?
options: It determines the focal length of a lens
It indicates the maximum angle of refraction
It defines the minimum angle for dispersion
It is the threshold for total internal reflection
questions.explanation: The critical angle is the angle of incidence above which total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a rarer medium. At this angle, the refracted ray grazes the boundary (angle of refraction = 90°), and beyond it, all light is reflected back, enabling applications like optical fibers.

questions.question_text: What is the critical angle for a diamond (\( n = 2.42 \)) to glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) interface?
questions.explanation: Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \). Diamond (\( n_1 = 2.42 \)), glass (\( n_2 = 1.5 \)). \( \sin i_c = \frac{1.5}{2.42} \approx 0.620 \). \( i_c = \sin^{-1}(0.620) \approx 38.4^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from glass (\( n = 1.52 \)) to air at an angle of incidence of \( 45^\circ \). What happens?
questions.explanation: Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{1}{1.52} \approx 0.658 \Rightarrow i_c \approx 41.1^\circ \). Since \( i = 45^\circ > i_c \), total internal reflection occurs.

questions.question_text: A prism of angle \( 60^\circ \) has a refractive index of \( 1.4 \). What is the angle of minimum deviation?
In a concave mirror, under what condition is the image formed virtual and magnified?
options: Object beyond the center of curvature
Object between focal point and pole
Object at the center of curvature
questions.explanation: For a concave mirror, a virtual and magnified image is formed when the object is placed between the focal point (F) and the pole (P). Here, the reflected rays diverge, and their backward extensions converge behind the mirror, producing a virtual, erect, and magnified image.

questions.question_text: In a refracting telescope, why does the objective lens have a larger aperture than the eyepiece?
options: To gather more light for brightness
questions.explanation: The objective lens in a refracting telescope has a larger aperture to collect more light from distant objects, enhancing brightness and resolution. The eyepiece, with a smaller aperture, magnifies this image, requiring less light-gathering capacity for viewing.

questions.question_text: A convex lens (\( f = 30 \, \text{cm} \)) and a concave lens (\( f = 15 \, \text{cm} \)) are in contact. What is the effective focal length?
In a plane mirror, why does the image distance equal the object distance?
options: Due to light converging behind the mirror
Due to equal angles of incidence and reflection
questions.explanation: In a plane mirror, light reflects such that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. This symmetry ensures that the perpendicular distance from the object to the mirror equals the apparent distance of the image behind it, as the image forms along the normal extended backward.

questions.question_text: A prism of angle \( 40^\circ \) and refractive index \( 1.5 \) produces what minimum deviation?
An object at a depth of \( 19.95 \, \text{cm} \) in water (\( n = 1.33 \)) is viewed normally. What is the apparent depth?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = \( \frac{\text{real depth}}{n} \). Real depth = \( 19.95 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.33 \). Apparent depth = \( \frac{19.95}{1.33} \approx 15 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: In a plane mirror, what property ensures that the image is not distorted?
questions.explanation: The flat surface of a plane mirror ensures that all incident rays reflect with equal angles of incidence and reflection, maintaining the object’s proportions and shape. Curved surfaces would distort the image by altering ray directions unevenly.

questions.question_text: What is the primary advantage of using a combination of lenses in optical instruments like microscopes?
options: Reduces the weight of the instrument
Eliminates the need for a light source
questions.explanation: A combination of lenses allows for greater magnification and improved image quality. The objective lens forms an initial image, which the eyepiece magnifies further, while multiple lenses can correct aberrations (e.g., chromatic, spherical), enhancing sharpness and clarity.

questions.question_text: A lens has a power of \( +2.5 \, \text{D} \). What is its focal length in centimeters?
questions.explanation: Power: \( P = \frac{1}{f} \) (in meters). \( P = +2.5 \, \text{D} \Rightarrow 2.5 = \frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow f = \frac{1}{2.5} = 0.4 \, \text{m} = 40 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: Why does a convex lens produce chromatic aberration when used with white light?
questions.explanation: Chromatic aberration occurs in a convex lens because different wavelengths of white light refract by different amounts due to the lens material’s varying refractive index for each wavelength. Shorter wavelengths (e.g., blue) focus closer than longer ones (e.g., red), causing color fringing.

questions.question_text: Why does a concave mirror used in a reflecting telescope require precise curvature?
options: To ensure rays converge to a single point
questions.explanation: The precise curvature of a concave mirror ensures that all parallel rays from a distant object converge accurately to a single focal point. Any deviation in curvature causes spherical aberration, blurring the image and reducing the telescope’s resolving power.

questions.question_text: A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 25 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification?
An object is at a depth of \( 13.3 \, \text{cm} \) in a medium with refractive index \( 1.33 \). What is the apparent depth?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = \( \frac{\text{real depth}}{n} \). Real depth = \( 13.3 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.33 \). Apparent depth = \( \frac{13.3}{1.33} = 10 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A concave mirror of radius of curvature \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) from the mirror. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = \frac{R}{2} = \frac{-20}{2} = -10 \, \text{cm} \) (concave mirror). Image distance: \( v = -20 \, \text{cm} \) (real image). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{-20} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-10} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{-2 + 1}{20} = \frac{-1}{20} \). \( u = -20 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from water (\( n = 1.33 \)) to air at an angle of incidence of \( 50^\circ \). What happens?
questions.explanation: Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{1}{1.33} \approx 0.752 \Rightarrow i_c \approx 48.75^\circ \). Since \( i = 50^\circ > i_c \), total internal reflection occurs.

questions.question_text: An object of height \( 3 \, \text{cm} \) is placed \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \). What is the height of the image?
questions.explanation: \( f = -15 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -20 \, \text{cm} \). \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-20} = \frac{1}{-15} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-15} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{-4 + 3}{60} = \frac{-1}{60} \). \( v = -60 \, \text{cm} \). Magnification: \( m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-60}{-20} = -3 \). Image height: \( h' = m \times h = -3 \times 3 = -9 \, \text{cm} \) (inverted). Magnitude = \( 9 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: An object is placed \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) from a convex mirror of focal length \( 18 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 18 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -12 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-12} = \frac{1}{18} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{18} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{2 + 3}{36} = \frac{5}{36} \). \( v = \frac{36}{5} = 7.2 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image).

questions.question_text: A prism of angle \( 50^\circ \) and refractive index \( 1.4 \) produces what minimum deviation?

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 1 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 4 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 14 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?
questions.explanation: Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{14}{1} = 14 \). Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{4} = 6.25 \). Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 14 \times 6.25 = 87.5 \).

questions.question_text: A light ray passes from water (\( n = 1.33 \)) to glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 30^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). \( 1.33 \sin 30^\circ = 1.5 \sin r \). \( \sin 30^\circ = 0.5 \Rightarrow 1.33 \times 0.5 = 1.5 \sin r \Rightarrow 0.665 = 1.5 \sin r \). \( \sin r = \frac{0.665}{1.5} \approx 0.443 \Rightarrow r = \sin^{-1}(0.443) \approx 26.3^\circ \).

questions.question_text: What is the critical angle for a dense flint glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) to air interface?
questions.explanation: Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \). Glass (\( n_1 = 1.62 \)), air (\( n_2 = 1 \)). \( \sin i_c = \frac{1}{1.62} \approx 0.617 \). \( i_c = \sin^{-1}(0.617) \approx 38.1^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A concave lens of focal length \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 8 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -20 \, \text{cm} \) (concave lens). Image distance: \( v = -8 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{-8} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-20} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-8} - \frac{1}{-20} = \frac{-5 + 2}{40} = \frac{-3}{40} \). \( u = -\frac{40}{3} \approx -13.33 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A convex lens of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 10 \, \text{cm} \). Image distance: \( v = 20 \, \text{cm} \) (real image). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{10} = \frac{1 - 2}{20} = \frac{-1}{20} \). \( u = -20 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of \( 40 \, \text{cm} \). An object of height \( 2 \, \text{cm} \) is placed \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) in front of it. What is the height of the image formed?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = \frac{R}{2} = \frac{-40}{2} = -20 \, \text{cm} \) (negative for concave mirror). Object distance: \( u = -30 \, \text{cm} \). Using mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-30} = \frac{1}{-20} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-20} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{-3 + 2}{60} = \frac{-1}{60} \). \( v = -60 \, \text{cm} \) (real image). Magnification: \( m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-60}{-30} = -2 \). Image height: \( h' = m \times h = -2 \times 2 = -4 \, \text{cm} \) (inverted, so negative). Magnitude of height = \( 4 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: An object is at a depth of \( 26.6 \, \text{cm} \) in a medium with refractive index \( 1.33 \). What is the apparent depth?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = \( \frac{\text{real depth}}{n} \). Real depth = \( 26.6 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.33 \). Apparent depth = \( \frac{26.6}{1.33} = 20 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A converging beam meets a convex lens (\( f = 10 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?
questions.explanation: Object distance: \( u = -5 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual object), \( f = 10 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-5} = \frac{1}{10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{5} = \frac{1}{10} \). \( \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{1 - 2}{10} = \frac{-1}{10} \). \( v = -10 \, \text{cm} \) (10 cm to the left).

questions.question_text: In a prism, when light is incident at a very small angle, what is the approximate relationship between deviation and the prism’s properties?
questions.explanation: For a thin prism with a small angle of incidence, the deviation is approximately equal to the product of the prism’s refractive index minus one and the prism angle (D ≈ (n - 1)A). This simplification holds because the angles of refraction are small, minimizing higher-order effects.

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from air (\( n = 1 \)) to glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 30^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Air (\( n_1 = 1 \)), glass (\( n_2 = 1.62 \)), \( i = 30^\circ \). \( 1 \times \sin 30^\circ = 1.62 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 30^\circ = 0.5 \Rightarrow 0.5 = 1.62 \sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \frac{0.5}{1.62} \approx 0.309 \). \( r = \sin^{-1}(0.309) \approx 18^\circ \).

questions.question_text: An object of height \( 3 \, \text{cm} \) is placed \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \). What is the height of the image?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -10 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -15 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-15} = \frac{1}{-10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-10} + \frac{1}{15} = \frac{-3 + 2}{30} = \frac{-1}{30} \). \( v = -30 \, \text{cm} \). Magnification: \( m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-30}{-15} = -2 \). Image height: \( h' = m \times h = -2 \times 3 = -6 \, \text{cm} \) (inverted). Magnitude = \( 6 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A convex lens (\( f = 40 \, \text{cm} \)) and a concave lens (\( f = 20 \, \text{cm} \)) are in contact. What is the effective focal length?
An object is placed \( 16 \, \text{cm} \) from a convex mirror of focal length \( 24 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 24 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -16 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-16} = \frac{1}{24} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{24} + \frac{1}{16} = \frac{2 + 3}{48} = \frac{5}{48} \). \( v = \frac{48}{5} = 9.6 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image).

questions.question_text: In a concave mirror, when the object is placed at the center of curvature, where is the image formed?
options: Between focal point and center of curvature
questions.explanation: For a concave mirror, when the object is at the center of curvature (C), the reflected rays converge back to the same point after reflection. This results in a real, inverted image formed at the center of curvature, with the same size as the object.

questions.question_text: In a compound microscope, what role does the eyepiece play in the final image formation?
options: Inverts the image to make it erect
questions.explanation: The eyepiece in a compound microscope acts as a magnifying lens, taking the real, inverted image formed by the objective and producing a larger, virtual image for the observer. It enhances the angular size of the intermediate image, making it appear magnified without altering its orientation.

questions.question_text: In a concave lens, what property of the lens determines the position of the virtual focal point?
questions.explanation: The virtual focal point of a concave lens is where diverging rays appear to originate when traced backward. This position is determined by the lens’s focal length, which depends on its curvature and refractive index, defining the extent of divergence.

questions.question_text: A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.55 \) has radii of curvature \( 22 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -22 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?
In a convex lens, what happens to the image if the object is placed between the focal point and twice the focal length?
questions.explanation: For a convex lens, when the object is between the focal point (F) and twice the focal length (2F), the image is real, inverted, and magnified. It forms beyond 2F on the opposite side, as the rays converge after refraction.

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) to water (\( n = 1.33 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 30^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Glass (\( n_1 = 1.5 \)), water (\( n_2 = 1.33 \)), \( i = 30^\circ \). \( 1.5 \times \sin 30^\circ = 1.33 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 30^\circ = 0.5 \Rightarrow 1.5 \times 0.5 = 1.33 \sin r \Rightarrow 0.75 = 1.33 \sin r \). \( \sin r = \frac{0.75}{1.33} \approx 0.564 \Rightarrow r = \sin^{-1}(0.564) \approx 34.3^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A convex lens of focal length \( 18 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 36 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 18 \, \text{cm} \). Object distance: \( u = -36 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-36} = \frac{1}{18} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{36} = \frac{1}{18} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{18} - \frac{1}{36} = \frac{2 - 1}{36} = \frac{1}{36} \). \( v = 36 \, \text{cm} \) (real image).

questions.question_text: A prism of angle \( 50^\circ \) and refractive index \( 1.5 \) produces what minimum deviation?
A prism of angle \( 50^\circ \) has a minimum deviation of \( 30^\circ \). What is the refractive index?
questions.explanation: Refractive index: \( n = \frac{\sin \left( \frac{A + D_m}{2} \right)}{\sin \left( \frac{A}{2} \right)} \). \( A = 50^\circ \), \( D_m = 30^\circ \). \( n = \frac{\sin \left( \frac{50 + 30}{2} \right)}{\sin \left( \frac{50}{2} \right)} = \frac{\sin 40^\circ}{\sin 25^\circ} \). \( \sin 40^\circ \approx 0.643 \), \( \sin 25^\circ \approx 0.423 \). \( n = \frac{0.643}{0.423} \approx 1.52 \).

questions.question_text: An object is placed \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) from a convex mirror of radius of curvature \( 30 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
Why does the image in a reflecting telescope remain free of chromatic aberration?
options: Due to uniform reflection of all wavelengths
questions.explanation: A reflecting telescope uses mirrors instead of lenses as the objective. Mirrors reflect all wavelengths of light uniformly, avoiding the wavelength-dependent refraction that causes chromatic aberration in lenses, resulting in a clearer, color-corrected image.

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from air (\( n = 1 \)) to water (\( n = 1.33 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 60^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Air (\( n_1 = 1 \)), water (\( n_2 = 1.33 \)), \( i = 60^\circ \). \( 1 \times \sin 60^\circ = 1.33 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 60^\circ = 0.866 \Rightarrow 0.866 = 1.33 \sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \frac{0.866}{1.33} \approx 0.651 \). \( r = \sin^{-1}(0.651) \approx 40.6^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A glass slab (\( n = 1.6 \)) of thickness \( 8 \, \text{cm} \) is placed over a point. What is the apparent shift?
questions.explanation: Shift = \( t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{n} \right) \). \( t = 8 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.6 \). Shift = \( 8 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1.6} \right) = 8 \left( 1 - 0.625 \right) = 8 \times 0.375 = 3 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A convex mirror of focal length \( 16 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 8 \, \text{cm} \) behind the mirror. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = 16 \, \text{cm} \) (convex mirror). Image distance: \( v = 8 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{16} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{16} - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1 - 2}{16} = \frac{-1}{16} \). \( u = -16 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: When light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds a certain value, what phenomenon occurs?
options: Refraction with bending away from normal
questions.explanation: When light travels from a denser to a rarer medium (e.g., glass to air) and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, total internal reflection occurs. This is because the refracted ray would otherwise require a sine value greater than 1, which is physically impossible.

questions.question_text: A ray of light passes from water (\( n = 1.33 \)) to glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 45^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell’s law: \( n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \). Water (\( n_1 = 1.33 \)), glass (\( n_2 = 1.62 \)), \( i = 45^\circ \). \( 1.33 \times \sin 45^\circ = 1.62 \times \sin r \). \( \sin 45^\circ = 0.707 \Rightarrow 1.33 \times 0.707 = 1.62 \sin r \Rightarrow 0.941 = 1.62 \sin r \). \( \sin r = \frac{0.941}{1.62} \approx 0.581 \Rightarrow r = \sin^{-1}(0.581) \approx 35.5^\circ \).

questions.question_text: What happens to the image formed by a convex mirror if the object is moved closer to the mirror from a distant position?
options: Image size increases but remains diminished
questions.explanation: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, and diminished image. As the object moves closer, the image size increases slightly but remains diminished (less than the object size), and the image distance increases, approaching the focal length as a limit, though it never exceeds it.

questions.question_text: In a compound microscope, why is the final image inverted with respect to the object?
options: Due to the eyepiece forming an erect image
Due to the objective forming an inverted real image
Due to light dispersion in the lenses
Due to the object being placed at infinity
questions.explanation: In a compound microscope, the objective lens forms a real, inverted image of the object. The eyepiece then acts as a magnifying lens, forming a virtual image of this inverted intermediate image. Since the eyepiece does not reinvert the image, the final image remains inverted relative to the original object.

questions.question_text: A convex lens (\( f = 60 \, \text{cm} \)) and a concave lens (\( f = 30 \, \text{cm} \)) are in contact. What is the effective focal length?
An object is placed \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) from a convex mirror of focal length \( 20 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification?
In a concave lens, why is the image always formed on the same side as the object?
options: Because the lens is thicker at the edges
Because rays diverge and appear to come from the same side
questions.explanation: A concave lens diverges light rays, making them appear to originate from a point on the same side as the object when traced backward. This results in a virtual image that cannot be projected on a screen, always forming on the object’s side regardless of its position.

questions.question_text: A concave lens of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -10 \, \text{cm} \) (concave lens). Image distance: \( v = -5 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual image). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \). \( \frac{1}{-5} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-5} - \frac{1}{-10} = \frac{-2 + 1}{10} = \frac{-1}{10} \). \( u = -10 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: In a convex lens, if an object is placed at the focal point, where is the image formed?
options: At the focal point on the other side
Between the lens and focal point
questions.explanation: For a convex lens, when the object is at the focal point (F), the rays after refraction become parallel and do not converge to a point on the other side. The image is formed at infinity, as the rays appear to diverge from an infinitely distant point when traced backward.

questions.question_text: Why does the apparent depth of an object in a denser medium appear less than its real depth when viewed from air?
options: Due to refraction bending rays away from the normal
Due to reflection at the surface
questions.explanation: When light travels from a denser medium (e.g., water) to a rarer medium (air), it bends away from the normal. This refraction makes the rays appear to diverge from a point closer to the surface than the actual object, reducing the apparent depth compared to the real depth.

questions.question_text: What is the primary reason optical fibers can transmit light over long distances with minimal loss?
options: High absorption of light by the core
Total internal reflection within the core
questions.explanation: Optical fibers use total internal reflection to transmit light. The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, ensuring that light rays striking the boundary at angles greater than the critical angle are fully reflected, preventing loss of light intensity over distance.

questions.question_text: A converging beam meets a concave lens (\( f = 15 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?
questions.explanation: Object distance: \( u = -6 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual object), \( f = -15 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-6} = \frac{1}{-15} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{-15} \). \( \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-15} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{-2 - 5}{30} = \frac{-7}{30} \). \( v = -\frac{30}{7} \approx -4.29 \, \text{cm} \) (4.29 cm to the left).

questions.question_text: An object of height \( 4 \, \text{cm} \) is placed \( 16 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 8 \, \text{cm} \). What is the height of the image?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -8 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -16 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-16} = \frac{1}{-8} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-8} + \frac{1}{16} = \frac{-2 + 1}{16} = \frac{-1}{16} \). \( v = -16 \, \text{cm} \). Magnification: \( m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-16}{-16} = -1 \). Image height: \( h' = m \times h = -1 \times 4 = -4 \, \text{cm} \) (inverted). Magnitude = \( 4 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: Why does the image in a refracting telescope appear inverted without additional optics?
options: Due to dispersion in the eyepiece
Due to reflection in the objective
Due to the real, inverted image formed by the objective
Due to the eyepiece forming an erect image
questions.explanation: In a refracting telescope, the objective lens forms a real, inverted image of the distant object at its focal plane. The eyepiece magnifies this inverted image without reinverting it, so the final image remains inverted unless an additional lens or prism system is used.

questions.question_text: A glass slab (\( n = 1.6 \)) of thickness \( 9.6 \, \text{cm} \) is placed over a mark. What is the apparent shift?
questions.explanation: Shift = \( t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{n} \right) \). \( t = 9.6 \, \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.6 \). Shift = \( 9.6 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1.6} \right) = 9.6 \left( 1 - 0.625 \right) = 9.6 \times 0.375 = 3.6 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.55 \) has both radii of curvature equal to \( 25 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?
What is the key factor that determines whether light undergoes total internal reflection at an interface?
options: Angle of incidence relative to the critical angle
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle. The critical angle depends on the refractive indices of the two media, making the angle of incidence the decisive factor for the phenomenon.

questions.question_text: An object of height \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) is placed \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \). What is the height of the image?
questions.explanation: Focal length: \( f = -15 \, \text{cm} \), \( u = -30 \, \text{cm} \). Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-30} = \frac{1}{-15} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-15} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{-2 + 1}{30} = \frac{-1}{30} \). \( v = -30 \, \text{cm} \). Magnification: \( m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-30}{-30} = -1 \). Image height: \( h' = m \times h = -1 \times 5 = -5 \, \text{cm} \) (inverted). Magnitude = \( 5 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: A converging beam meets a concave lens (\( f = 20 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?
questions.explanation: Object distance: \( u = -5 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual object), \( f = -20 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-5} = \frac{1}{-20} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{5} = \frac{1}{-20} \). \( \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-20} - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{-1 - 4}{20} = \frac{-5}{20} = \frac{-1}{4} \). \( v = -4 \, \text{cm} \) (4 cm to the left).

questions.question_text: Why does a convex mirror never produce a real image regardless of the object’s position?
options: Because it has a negative focal length
Because the object is always beyond the focal point
Because it reflects light towards the object
questions.explanation: A convex mirror reflects light such that the rays diverge after reflection. These diverging rays appear to originate from a point behind the mirror, forming a virtual image. Since the rays do not actually converge, a real image (which requires convergence) cannot be formed.

questions.question_text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 120 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 6 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
questions.explanation: Magnifying power: \( m = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \). \( f_o = 120 \, \text{cm} \), \( f_e = 6 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{120}{6} = 20 \).

questions.question_text: A converging beam meets a convex lens (\( f = 20 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 8 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?
questions.explanation: Object distance: \( u = -8 \, \text{cm} \) (virtual object). Focal length: \( f = 20 \, \text{cm} \). Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-8} = \frac{1}{20} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{20} \). \( \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{2 - 5}{40} = \frac{-3}{40} \). \( v = -\frac{40}{3} \approx -13.33 \, \text{cm} \) (13.33 cm to the left).

questions.question_text: A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.5 \) has radii of curvature \( 18 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -18 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?
What is the critical angle for a crown glass (\( n = 1.52 \)) to air interface?
questions.explanation: Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \). Crown glass (\( n_1 = 1.52 \)), air (\( n_2 = 1 \)). \( \sin i_c = \frac{1}{1.52} \approx 0.658 \). \( i_c = \sin^{-1}(0.658) \approx 41.1^\circ \).

questions.question_text: A double convex lens has radii of curvature \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -30 \, \text{cm} \) with refractive index \( 1.6 \). What is its focal length?
Why is the image formed by a plane mirror always virtual?
options: Due to light converging in front of the mirror
Due to apparent divergence from behind the mirror
questions.explanation: In a plane mirror, the reflected rays do not actually converge but appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror when traced backward. This apparent origin of rays behind the mirror results in a virtual image that cannot be projected onto a screen.

questions.question_text: A simple microscope uses a lens of focal length \( 8 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification when the image is at infinity?
questions.explanation: Magnification at infinity: \( m = \frac{D}{f} \). \( D = 25 \, \text{cm} \), \( f = 8 \, \text{cm} \). \( m = \frac{25}{8} = 3.125 \).

questions.question_text: In optical fibers, what ensures that light remains confined within the core during transmission?
options: Higher refractive index of core than cladding
Lower refractive index of core than cladding
questions.explanation: In optical fibers, the core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, enabling total internal reflection. When light strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, it reflects back into the core, ensuring confinement and minimal loss.

questions.question_text: A lens has a power of \( +3 \, \text{D} \). What is its focal length in centimeters?
questions.explanation: Power: \( P = \frac{1}{f} \) (in meters). \( P = +3 \, \text{D} \Rightarrow 3 = \frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow f = \frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333 \, \text{m} \approx 33.3 \, \text{cm} \).

questions.question_text: An object is placed \( 18 \, \text{cm} \) from a convex mirror of focal length \( 12 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
